item.title: Physically inspired geometry-to-photometry rendering and lightweight convolutional neural network for real-time weld defect detection
item.description:
The problem

The weld seam on a lithium-ion battery top cover decides how well the cell is sealed, and defects in it can lead to electrolyte leakage or thermal runaway. Inspecting it automatically is hard for three reasons, according to the authors. The height difference between a defect and the sound weld is only sub-millimetre, and on a reflective, weakly textured metal surface it produces no stable brightness contrast, so an ordinary 2D camera image carries almost no usable defect signal. A 3D scanner does record the deviation, but point-cloud networks are too slow and heavy for a production line. And when the depth map is fed directly to a 2D convolutional network, the network sees a scalar grey-level field in which tiny defects are easily overlooked.

The paper therefore keeps the 3D measurement but changes how it is shown to the detector. A deterministic, physically interpretable rendering turns the depth map into a colour image in which small geometric changes become strong photometric contrast, and a lightweight 2D detector then works on that image. No multi-sensor fusion or point-cloud processing is needed at inference.

How it works

The framework has two stages (Fig. 1 of the paper): depth-normal guided illumination rendering, and detection with a network the authors call YOLO-WaveletTiny (YOLO-WT).

  1. Depth acquisition. A 3D line-laser profile scanner (OPT-LPC61) scans the weld and produces a single-view depth map. No multi-view registration or fusion is used anywhere in the experiments.
  2. Depth-to-RGB mapping. Instead of a fixed colour map, the lookup table is built from the statistics of each depth map. The histogram bin width comes from the Freedman–Diaconis rule, h = 2·IQR / ∛N. The cumulative distribution of the histogram is scaled to the index range 0–255, and a segmented RGB gradient turns each index into a colour. This pseudo-colour image carries the global depth hierarchy of the weld.
  3. Surface normals. For each pixel, two diagonal vectors to its neighbours are formed and their cross product, normalised, gives the surface normal. On a sound weld the normals are consistent; at pits and bumps they change abruptly.
  4. Phong shading. The normals drive a Phong model: ambient, diffuse (N·L) and specular ((R·V)ⁿ) terms are summed into an intensity I, and the rendered image is I times the pseudo-colour image. Because the result depends on the dot products of the normals, small normal perturbations from micro-defects cause large intensity changes. The rendering runs in C++ with OpenCV; its parameters (Table 3 of the paper) are empirical, for example ambient weight 0.1, diffuse 0.5, specular 0.3 and highlight index 32.
  5. YOLO-WaveletTiny. The detector starts from YOLOv11n and adds two wavelet modules. WDSConv in the backbone replaces the 3×3 depthwise convolution with a Haar wavelet split into one low-frequency and three high-frequency subbands, filters each subband with a depthwise convolution, reconstructs by inverse wavelet transform and projects with a 1×1 convolution. IWUpsample in the neck replaces interpolation-based upsampling with a multi-level inverse wavelet reconstruction, so that fine high-frequency defect detail is not blurred during feature fusion.

Results

Rendering alone lifts the YOLOv11n baseline from 85.1% to 91.0% mAP@50, against 85.7% on pseudo-colour images and 88.9% on normal maps; recall rises from 74.6% to 87.3% (Table 8).
The full YOLO-WT reaches 93.8% mAP@50 and 88.7% recall with 2.47M parameters and 5.7 GFLOPs, the highest mAP@50 and recall and the smallest model among the compared detectors (Tables 10 and 12).
Against point-cloud segmentation networks, YOLO-WT has the highest defect-level F1 (89.0%) at 7.3 ms per image; the 3D methods take 168.5 to 573.2 ms (Table 13).

The dataset comes from real production inspection of automotive battery top cover welds and holds six defect classes, from 104 bumps to 381 pinholes, so the classes are clearly imbalanced (Table 2). Each sample is a single-view depth map, cropped to 640 × 640 pixels and split 8:1:1 into training, validation and test sets. Training uses 250 epochs, SGD and no pretrained weights; detection runs on an RTX 3080.

Why the rendering helps. The paper first measures how well each representation separates defect from background (Table 5). The rendered image has the highest edge gradient gain (4.130), but not every metric: the pseudo-colour image has the largest mean intensity contrast (0.064) and the specular component alone has the highest signal-to-noise ratio (1.557). The rendered image combines these with 0.051 and 0.771. A second analysis correlates, over 16 × 16 pixel patches, how much the normals vary with the local Michelson contrast (Table 6). Here the rendered image correlates most strongly of all modalities (Pearson 0.489, Spearman 0.737, Kendall 0.557), while the pseudo-colour image barely correlates (Pearson 0.121).

A Morris sensitivity analysis over the six rendering parameters shows that the ambient weight and the light direction dominate all three visibility metrics, while the diffuse weight and highlight index have weak, stable effects and can be left at typical values (Table 7). Under added Gaussian noise, pulse noise and random occlusion of the depth map, intensity contrast and SNR fall gradually. Under occlusion the edge gain rises artificially, because the missing blocks create spurious edges; the authors conclude that occluded scans need hole filling before edge-based analysis.

Choice of shading model. Six classical models were compared with the same YOLOv11n detector (Table 9). Phong and Blinn-Phong tie at 91.0% mAP@50, and Phong has the best precision (90.3%, tied with Gooch) with recall of 87.3%. Minnaert is marginally higher on mAP@50-95 (46.5% against 46.3%) and Rim Lighting on recall (88.2%). Phong is also the slowest of the six on CPU, at 15.2 ms per image; the authors consider this acceptable given the cost of missed defects.

The detector. In the ablation (Table 10), IWUpsample alone raises mAP@50 from 91.0% to 93.2% at slightly higher cost, while WDSConv alone makes the model smaller (2.45M parameters, 5.6 GFLOPs) but less accurate (90.7%). Together they reach 93.8% mAP@50, 47.6% mAP@50-95 and 88.7% recall, with 4.6% fewer parameters and 10.9% less computation than the baseline. Latency rises from 5.5 ms to 7.3 ms per image, which the authors judge still real-time for the line. Precision drops slightly (89.9% against 90.3%): the model trades a few false alarms for fewer missed defects, which the authors note is usually preferred in inspection. Five-fold cross-validation gives 94.8 ± 1.03% mAP@50 (Table 11).

Among the compared 2D detectors (Table 12), YOLOv8n comes second on mAP@50 with 92.3%. On mAP@50-95 YOLO-WT (47.6%) is slightly behind DFINE-Nano (48.6%), DEIM-Nano (48.3%) and DEIMv2-Nano (47.7%), which are larger and slower (3.6–3.7M parameters, 14.9–18.0 ms against 7.3 ms). The authors name three limitations: the rendering parameters are fixed at one operating point, precision is slightly lower in exchange for recall, and the data come from a single production line. Future work is to tune parameters automatically, improve precision, and extend the data to other materials and welding processes.

item.title: SciVision Machine Vision SDK
item.description:
SciVision is OPT’s industrial visual-development SDK for building deployable machine-vision applications around cameras, 2D/3D measurement, deep-learning inference, robot guidance, and production-line communication. It sits below visual workflow software such as Smart3 and exposes the algorithm layer directly for engineering teams that need C++/C#/Python/VB integration.

Official product feature overview: 2D, 3D, deep learning, secondary development, cross-platform deployment, controls, communications, and multi-language support.

Product role

SciVision is positioned as a full-function development kit rather than a single algorithm library. The official product page presents it as a platform for 2D vision, 3D vision, and deep learning, with GPU acceleration, multithreading, instruction-set optimization, more than 300 algorithm APIs, and cross-platform support across Windows, MacOS, Ubuntu, CentOS, and Arm.

Architecture

The SDK is organized around an application-development layer, controls and communication modules, and a broad algorithm layer. It is intended to help teams move from proof-of-concept scripts to production applications with reusable UI controls, measurement tools, communication adapters, and sample projects.

Official architecture graphic showing the SDK’s development modules and algorithm coverage.

Engineering capabilities

The product material highlights fast calls into both interface and algorithm layers, rich example projects, image controls, CPK/GRR controls, TCP/serial/PLC communication, and multi-language bindings. For production use, the practical value is that image acquisition, measurement, inspection, result visualization, and factory communication can be developed within one SDK surface.

Official heterogeneous-computing benchmark slide for SDK-side acceleration.

Companion book and examples

The companion book, Machine Vision Algorithms: Principles and Industrial Practice, is a bilingual Quarto book with 42 chapters, 9 parts, dual HTML/PDF output, and runnable SciVision SDK C++ examples. The book explains the algorithms independently from the API, then connects them back to SciVision examples where code-level implementation details matter.

The mvbook repository links algorithm principles, industrial cases, and runnable SciVision SDK C++ examples.

item.title: Fusing Phase Map Servoing and MPC for High-Precision Robotic Tracking of Dynamic Objects
item.description:
The problem

Industrial robots often work stop-and-go: move to a fixed pose, take an image, then act. To work on parts that keep moving on a conveyor, the robot must instead close the loop on continuous visual feedback, which is visual servoing. Conventional visual features such as points, edges and contours struggle on the textureless or specular surfaces common in industry. Phase maps from fringe projection are an alternative: a projector casts sinusoidal fringes, and the recovered phase gives dense, subpixel geometric information without a 3D reconstruction step. Earlier phase-map servoing work, however, dealt with static or slowly varying scenes.

A moving target adds two difficulties. Sensing and image processing delays make the measured phase map lag behind the object’s actual state, and the lag grows with target speed. Model predictive control (MPC) is well suited to dynamic tracking because it plans over future states under constraints, but applied directly to the thousands of phase pixels in a map it becomes too expensive to solve at a high rate.

How it works

The framework keeps the dense phase map as the feedback signal but shrinks the control problem built from it, so that MPC can run at the camera rate, and adds an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) to look ahead past the sensing delay.

  1. Phase map as the feature. The camera and projector are mounted on the robot’s end effector. The difference between the observed and the desired phase map is mapped to a 6-DoF end-effector velocity through an analytically derived phase interaction matrix L, one row per phase pixel.
  2. Gradient-guided sparsification. Pixels whose phase gradient falls below a threshold ε carry little information about motion, so their rows of L are removed. In all experiments ε is 0.15 times the largest gradient magnitude.
  3. PCA embedding. The remaining phase features are projected onto d = 8 principal components, so MPC works with an 8 × 6 interaction matrix instead of an m × 6 one (m is the number of pixels in the phase map). In scenes with enough phase gradient, the reduced matrix keeps rank 6 and all six motion directions stay controllable.
  4. Adaptive prediction horizon. The MPC horizon follows the phase change rate: it stays at Nmin = 3 when the phase changes slowly and grows smoothly, through a tanh function, towards Nmax = 10 as the target speeds up.
  5. EKF prediction as the MPC reference. An EKF estimates the target’s position and velocity, propagates them over the horizon and converts each predicted position into a predicted phase map. MPC tracks this sequence as its reference, compensating for latency, and applies only the first control input of each solution.

Results

MPC quadratic-programming (QP) solve time 6.8 → 1.9 ms (median, Table 4) and closed-loop latency 12.9 → 8.3 ms (median; 19.2 → 10.4 ms at the 95th percentile), baseline vs the proposed M6 configuration (the baselines and M1–M6 are defined below; Table 4).
Target moving at 0.1 m/s: 100 % tracking success vs 33 % for the baseline, with a final error of 0.05 ± 0.02 mm over 12 trials (Table 5).
At 0.05 m/s: final error 0.04 ± 0.01 mm vs 0.07 ± 0.02 mm and convergence in 290 ± 40 ms vs 420 ± 55 ms (Table 5).

The simulation, run in MATLAB, compares eight controllers: two baselines (A, which uses the full phase map and recomputes the interaction matrix at every step, and B, which adds warm start to A) and six variants that use one, two or all three of the reductions (M1–M6). M6, which combines PCA, the sparse interaction matrix and the adaptive horizon, converges within about 20 iterations and has the lowest RMS error and the lowest, most compact solve-time distribution. A sweep of the reduction settings supports ε = 0.15 and d = 8 as the balance point: they give a 1.9 ms solve time and 0.048 mm RMS error (Table 2), against 3.5 ms and 0.042 mm for a looser setting (ε = 0.05, d = 12) and 1.3 ms with 0.081 mm for a more aggressive one (ε = 0.30, d = 6) (Table 2). Camera exposure, phase computation and the EKF update cost the same with or without the reductions; the time saved comes from the MPC/QP step. The tests used a 640 × 480 camera at 120 Hz and a single CPU thread on an Intel Core i7-12700, with the qpOASES solver.

In the physical experiments, the projector–camera head rode on the robot arm and the object travelled on a conveyor. With a stationary object, the proposed controller reached the same accuracy as the original phase-map servo law, with errors around 0.3 mm, but converged in about 20 iterations instead of 30. The EKF matters most once the target moves fast: without it the phase error shows peaks approaching 0.2 rad, with it typical peaks stay below 0.1 rad.

The authors state that the reachable speed is limited by sensing throughput. With the 120 Hz camera and a control period of about 8.3 ms, tracking is stable up to about 0.12 m/s; above that, phase noise rises as phase-map generation cannot keep up, so results for faster targets are not reported. The current implementation tracks a single target under relatively controlled visual conditions; faster phase-map generation and multi-object tracking are left to future work.

item.title: OPT 3D Camera Product Line
item.description:
OPT’s 3D camera portfolio is organized around the major industrial sensing routes: laser profile cameras for scanning and micrometer-level measurement, projected structured-light cameras for one-shot high-precision reconstruction, speckle/RGB-D cameras for large field-of-view depth and color capture, and ToF cameras for high-frame-rate perception.

Product matrix covering laser profile, projected structured light, speckle structured light, and ToF cameras.

My role

My role is centered on the algorithm and software layer that turns 3D camera data into deployable inspection workflows: reconstruction, calibration, point-cloud/mesh processing, measurement, defect detection, registration, robot guidance, and Smart3 integration.

Product architecture

The product line is designed as a hardware and software suite rather than a set of isolated sensors. Camera families cover close-range high-precision measurement, large-format depth acquisition, 2D/3D aligned inspection, and robot guidance. The Smart3 algorithm platform connects the camera output to visual workflow design, point-cloud processing, measurement tools, and production deployment.

The portfolio compares laser triangulation, temporal coded structured light, and binocular speckle depth sensing.

Technology routes

Laser profile cameras emphasize mature motion-assisted measurement with um-level precision. Projected structured light emphasizes one-shot reconstruction and high repeatability for static or indexed parts. Speckle/RGB-D cameras emphasize wide field-of-view capture, RGB-depth alignment, and cost-effective logistics or robot-vision use cases.

Different routes are positioned by speed, precision, and application scenarios.

System deployment

The camera line is paired with the Smart3 visual algorithm platform, allowing inspection workflows to be configured with camera acquisition, preprocessing, point-cloud reconstruction, measurement, defect detection, and user-defined visualization.

Hardware: OPT 3D camera series. Software: Smart3 algorithm platform.

Industry coverage

The product line is positioned for lithium batteries, 3C electronics, photovoltaic, semiconductor, automotive, robotics, food, medicine, chemical, and warehouse automation scenarios, with applications including glue inspection, PCB measurement, welding inspection, dimensional checking, robot guidance, and volume measurement.

Industrial application coverage across more than 30 market segments.

item.title: 3D Surface Matching Based on Adaptive Threshold and Curvature Map
item.description:
The problem

In industrial defect inspection and robotic sorting, a 3D scanner has a limited acquisition range, so each scan gives a single point cloud or depth map from one viewpoint, covering only part of the surface. Matching a workpiece model against such a scan is hard: feature points are sparse, there is a lot of redundant data, and the overlap is low.

The standard tools each have a weak spot, according to the authors. ICP (iterative closest point) aligns very accurately from a good starting pose, but is sensitive to initialisation and can get stuck in a local minimum when the geometry is incomplete or ambiguous. RANSAC-based methods struggle to separate adjacent or continuous surfaces. The integral volume descriptor (IVD) makes coarse matching more robust to noise, but its cost grows quickly on dense or noisy clouds. Learning-based registration, in turn, typically needs large annotated datasets and heavy computation, and generalises poorly across industrial scenes. This paper aims at a geometric method that keeps only the points that matter, so that IVD and ICP have less to process.

How it works

The method targets workpieces with pronounced curvature. It first shrinks the model point cloud to its high-curvature points, with a threshold that it finds by itself, and then matches in two stages: a coarse pose from IVD correspondences, and a fine pose from ICP.

  1. Depth map and curvature map. The model point cloud is converted into a depth map. For each pixel, a quadratic surface is fitted to its neighbourhood, and the resulting average curvature becomes the pixel value of the surface curvature map.
  2. Adaptive threshold iteration. From the histogram of curvature values (bin width by Scott’s rule), the method fixes a target share of high-curvature points: the points above an upper percentile. The threshold is β = μ + Kσ, with the mean μ and standard deviation σ of the curvature map. If the share of points above the threshold is too large, K is increased by 1%; if too small, decreased by 1%. This repeats until the share lies within a tolerance of the target. The points above the final threshold are the model point cloud used for matching.
  3. IVD correspondences. The IVD of a point is the volume where a sphere around it overlaps the inside of the surface; it is computed by convolving a voxel occupancy grid with a spherical grid, which avoids the noise sensitivity of differential features. Model points and scene points with similar IVD and position give preliminary point pairs.
  4. Coarse pose by SVD. After removing the centroids of both point sets, the covariance matrix of the pairs is decomposed by SVD, giving the approximate pose of the target in the scene.
  5. Fine matching by ICP. The model is moved by the coarse pose, and ICP then minimises the squared distances to the scene points, stopping when the objective changes by less than a set value.

Results

Lowest RMSE of the compared methods on both workpieces: 0.681 on Workpiece 1 and 0.405 on Workpiece 2, against 1.194 and 0.521 for IVD-SVD+ICP without feature selection (Table III).
The thresholds adapt per model, so no manual tuning is needed: the converged K was 0.405, 0.605 and 0.368 for the three models (Table II).
Under added Gaussian noise (std 0.1, 0.3, 0.5) the RMSE stays below IVD-SVD+ICP in every case, for example 0.826 against 1.01 at std 0.3 on Workpiece 1 (Table IV).

The experiments use point clouds from a structured-light camera of two workpieces (Fig. 4 of the paper). Workpiece 1 is matched with two models, front and back, in a scene of 149,469 points; Workpiece 2 uses one model (Table I). Accuracy is measured by RMSE between matched points, averaged over all targets when the scene holds several.

The segmentation takes the top 20% of curvature values as the target (80th percentile). The segmented clouds are much sparser than the originals, yet the edges and other geometrically significant points remain. Table II lists the converged parameters: the three models needed 502, 904 and 622 iterations and ended with 3,671, 3,369 and 4,860 feature points.

For matching, the paper compares IVD-SVD+ICP, the same pipeline with the threshold set by hand through three fixed K values (0.3, 0.6, 0.9), and the proposed method. The proposed method has the lowest RMSE on both workpieces. The margin is small on Workpiece 2, where K = 0.3 reaches 0.406 against 0.405. The fixed-K runs show how much the choice of K matters on Workpiece 1: RMSE ranged from 0.752 to 0.991, whereas the adaptive threshold needs no such tuning. Running time (Table III) is in the same range: 543 ms and 337 ms for the proposed method, against 532 ms and 489 ms for IVD-SVD+ICP, and some fixed-K variants were faster on Workpiece 2.

To test noise robustness, Gaussian noise with standard deviation 0.1, 0.3 and 0.5 was added to the point clouds, as low, medium and high noise, and the method was compared with IVD-SVD+ICP. The proposed method’s RMSE grows with noise but stays lower in all six cases: 0.748, 0.826 and 0.978 on Workpiece 1 (against 0.811, 1.01 and 1.121), and 0.417, 0.497 and 0.557 on Workpiece 2 (against 0.656, 0.667 and 0.728) (Tables IV and V). In low and medium noise, the matching shows no positional deviation. The authors state that the method still has limitations on high-noise point clouds, and name further work on feature extraction, more data for cross-scenario validation, and error analysis for heterogeneous point clouds.

item.title: A Grayscale-Compatible Color Encoding via 8-bit HSV Bit-Packing and Lightweight Refinement
item.description:
The problem

Converting a colour image to grayscale makes it compact and keeps it compatible with grayscale pipelines, but it throws away all chrominance. Colourization networks try to bring the colour back from the gray image alone. They are typically large, and because the input carries no explicit colour anchor, the colours they produce come from learned priors and can be wrong for the scene.

Invertible-grayscale methods instead hide colour inside an 8-bit gray-like image, either by modifying pixel values (reversible data hiding) or with learned invertible networks. The image they produce looks like a grayscale picture but is not guaranteed to be bit-identical to the standard grayscale, and the neural variants usually require heavier encoder–decoder networks. This paper takes a different design point: a 16-bit single-channel carrier whose high byte is the standard BT.601 grayscale, with the second byte spent on an explicit colour hint. It is intentionally not a replacement for strict 8-bit storage: it uses 16 instead of 8 bits per pixel, still down from 24 for RGB.

How it works

The encoder is a fixed bit-packing rule with no learned parameters. The decoder first rebuilds a coarse colour image deterministically from the packed bits, then a small U-Net refines it.

  1. Gray in the high byte. For each pixel, the standard ITU-R BT.601 grayscale value (0.299 R + 0.587 G + 0.114 B, rounded to 8 bits) is stored in the 8 most significant bits of a 16-bit word.
  2. Quantize hue and saturation. The pixel’s hue (OpenCV range 0–179) and saturation (0–255) are each quantized to 4 bits. This balanced split, H4S4, was chosen by the bit-allocation ablation.
  3. Pack the low byte. The 4-bit hue and 4-bit saturation are packed into the low byte (8 bits in all), the HSV hint. Shifting the word right by 8 bits returns the standard grayscale exactly: gray PSNR is infinite and gray SSIM is 1.0.
  4. Direct decoder. Without any training, the word is unpacked, hue and saturation are dequantized, the gray value is used as V, and HSV is converted back to RGB. This gives a coarse colour image.
  5. Residual refinement. The main model (UNet-residual) is a two-level U-Net with 0.47 M parameters. It takes the coarse RGB together with the gray, hue and saturation planes (6 channels) and adds a residual scaled by 0.25; the result is clipped to the valid range. Two direct-prediction variants of the same size serve as ablations: UNet-gray sees only the gray plane, and UNet-hints sees gray, hue and saturation (3 channels).

Results

Grayscale plane bit-identical to BT.601: gray PSNR = ∞ and SSIM = 1.0 by construction (Section II-E, Table XI).
Kodak 24 PSNR from 23.89 dB to 40.64 dB, and CIEDE2000 ΔE00 from 10.40 to 1.63, as the explicit chroma hint given to the U-Net grows from 0 bits (UNet-gray) to 8 bits per pixel (UNet-hints) (Table VIII).
0.47 M parameters, 14.77 GFLOPs, 1474 FPS at 256 × 256 for UNet-hints (the residual variant runs at 757 FPS), against two invertible-grayscale baselines with an 8-bit carrier: WIN 2025 at 2.34 M / 76.75 GFLOPs / 68 FPS and Zhao 2021 at 14.63 M / 129.05 GFLOPs / 18 FPS (Table VI). WIN 2025 reaches higher PSNR than UNet-hints on Kodak 24.

All networks are trained on the 5,000-image PASCAL VOC 2012 subset (80/20 train/val) and tested at 256 × 256 on Kodak 24, the DIV2K validation set (100 images) and McMaster 18. The low-byte hint carries most of the colour: the U-Net that sees gray, hue and saturation (UNet-hints) reaches 40.64 dB on Kodak 24, 38.10 dB on DIV2K and 35.41 dB on McMaster, while the same network given only the gray plane reaches 23.89, 22.98 and 18.61 dB. The direct decoder alone, with no network, gives 26.05 dB on Kodak 24. The residual variant reaches 37.88, 37.60 and 31.26 dB; the authors attribute its gap on the saturated McMaster images to the residual scale of 0.25, which limits how far it can correct a weak direct reconstruction. Among the re-measured baselines, WIN 2025 scores higher on most metrics (40.96 dB on Kodak 24, 38.16 dB on DIV2K and 39.43 dB on McMaster). The authors stress that these comparisons are not rate-normalized, since the baselines use an 8-bit carrier and this method a 16-bit one.

The format is fragile under lossy processing of the 16-bit image. JPEG at quality 90 lowers Kodak PSNR of the residual pipeline from 37.88 dB to 22.02 dB, and a Gaussian blur of σ = 0.5 to 16.32 dB, because both mix or discard the bits of the hint byte. If the hint byte is dropped entirely, the output falls back to a near-grayscale image (22.79 dB, SSIM 0.931). The authors therefore recommend the format for pipelines that keep the 16-bit image lossless, for example 16-bit PNG.

item.title: An Improved Graph Attention Network for Semantic Segmentation of Industrial Point Clouds in Automotive Battery Sealing Nail Defect Detection
item.description:
The problem

Sealing nails plug the electrolyte injection holes of automotive batteries and are laser-welded in place. Welding can leave defects such as bursts, molten beads and pinholes that compromise the battery’s safety and durability. The metal surface is highly reflective and textureless, which makes 2D imaging unreliable: it needs frequent lighting re-tuning and suffers from high false-detection rates. Traditional inspection therefore combines 2D vision to locate a defect with 3D vision to measure it, a multi-stage workflow that is complex, less efficient and accumulates errors from one stage to the next.

A 3D point cloud gives direct access to the shape of the surface, but many state-of-the-art segmentation networks, such as Point Transformer and Swin3D, rely heavily on RGB-D or intensity input. That limits their robustness when only geometry is available, which is common on reflective industrial parts. The defects themselves are also hard to learn. Defects of the same type can take very different shapes, a scan of about 100,000 points contains only about 1,000 defect points, and near a defect boundary the point coordinates barely differ from those of the surrounding surface.

How it works

LGASS (Local Graph Attention for Semantic Segmentation) segments defects directly in the 3D point cloud, so localisation and measurement happen in a single stage. It uses geometry only: the network input is each point’s surface normal, and the point coordinates determine which points are neighbours. The network is a U-Net-style encoder–decoder built around two new modules, one for attention and one for pooling.

  1. Scan the weld. A 3D laser profiler (OPT-LPC20, blue 405 nm laser stripe) scans the sealing nail at a lateral resolution of about 0.05 mm. An improved RANSAC algorithm fits the reference planes of the nail and the battery cover, and a circular region around the nail’s centre isolates the weld region for inspection.
  2. Watch the normals. Nearly every defect region shows clear changes in height and surface normal. Near a defect boundary, two adjacent points can have almost the same coordinates but clearly different normals, so the difference in normals between neighbours is a key indicator of a defect.
  3. Local Graph Attention Filter (LGAF). Each point is linked to its k nearest neighbours. For each neighbour, LGAF correlates the point’s own feature with its feature difference to that neighbour and weights the result by their spatial distance. The resulting attention weights are used to aggregate the neighbours’ features. A large normal difference produces a high attention weight, which focuses the network on defect boundaries.
  4. Spatial Attention Graph Pooling (SAG-Pooling). When the encoder downsamples, each point is scored by multiplying a learned spatial attention weight with its normal difference to a neighbour. Only the top-ranked points are kept, so points survive only if they are both spatially important and geometrically distinctive, such as those on defect edges.
  5. Label every point. The decoder uses graph-convolution blocks with positional encoding to upsample back to the full point set, with skip connections from the encoder. It assigns each point one of six classes: normal surface or one of the five defect types (burst, pit, warpage, molten bead, pinhole). A class-weighted loss gives the rarer defect classes more influence during training.

Results

mIoU (mean intersection-over-union over the classes) 79.26% and overall accuracy (OA) 99.43% on the sealing-nail dataset (mean of five runs), ahead of PTv3 (75.13% mIoU) and OA-CNN (74.04%) (Table 4).
Pinhole IoU 65.23%, against at most 60.04% for the compared methods (Table 4).
+2.59 points mIoU from LGAF and SAG-Pooling together over a baseline with standard graph convolution and pooling (Table 5).
220.9 ms to process one sample on an RTX 4070 GPU (Table 6).

The authors built a new dataset for this work from real sealing nails on inspection lines, with naturally occurring defects: 271 normal and 658 defective samples covering five defect types (170 burst, 112 pit, 132 warpage, 102 molten bead and 142 pinhole; Table 1). Code and dataset are released online. LGASS was compared with GACNet, PointNet, PointNet++, Point Transformer (PTv1 and PTv3) and OA-CNN in this geometry-only setting. Over five runs with different random seeds its mIoU stayed between 78.97% and 79.61%, and it achieved the best IoU on four of the five defect classes: pit, molten bead, warpage and pinhole.

The ablations show where the gain comes from. Replacing graph convolution with LGAF adds 2.19 points of mIoU, SAG-Pooling alone adds 0.46, and the two together add 2.59 (Table 5). Normals are the better input: in the input ablation, normals only give 79.23% mIoU, against 76.94% with coordinates only and 78.31% with both (Table 7). The class-weighted loss raises IoU on the minority classes, by 2.3 points for pinholes and 2.13 for molten beads, and lifts mIoU from 78.73% to 79.26% (Table 8). Inference needs about 2.8 GB of GPU memory. The authors note that LGASS may struggle with highly concave geometry, such as recessed nails with overlapping defects, where a fixed k-nearest-neighbour graph limits long-range context, and that rare classes such as pinholes still have lower IoU than the others.

item.title: Automatic geometric calibration and unwarping of rotating line-scan imaging systems using elliptical distortion of circular patterns
item.description:
The problem

A line-scan camera captures one line at a time, and motion supplies the second image dimension. How the image is formed therefore depends on that motion, and calibration has to describe it. Most line-scan calibration methods assume the object moves past the sensor in a straight line. Many inspection systems instead rotate the object: cylindrical workpieces, rotary surface profiling, panoramic imaging of rotationally symmetric parts. Each scan line is then taken at a different angle, a sector-scan (polar) geometry that distorts both the 2D intensity image and the 3D height profile. Calibration methods for rotating scanners typically rely on known angular motion, mechanical measurements or rotary encoders, which add complexity to the system.

The distortion itself carries the missing information. Under rotational scanning, the circular holes of a calibration plate appear as ellipses, and how the ellipses’ centres and aspect ratios change across the image encodes the rotation geometry. Earlier work used circular targets and ellipse fitting, but usually treated the deformation of the ellipses as a side effect of projection or misalignment, not as a record of the scanning geometry.

How it works

The method treats the image as polar data. A pixel’s column gives its distance from the rotation centre, r = x − xc, and its row gives the rotation angle, θ = k(y − yc), where k is the angular sampling rate in radians per row. The rotation centre (xc, yc) and k are unknown. All three are estimated from the ellipses in an image of a simple circular-hole plate, without encoders, mechanical measurements or auxiliary sensors. One polar-to-Cartesian mapping then corrects the 2D image and the 3D height map.

  1. Scan. The sensor stays still while the plate turns on a rotary stage. Each scan line becomes one image row at a new angle, so rows record angle and columns record distance from the rotation centre.
  2. Circles become ellipses. Under this sector-scan mapping, each round hole appears as an ellipse whose shape depends on its position. A single ellipse may be perturbed by noise, partial occlusion or imperfect edges, but together the ellipses follow stable trends, and the method estimates the calibration parameters from these collective trends rather than from any single precise measurement.
  3. Fit an ellipse to every hole. Hole regions are located (manually or automatically), segmented with an adaptive threshold, and their edges are refined to subpixel accuracy along the image gradient. After outlier edge points are removed, each contour is fitted with a direct least-squares ellipse fit. The centre and the aspect ratio ρi = rx,i / ry,i are recorded; ellipses with large residuals or unreasonable aspect ratios are rejected.
  4. Regress to find the rotation centre and sampling rate. The aspect ratio varies approximately linearly with the ellipse’s horizontal centre position, ρ = a·cx + b, so the rotation centre is where the line crosses zero, xc = −b/a. Because a small error in the slope a shifts xc strongly, the line is fitted robustly: RANSAC first removes gross outliers, then an iterative residual-based least-squares refinement (ILS) drops measurements with large residuals and refits, typically converging in 2–3 iterations. A second linear regression, of the angle against the vertical positions of the ellipse centres, θ = k·cy + d with d = −k·yc, gives the angular sampling rate k from its slope and the vertical centre yc from its intercept.
  5. Unwarp. Each pixel of the corrected image is mapped back to the raw image with the estimated xc, yc and k, and its value is found by bilinear interpolation. The ellipses become circles again. For 3D data, each height value becomes a point X = r cos θ, Y = r sin θ, with its height Z unchanged. The laser profiler produces the 2D intensity image and the 3D height map from the same measurements, so one transformation corrects both.

Results

Rotation centre xc = −516.76 px with R² = 0.998 for the aspect-ratio regression, and angular sampling rate k = 0.00402 rad/pixel with residual angular error below 0.12° across all calibration holes (Section 4.4).
Circularity error ε from 0.21 ± 0.08 before unwarping to 0.02 ± 0.01 after, where ε = |rx − ry| / rx is 0 for a perfect circle (Section 4.5).
Standard deviation of xc: 0.5 px with ILS, against 1.4 px with RANSAC and 3.8 px with ordinary least squares (Table 3).

All experiments ran on a real system: a single industrial laser triangulation profiler (LPF2-050, OPT Machine Vision, 405 nm blue laser, 3,200 points per scan line) mounted above a programmable precision rotary stage. The profiler stays still while the calibration target rotates at constant speed, and it records the 2D intensity image and the 3D height profile from the same measurements. Three circular-hole calibration plates of different materials, metallic and ceramic, with different hole layouts, gave consistent estimates of the rotation centre and angular sampling parameters. Ellipse fitting reached an average RMS algebraic fitting error of 0.42 pixels. Unwarping restored the circular holes in the 2D image, and the same transformation reduced residual geometric distortion and improved the spatial regularity of the reconstructed 3D surfaces.

The estimate becomes more stable as more ellipses are used. Over 50 random repeats, the standard deviation of xc fell from 2.1 px with 5 ellipses to 0.6 px with 10 and 0.3 px with 20, and automatic detection with ILS also reached 0.3 px (Table 1). Spreading the ellipses widely across the field of view matters more than adding more of them: the paper recommends about 8–30 well-distributed ellipses covering at least 30–50% of the field of view. The method also stayed stable under simulated partial occlusion, salt-and-pepper and speckle noise, and defocus blur (Fig. 10). When the scanned angle exceeds about 10°, the regression is stable, with R² > 0.99 in most experiments.

The authors also state the method’s limits. The model assumes the rotation axis is perpendicular to the image plane and that the scan line passes through the centre of the calibration disk; axis tilt, wobble or a lateral offset of the scan line would need extra parameters. Very small scanned angles make the ellipses nearly circular, so xc and k become hard to observe. Strong lens distortion should be corrected first, and a warped or non-planar plate can bias the ellipse centres. For 3D data, the correction addresses distortion from the scanning geometry only; it does not model laser-plane calibration or focal-length variation.

item.title: Deep diffusion model-based dual structured light for large-format complex surface imaging
item.description:
The problem

Phase-shifting structured light measures 3D shape with high accuracy by projecting sinusoidal fringes and reading their phase in a camera image. A single projector–camera unit, however, sees an object from only one angle. On large or complex surfaces, protrusions block the projected light or the camera’s view, leaving shadowed and blind regions without phase information, and the measurable area is limited. Measuring from several viewpoints, or turning the object on a turntable, fills the gaps but is slow and impossible for objects that cannot be moved.

Adding a second projector–camera head covers what the first cannot see, but only if the two heads can measure at the same time with overlapping views. When both projectors are on, each camera records the two fringe patterns superimposed in the overlap, an aliased pattern that leads to incorrect reconstruction. Earlier ways of separating such patterns need extra hardware (colour filters, special optical paths), colour or orientation multiplexing, or a strict projection order, and some give up simultaneous measurement altogether.

How it works

The system pairs two synchronised projector–camera heads with locally overlapping fields of view and runs them simultaneously. Instead of preventing the aliasing with hardware, it removes it in software: a conditional diffusion model learns to recover, from each aliased image, the clean fringe pattern of one projector. After that, each head works as a conventional structured-light unit, and the overlap is used to fuse the two results.

  1. Two synchronised heads. Two projectors and two cameras are connected by synchronous control lines, so both heads project and capture at the same time. Each head measures part of the surface, and their fields of view overlap locally.
  2. Aliasing as a sum. In the overlap a camera pixel integrates light from both projectors, so its intensity is the sum of the two projected patterns’ contributions. Writing u for the pixel and ln for the pattern of projector n, I(u) = I(u; l1) + I(u; l2) (background light is assumed not to affect the phase). One head’s pattern is therefore the measured intensity minus the other head’s pattern, I(u; ln) = I(u) − I(u; l3−n), which the authors read as a denoising problem, with the other head’s pattern as the noise.
  3. Conditional diffusion recovers the clean fringe. A U-Net with self-attention is trained in a conditional denoising diffusion framework. Training pairs come from the system itself: one head on alone gives the clean pattern x0, both heads on give the aliased pattern y, which serves as the condition. At inference the model starts from Gaussian noise and denoises it step by step, guided by y, until it reaches the dealiased fringe.
  4. Phase and 3D per head. With clean fringes, the four-step phase-shifting algorithm gives the wrapped phase and multi-frequency heterodyne unwrapping the absolute phase. Triangulation with each head’s calibrated projector and camera parameters then turns it into a partial 3D point cloud.
  5. Fusion with ICP. The overlapping region provides corresponding points, and the iterative closest point (ICP) algorithm estimates the rotation and translation that merge the two partial point clouds into the complete surface.

Results

Fringe recovery: PSNR 45.80 dB, MSE 1.85, SSIM 0.98 against the non-aliased fringe pattern (Section 3.2, Fig. 7).
Phase: at most 0.05 rad difference from the phase of the non-aliased pattern along a test row (Fig. 8).
3D: RMS error 0.057 mm for the dealiased reconstruction against a reference from separate, non-aliased measurements (Fig. 9).
Reconstruction error within 8 µm along sampled depth profiles of a prism with prominent protrusions (Fig. 12).

The prototype uses two TJ20U2 projectors and two CMOS cameras with a resolution of 3072 × 2048. Fringe patterns with periods of 100, 110, 120 and 130, each in four phase steps of 0.5π and with varied initial phase, produced 4043 training and 1583 test samples of 512 × 512 pixels; the model was trained with T = 4000 diffusion steps for 800 epochs. Without dealiasing, fringe aliasing introduces significant errors in both heads’ point clouds and in the fused result; with the diffusion model, the object is reconstructed successfully. An earlier derivative-based recovery method, applied to the same aliased fringes, distorts the fringes (noticeably denser, with local intensity amplification) and gives a noisy point cloud with pronounced layering. On a prism chosen to accentuate occlusion, fusion widened the reconstruction range and filled sparse areas that a single head leaves.

The authors define the scope of the evaluation as truly simultaneous dual-head measurement with a local overlap. Other aliasing-removal methods depend on specific hardware or projection schemes, such as colour or orientation multiplexing, optical-path separation or controlled projection sequences, and could not be run on this configuration without changing it. Results are therefore compared with non-aliased single-projector measurements as the reference and with conventional phase shifting applied directly to the aliased fringes as the baseline.

item.title: Depth-adaptive calibration of line-laser 3D measurement systems using rational polynomial mapping and depth-independent misalignment compensation
item.description:
The problem

A line-laser profiler measures a surface by triangulation. A camera watches the laser stripe on the object and converts each stripe pixel (u, v) into physical coordinates (X, Z) in the laser plane. A full 3D point cloud is then built by stitching many such profiles while a motion stage scans the part. Measurement accuracy is therefore set by calibration, and two different errors erode it across the working depth of field.

The first error is internal. Conventional calibration rests on a single-plane homography, a strictly linear pixel-to-physical mapping. In a real system, slight tilt of the lifting stage, local non-flatness of the target, radial and tangential lens distortion and stripe-centre extraction noise push the observations away from that ideal perspective, and a pure homography cannot represent the non-linear deviation. The second error is external. If the sensor is not aligned with the motion axis, the stitched cloud carries a systematic shear, and an orthogonal rectangle comes out as a parallelogram. Tuning intrinsics or distortion coefficients cannot remove this shear, and correcting each depth with its own parameters multiplies the parameter count. Existing pipelines usually address either the internal mapping or the external installation geometry, and their joint effect across the depth of field is seldom modelled.

How it works

The method handles the two errors in two separate stages. The internal stage is a one-off factory calibration that fixes the pixel-to-physical mapping inside each profile. The external stage is an on-site compensation that removes the installation shear from the stitched cloud. An automated, motion-triggered workflow runs both, so no manual multi-pose target placement is needed.

  1. Sample the full depth range. The camera and line laser are mounted on a precision Z-axis stage that moves through programmed positions. At each height the system captures a laser-on/laser-off image pair, which yields a clean stripe centreline. In the experiments, six depths Z1–Z6 are spaced 30 mm apart over a 150 mm range. Five are used for fitting, and Z3 is held out for testing.
  2. Fit one rational polynomial mapping. The model keeps the perspective (homography) backbone and adds a bivariate cubic residual in the height direction. Merged into one ratio, it maps (u, v) to X and to Z with a cubic numerator over a shared linear denominator, 22 coefficients in total. Cross-multiplying makes the problem linear, and the correspondences from all training depths form one overdetermined system, solved by least squares.
  3. Model the shear. The installation error is split into three rotations: roll α, pitch β and yaw γ. With a yaw angle γ, a scan step Δy pushes points sideways by Δx = Δy tan γ, so a rectangle turns into a parallelogram. In the tested push-broom setup, pitch rotates the laser plane about its own axial direction and causes no in-plane shear, so β is set to zero.
  4. Measure α and γ. A RANSAC line fit to a scan of the empty platform gives a reference line L. Roll comes from a standard height block of nominal height H and width W: α = arctan((H′ − H) / W), where H′ is the measured mean height of its upper face above L. Yaw comes from a checkerboard: requiring adjacent edges of a corrected cell to be perpendicular gives a quadratic equation in sin γ. It is solved for every interior 2 × 2 corner cell, and the median is used.
  5. Undo the rotation, once for all depths. Every point is mapped through the inverse rotation in Z–Y–X order, Rx(α) Ry(β) Rz(γ), which reduces to Rx(α) Rz(γ) with β = 0. The correction does not depend on depth, so angles estimated once at Z3 are reused across the whole volume.

Results

Mean absolute error 17.5% lower in X and 11.8% lower in Z than the HALCON calibration baseline on the held-out depth Z3: 8.745 vs 10.600 µm and 3.820 vs 4.332 µm (Table 5).
Error in the measured angle of a 25° standard block, tilted installation: 0.7591° → 0.0387° (deviation from 25°), depth-mean, a 94.90% reduction (Table 7).
Checkerboard orthogonality error, tilted installation: 10.007° → 0.309° (deviation of adjacent edges from perpendicular), depth-mean, a 96.92% reduction (Table 8).

All experiments use one commercial line-laser profiler (OPT-LPF2-006-01) on a programmable Z-stage and a push-broom rig. Ground truth comes from certified standards: a grid distortion target with a 49 × 49 dot array at 1 mm pitch, a metal checkerboard with 25 mm cells, a 25° standard angle block and a height block. For the internal stage, the HALCON baseline and the proposed mapping used the same image stack, the same stripe-centre extractor and the same train/test depth split. Besides the lower mean absolute errors, the proposed mapping improved repeatability by 33.8% in X and 70.0% in Z. The largest gain is in Z repeatability, the metric most sensitive to height-direction nonlinearity, which the cubic residual is designed to absorb.

A sweep over the residual order supports the cubic choice: a quadratic residual underfits, and a quartic one reaches the lowest training error, but its held-out error rises to 12.155 µm in X and 5.130 µm in Z, against 8.745 and 3.820 µm for the cubic residual (Table 11).

For the external stage, the sensor was deliberately tilted (roll α ≈ 5°, yaw γ ≈ 10°) and measured at all six depths in three states: normal installation, tilted without compensation, and tilted with compensation, with 10 trials each. Compared with normal installation, the tilt raised the angle-block error by a factor of 18.84 and the orthogonality error by a factor of 31.87. With the angles frozen from Z3, compensation brought both back to the level of normal installation (0.96× and 0.98× of it). The per-depth reduction stayed within 94.69%–95.04% for the angle and 96.87%–96.97% for orthogonality, so one compensator handles every depth without retuning.

Both stages are needed. With the external compensator disabled, the mapping errors match the full pipeline, but the angle and orthogonality errors stay at their uncompensated levels. With HALCON’s mapping plus the external compensator, the geometric errors drop to 0.0506° and 0.519°, but stay above the full pipeline’s 0.0387° and 0.309°, and the mapping errors return to the baseline (Table 10). The compensator also kept working beyond the vendor’s nominal 5° mounting tolerance: at Z3, with roll swept up to 20° at a yaw of about 10°, the corrected angle error stayed within 0.037°–0.101° and the orthogonality error within 0.16°–0.59° (Table 9). The numerical part of a full calibration takes about 2.3 s, and the total of about 11 minutes is dominated by physical scanning (Table 12).

The authors scope these results to the single tested device and working-distance range. Validation on a second camera, additional standard angles and the repeatability of the estimated angles across independent re-mountings are left to future work.

item.title: Dynamic correlation network and structure-aware matching for robust point cloud registration
item.description:
The problem

Point cloud registration finds the rotation and translation that align two partially overlapping 3D scans of the same scene, for example LiDAR or RGB-D scans captured from different viewpoints. Learned methods describe each point by features aggregated from its neighbourhood and then match points across the scans. When the relative rotation between the scans is large, these features, and the correlations between them, can change with the orientation, and the matches become unstable.

The common remedy is to train with randomly rotated scans, but augmentation cannot cover the continuous space of 3D rotations, SO(3), so orientations not seen in training still degrade performance. Rotation-equivariant networks such as PARE-Net help, yet they still combine neighbouring features through a fixed multi-layer perceptron (MLP) that applies the same correlation model to every neighbourhood. And even when two superpoints (coarsely sampled points, each standing for a local patch of the scan) are correctly matched, the individual points inside them can still be paired wrongly.

How it works

The method follows the coarse-to-fine pattern: a backbone extracts coarse superpoints (a sparse set of points, each standing for a local patch of the scan) and dense point features, superpoints are matched first, and points are then matched only inside matched superpoint patches. It changes two parts of this pipeline. A Dynamic Correlation Network (DCN) inside the PAREConv-FPN backbone decides how to combine neighbouring features from rotation-invariant cues, and a Structure-Aware Point Matching (SAPM) module refines the point matches inside each patch.

  1. Rotated input. The two scans arrive at an arbitrary relative rotation; the network has to estimate the rigid transform between them even when that orientation was not seen during training.
  2. A rotation-invariant cue. For each point and its nearest neighbours, a vector-neuron encoder builds features from the relative offsets, the mean offset of the neighbourhood and their cross product. These features rotate with the scan; their magnitudes do not, so the magnitudes serve as a rotation-invariant descriptor.
  3. Dynamic kernels. A channel reallocation network turns that descriptor into softmax scores over a small bank of learnable kernels (four in the experiments), and each neighbour’s kernel is the score-weighted sum of the bank. Because the scores depend only on invariant quantities, kernel selection does not change with rotation, while the aggregated features remain rotation-equivariant.
  4. Context inside each patch. Each matched superpoint pair defines two local patches. SAPM refines every point’s descriptor with linear self-attention over its own patch, at a cost linear in the patch size; points that lie closer to a different superpoint are masked out.
  5. Consistent matches and the pose. A row-wise and a column-wise masked softmax over the patch similarity matrix are fused with per-point confidence scores. Entries that are in the top k in both directions become dense matches. Each patch yields a pose hypothesis by SVD, and a feature-based hypothesis proposer keeps the best one, without RANSAC.

Results

Registration recall (share of scan pairs aligned to an RMSE below 0.2 m) 95.4 % on 3DMatch and 79.6 % on 3DLoMatch; the 3DLoMatch result is the highest of all methods compared (Table 3).
Transformation recall (share of pairs with rotation error below 15° and translation error below 0.3 m) 82.3 % on 3DLoMatch and 82.7 % on rotated 3DLoMatch, where FCGF drops by 15.1 points relative to unrotated 3DLoMatch (Table 4).
Rotation error 0.21° on KITTI, the lowest of the compared methods, with 4.8 cm translation error and 99.8 % recall (Table 2).

3DMatch and 3DLoMatch are indoor benchmarks with overlaps above 30 % and between 10 % and 30 %; KITTI consists of outdoor driving scans. On 3DMatch the method is close to the best RANSAC-based method, BUFFER-X (95.6 %), and slightly ahead of DFAT and PARE-Net (both 94.9 %); with RANSAC in place of its own estimator it still reaches 95.2 % and 79.3 %. When arbitrary rotations are applied to 3DLoMatch, methods that rely mainly on rotation augmentation, such as FCGF and Predator, lose transformation recall, whereas methods with rotation-invariant or equivariant designs, this one included, stay stable. On KITTI, CAST has a lower translation error (2.5 cm), while this method has the lowest rotation error. In the KITTI ablation, DCN and SAPM each reduce the errors on their own, and together they lower the rotation error from 0.239° to 0.211° and the translation error from 5.5 cm to 4.8 cm (Table 6). The model has 4.04 M parameters and takes 100.29 ms on an RTX 4090, faster than CAST (129.80 ms) and PARE-Net (122.80 ms) (Table 5).

The authors note two limitations: when the overlap is critically small, coarse superpoint matches can be wrong, and highly repetitive structures can produce ambiguous descriptors that mislead hypothesis selection.

item.title: Few-Shot 6D Object Pose Estimation via Decoupled Rotation and Translation with Viewpoint Encoding
item.description:
The problem

6D pose estimation recovers an object’s 3D rotation and 3D translation relative to the camera, a core step for robotic grasping, autonomous driving and augmented reality. Depth sensors are affected by noise, occlusion and cost, and struggle with reflective or transparent objects, which motivates methods that use a single RGB image. Monocular methods based on keypoints, templates or direct regression have made steady progress, but they rely heavily on large annotated real datasets, and the scarcity of real pose annotations limits further gains.

This work decouples rotation from translation. Rotation is learned from synthetic images alone, so only the translation part is trained on real images, and the translation part does not have to learn rotation from them, which reduces the number of real samples needed.

How it works

An object detector first crops the object from the image. Rotation and translation are then estimated by two independent branches. The rotation branch factorises the full rotation R into an out-of-plane part Rγ (the object’s viewpoint) and an in-plane part Rθ (a rotation about the camera’s optical axis), R = RθRγ, and handles each with modules trained on synthetic images only. The translation branch builds on GDR-Net and is the only part trained on real images.

  1. Detect and crop. An object detector extracts a 128×128 region of interest (ROI) around the object from the RGB image; both branches work on this crop.
  2. Retrieve candidate viewpoints. A viewpoint encoder, trained on images rendered from ShapeNet, maps the ROI to a 64-dimensional vector that is sensitive to viewpoint but invariant to in-plane rotation. For the target object, 4,000 viewpoints are sampled uniformly on a sphere around its mesh and rendered to build a codebook; cosine similarity against the codebook gives the top-K candidate viewpoints.
  3. Regress the in-plane rotation. For each candidate, a regression head compares the ROI with the view rendered at that viewpoint and predicts the in-plane rotation, giving a complete 3D rotation hypothesis.
  4. Verify the orientation. A verification head scores how consistent each hypothesis is with the ROI, and the highest-scoring hypothesis is taken as the rotation estimate.
  5. Regress the translation. Following GDR-Net, a ResNet-34 predicts three 64×64 maps from the ROI (a dense 2D–3D correspondence map, a surface-region attention map and a visible-object mask), and a lightweight network regresses the scale-invariant translation from the correspondence and surface-region maps. This branch is trained with 600 real images per object.

Results

ADD(-S) is the share of poses with error below 10 % of the object’s diameter. 65.3 % ADD(-S) on LM-O, against 62.2 % for GDR-Net (Table 3).
65.9 % ADD(-S) and 92.4 % AUC of ADD-S on YCB-V, against 60.1 % and 91.6 % for GDR-Net (Table 5).
97.6 % ADD(-S) on LINEMOD with ground-truth ROIs, and 94.8 % with Fast R-CNN detections (Table 2).
Retrained with the same 600 real images, ZebraPose and CheckerPose reach 38.2 % and 40.5 % on LM-O, against 65.3 % here (Table 4).

The evaluation uses LINEMOD (13 objects in cluttered scenes), LM-O (8 partly occluded objects, 1,214 test images) and YCB-V (21 objects, with severe occlusion and several symmetric objects). A pose counts as correct when its ADD(-S) error is below 10 % of the object’s diameter; for YCB-V the area under the ADD(-S) curve up to 10 cm is reported as well. The rotation network is trained on synthetic images only and the translation network on 600 real images per object; for YCB-V, physically based rendered images are also used in training.

On LM-O the method is ahead of the compared methods on most objects, with the largest gains over GDR-Net on Holepuncher (74.5 % against 60.1 %), Duck and Ape; GDR-Net remains slightly better on Can and Eggbox. On YCB-V it also leads in AUC of ADD(-S), 86.9 % against 84.4 % for GDR-Net. The few-shot comparison shows the largest gap: when ZebraPose and CheckerPose are retrained with the same 600 real images, their YCB-V ADD(-S) falls to 35.7 % and 37.8 %, against 65.9 % here (Table 6). The rotation modules were also evaluated on their own on LINEMOD: on real images with predicted ROIs, viewpoint retrieval is within 10° in 72 % of cases, and in-plane rotation is within 10° in 74 % of cases with predicted viewpoints and ROIs and in over 90 % with ground-truth viewpoints (Figs. 5 and 6), so in-plane accuracy depends strongly on retrieval quality. The authors note that accuracy partly depends on the reliability of the object detector, and that generalisation to unseen object categories remains limited.

item.title: Learning-based reconstruction of moving transparent objects
item.description:
The problem

Transparent moving objects have long been challenging targets in optical imaging: they have high transmittance and weak texture, and their imaging involves both refraction and reflection. Unlike conventional opaque rigid objects, a transparent object reflects the fringe patterns projected by phase-shifting profilometry (PSP) from both its front and rear surfaces, so the captured images show severe fringe superposition. When the object moves, its refraction effects are further coupled with motion-induced errors, which makes accurate reconstruction significantly harder.

How it works

The paper systematically analyzes how the imaging mechanisms of transparent objects influence geometric modeling and motion estimation, and proposes a learning-based reconstruction method for moving transparent objects that works in two stages.

  1. Superimposed fringes. PSP fringe patterns are reflected by both the front and rear surfaces of the moving transparent object and overlap in the captured images.
  2. Fringe separation. A diffusion model separates the superimposed fringe patterns.
  3. Reconstruction of the moving object. The moving object is then reconstructed based on the SIFT algorithm and two-dimensional motion equations.

Results

Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the method in complex dynamic transparent scenarios.

This page summarises the paper’s abstract. The full paper is available from the publisher: doi.org/10.1117/12.3111340.

item.title: Method for segmenting and denoising triangle mesh

This work appears in US Patent 12,536,620.
