item.title: Robust Object 6D Pose Estimation Under High Dynamic Ambient Light
item.description:
The problem

Estimating an object’s 6D pose means recovering its 3D rotation and translation relative to the camera, here from a single RGB image. Gen6D is a model-free pose estimator: at test time it needs no high-quality object model, depth map or object mask, and works from reference images of the object instead. It runs in three stages: a detector finds the object and its size, a selector picks the most similar reference image for a rough rotation, and a refiner corrects the estimate.

Under high dynamic ambient light, with stark contrast between highlights and shadows, this pipeline breaks down. Reflections on the object’s surface change with the light, shadows alter its brightness and texture, and colours are distorted. The authors tested Gen6D in scenes where projected light sources make the object’s surface reflect unevenly, and its pose estimates were poor. The refiner often cannot repair this on its own, because it depends heavily on the rough estimates from the earlier stages, which the lighting has already affected.

How it works

The method keeps Gen6D’s detector–selector–refiner pipeline and changes the feature extractor that all three stages share. An efficient channel attention (ECA) module is embedded in the VGG backbone. The resulting VGG-ECA network weights informative feature channels up and noisy ones down, so the features are less disturbed by glare and shadow.

  1. Glare confuses the original model. On objects with metal parts, such as a knife or scissors, Gen6D often finds only the weakly reflective plastic handle and misses the highly reflective metal.
  2. Channel attention in the backbone. ECA modules are added after the VGG layers with 64, 128 and 256 filters. Each averages every channel to a single value, applies a 1D convolution across neighbouring channels (its kernel size is set adaptively from the number of channels), maps the result to weights between 0 and 1 with a sigmoid, and multiplies the channels by these weights. Unlike the squeeze-and-excitation (SE) module it builds on, ECA does not reduce the channel dimension first.
  3. Detector. VGG-ECA features of the reference images serve as convolution kernels on the query image’s features, at several predefined scales. The peak of the resulting heat map is the 2D projection of the object centre, and the scale map at that point gives the bounding-box size, from which the depth and the initial translation follow.
  4. Selector. The object region is compared with the reference images, and the most similar one gives the initial rotation.
  5. Refiner. A 3D CNN regresses the residual between the current pose and the true pose and updates the estimate.

Results

ADD-0.1d 51.48 vs 49.48 for Gen6D (percentage of poses within 10 % of the object diameter), averaged over seven GenMOP objects (Table 1).
Prj-5 91.94 vs 89.64, with the largest gain on the knife, 77.21 vs 69.73 (Table 1).
Inference time 0.5322 s vs 0.4965 s, 35.7 ms (7.19 %) more than the original VGG model (Table 2).

The model is trained on GenMOP, the official Gen6D dataset of 10 objects, and for testing the authors chose objects with highly reflective surfaces. ADD-0.1d counts poses whose average model-point distance from the ground truth is within 10 % of the object diameter; Prj-5 counts poses whose 2D projection error is within 5 pixels. On every one of the seven objects in Table 1, the improved model scores higher than Gen6D on both metrics.

Separately captured RGB images under high dynamic ambient light show the effect qualitatively. Where Gen6D boxes only the plastic handles of the knife and scissors, the improved model captures the whole object, and it also detects a transparent glass cup on which Gen6D fails. Across five light levels, from dark (L1) to bright (L5), Gen6D is much less accurate on the knife and scissors in both low (L1, L2) and high (L4, L5) light, while the improved model is more accurate, most visibly on the glass cup. The authors also report failures: strong light makes part of the knife blade appear black, so the improved model cannot detect the pose of those blade sections, and the metal scissors are still misaligned at L1 and L2. They name more objects and datasets, other attention mechanisms and tests in real industrial applications as future work.

item.title: Self-calibrating structured light three-dimensional imaging method with fringe projection
item.description:
The problem

Industrial inspection asks for 3D measurement that is efficient, economical and highly precise, and structured-light 3D measurement meets these requirements. In a monocular camera–projector system that reconstructs surfaces by phase-shifting fringe projection, long-term operational stability is the key bottleneck for measurement accuracy: external factors such as vibration make the system’s extrinsic parameters move slowly, which weakens the triangulation constraints and lowers the accuracy of the measurement results.

How it works

The paper develops a self-calibrating fringe-projection 3D imaging technique that integrates bundle adjustment. The surface of the object being reconstructed becomes a constraint in the calibration itself.

  1. Drifting extrinsics. Vibration slowly moves the extrinsic parameters of the camera–projector system, weakening the triangulation constraints.
  2. Initial values. The independent calibration parameters of the camera and of the projector serve as the initial values.
  3. Joint optimisation (the bundle adjustment). The surface point cloud of the object being reconstructed is added to the optimisation as a constraint, giving a collaborative optimisation model of the camera parameters, the projector parameters and the scene’s 3D points.
  4. Corrected extrinsics. With this model the system’s extrinsic parameters are corrected rapidly and accurately.

Results

In the experiments, the technique significantly reduces the reliance on high-precision targets and strict flatness requirements without interrupting the measurement process, and cuts the cost of manual intervention and operation while ensuring reconstruction accuracy and measurement efficiency.

This page summarises the paper’s abstract. The full paper is available from the publisher: doi.org/10.1117/12.3114025.

item.title: SuP: Sub-cloud Driven Point Cloud Registration
item.description:
The problem

Point cloud registration finds the rotation and translation that line up two 3D scans of the same scene. Modern methods do this precisely when the two scans share a lot of geometry. In applications such as large-scale mapping and autonomous navigation, though, the views often share only a small part of the scene. Once the shared surface falls below about 30 %, classic ICP and learned methods alike struggle to find reliable correspondences, and registration slows, drifts or fails.

The paper traces these failures to the regions that are not shared: they can still be geometrically or semantically similar to each other, and matching the two whole clouds then produces wrong correspondences that obscure the correct ones. Earlier work tried to predict which points lie in the overlap, but that prediction depends on consistent features and becomes less effective on low-overlap pairs. Later methods strengthen the features with attention, geometric encodings, semantics or colour, yet their accuracy still drops as overlap falls.

How it works

SuP changes what it looks for. Two scans may overlap only a little overall, but if each is cut into smaller pieces and the pieces are matched pairwise, a subset of these sub-cloud pairs has high overlap. SuP calls these high-overlap pairs anchor pairs. It finds them in two phases, then builds its matches only from inside them.

  1. Features for the whole scan. A KPConv backbone extracts point features at several scales, and attention layers exchange context within and between the two scans. By default SuP uses the colour-enhanced backbone and attention of ColorPCR.
  2. Subdivide. Each scan is split into k sub-clouds. Farthest point sampling picks well-spread centroids, and each sub-cloud collects a centroid’s nearest neighbours within a radius.
  3. Phase I: overlap-guided prior weighting (OPS). For every source–target pair of sub-clouds, SuP measures how strongly their point features agree, counting only mutual top-ranked correlations, and keeps the best-scoring pairs as candidates. This is an efficient first filter against pairs that do not overlap.
  4. Phase II: multi-scale post-weighting (MPN). Each candidate pair is aligned with a preliminary pose from a weighted SVD. A small learned network then checks whether points that now sit close together also have similar features, at two scales. The pairs with the highest feature-consensus weights become anchor pairs. During training, the network is supervised by how well each candidate actually aligns (an alignment-aware weighting loss).
  5. Merge-to-match. Inlier correspondences from all anchor pairs are merged, refined on the denser points, and passed to a standard estimator (RANSAC or the RANSAC-free LGR) to compute the final rotation and translation.

In the reported setup, each scan is cut into 6 sub-clouds, giving 36 possible pairs. OPS keeps 24 of them, and the top 8 by feature consensus become anchor pairs.

Results

Registration recall 97.8 % on Color3DMatch and 90.2 % on Color3DLoMatch with the RANSAC-free LGR estimator, the highest among the methods compared with LGR (Table 2).
98.1 % and 90.4 % with RANSAC, and the highest registration recall at every sampling level from 5,000 down to 250 correspondences (Table 1).
Lowest pose errors: 1.374° / 0.046 m on Color3DMatch and 2.493° / 0.074 m on Color3DLoMatch (Table 3).

The evaluation uses colour-enhanced versions of the indoor 3DMatch benchmark: Color3DMatch, with pairs overlapping by more than 30 %, and Color3DLoMatch, the harder split with 10–30 % overlap. Registration recall is the share of scan pairs aligned to within 0.2 m RMSE. SuP uses ColorPCR’s colour-enhanced backbone by default; compared with ColorPCR alone, the strongest baseline, it raises recall from 96.5 % to 97.8 % on Color3DMatch and from 88.3 % to 90.2 % on Color3DLoMatch under LGR. The share of correct matches rises as well: with 250 sampled correspondences on Color3DLoMatch, 76.0 % of SuP’s matches are correct (inlier ratio), against 68.0 % for ColorPCR.

The sub-cloud step also works as an add-on to other methods. Added to GeoTransformer, it raises Color3DLoMatch recall from 74.0 % to 76.7 %; added to PEAL, from 81.2 % to 83.4 % (Table 4). In the ablation study, adding the four components one at a time (OPS, the feature-consensus weights, MPN and the alignment-aware loss) raises recall at every step on both benchmarks (Table 5). Sub-cloud size matters as well: smaller sub-clouds may lower recall because of insufficient overlap, larger ones miss local detail, and the default radius setting τ = 0.35 gives the best balance (Table 6). The paper’s limitation section notes that features from scans captured with very different sensors could weaken OPS and MPN, and suggests feature normalisation or domain adaptation as a next step.

item.title: TTA-MAC: Test-Time Adaptive Metric Calibration with a Signed-SDF Trust Region for Monocular 6D Object Pose Alignment
item.description:
The problem

Zero-shot 6D object pose from a single RGB image has advanced quickly thanks to foundation detectors and monocular depth models. A central bottleneck remains, according to the authors: metric grounding. Monocular depth gives rich relative geometry, but its scale and shift are biased for each object instance. A global CAD-guided affine calibration such as CAD-MAC reduces this bias, yet the remaining residual can be strongly non-Gaussian: on LineMod-Occlusion with the DAv2 depth model, its skewness is +4.5 and its excess kurtosis +36. A Gaussian prior for per-instance refinement therefore fits the actual errors poorly.

How it works

TTA-MAC is a CAD-anchored refinement layer applied at test time. It takes a frozen detector, a frozen monocular depth backbone, a warm-start pose and the object’s CAD model, and refines only eight geometric variables: the two calibration scalars of the monocular depth and the 6D pose.

  • Per-instance MAP problem. The depth-derived point cloud is aligned to a signed distance field computed from the CAD model.
  • Heavy-tailed prior. A Student-t prior models the heavy-tailed calibration residuals.
  • Trust region. The refinement runs inside a trust region with three gates and restores the best state found so far. The key safeguard is a signed-SDF gate on the fraction of the pseudo-depth cloud that lies inside the CAD volume. This detects wrong-basin states where the cloud penetrates the object, a failure that ordinary ICP or unsigned-distance alignment cannot see.

Results

Compared with a CAD-MAC+ICP baseline, the median ADD error improves from 44.0 mm to 31.3 mm on LineMod-Occlusion, and the success rate (ADD below 10% of the object diameter) rises from 10.4% to 14.3%. On LineMOD, across 18,273 instances, the median ADD improves from 43.5 mm to 30.5 mm and the success rate from 17.3% to 23.3%. The transfer to other datasets is partial: the median ADD improves from 41.1 mm to 38.3 mm on YCB-V and from 59.5 mm to 55.6 mm on TUD-L, and these runs also expose remaining threshold and over-refinement failures. The authors name visibility-aware, symmetry-aware and occlusion-robust trust regions as future directions.

This page summarises the abstract of the manuscript; details will be added once the paper is published.

item.title: Underwater structured-light 3D imaging method based on FP-DiffNet
item.description:
The problem

Fringe-projection profilometry measures shape by projecting sinusoidal fringes onto an object and reading the phase of the fringes the camera sees. Its methods and accuracy were established with air as the medium. Under water, several effects act at once. Absorption and scattering attenuate the signal with distance. Small-angle forward scattering from suspended particles blurs the fringes, large-angle backscattering adds background light and noise, and refraction at the water–air interface shifts the light paths. The fringes lose contrast and blur, so phase retrieval accumulates errors and the point cloud can lose regions or be distorted.

Restoration methods such as polarization or stereo imaging rely on prior modelling of the water’s optical parameters, while enhancement methods such as histogram equalization or colour correction can introduce colour bias and extra noise. Deep networks trained end-to-end avoid the priors but act as black boxes without explicit physical constraints, which can distort the restored fringes and bias high-precision phase retrieval.

How it works

FP-DiffNet is a fringe-restoration front end placed between acquisition and phase retrieval. It treats restoration as a conditional denoising diffusion process (DDPM): a U-Net learns to turn noise into a clean fringe image, guided by the degraded underwater image, and a simplified physical model of the degradation keeps the result consistent with underwater light transport. The restored fringes then go through the usual phase-shifting pipeline.

  1. Model the degradation. Following the Jaffe–McGlamery model, the light reaching the camera splits into direct transmission (attenuated with distance), forward scattering (a Gaussian blur of the image) and backscattering (background light and noise). Refraction at the water–air interface adds a depth-dependent shift of the rays.
  2. Train a conditional diffusion model. High-SNR fringe images captured in air are the targets, and fringe images of the same scenes captured in turbid water are the conditions. A clean image is noised towards Gaussian noise over T = 1000 diffusion steps, and a U-Net with self-attention learns to predict the injected noise from the noisy image, the step index and the underwater image. The loss combines an image-similarity term (SSIM), the noise-prediction error and a physics-consistency term, plus an L1 sparsity penalty on the weights.
  3. Restore by reverse diffusion. Sampling starts from pure Gaussian noise and removes noise one step at a time, with the underwater observation fed to the network at every step, until a clean fringe image remains.
  4. Correct with physics. A simplified degradation operator, a Gaussian blur for forward scattering plus a noise term for backscattering, links the estimate to the observation. Every k = 50 reverse steps, a gradient step with strength α = 0.01 reduces the residual between the observation and the simulated degradation of the estimate. Refraction is not in this operator; the U-Net learns it from the data.
  5. Retrieve phase and shape. The restored images have the form of standard N-step phase-shifting fringes, so phase retrieval runs unchanged: the arctangent formula gives the wrapped phase, unwrapping gives the absolute phase, and its difference from a reference plane is converted into 3D coordinates with the calibrated projector–camera geometry.

Results

Fringe restoration at the highest turbidity T4 (T1 is the least turbid of the four levels): PSNR 42.42 dB, SSIM 0.9750, MS-SSIM 0.9974 (Table 2).
Wrapped-phase MAE 0.0354 rad at T4, 0.0260 rad at T1 (Table 3).
3D reconstruction RMSE 0.0890 mm at T4, 0.0317 mm at T1 (Table 4).

The system pairs an industrial camera (1800 × 1600 pixels) with a digital projector (1280 × 1024 pixels) mounted about 0.6 m above an acrylic tank, using a three-frequency four-step phase-shifting scheme. Turbidity was raised by adding 4, 5, 6 and 7 mL of milk to 13 L of clear water, giving four levels T1–T4. The dataset covers five objects in random poses, split 4:1 into 7200 training and 1800 test images, and all reported results are on the test set. Errors are measured against ground-truth fringe images, phases and reconstructions. From T1 to T4, PSNR falls only from 43.02 to 42.42 dB, and the cosine similarity of the wrapped phase to the reference stays between 0.9951 and 0.9962. The remaining phase errors concentrate at object boundaries, shadows and phase discontinuities. Restoring one 512 × 512 fringe image takes about 430 ms on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090.

The authors state the limits. T4 is the most turbid level tested; beyond it they expect restoration to fail once direct transmission falls below the noise floor and the fringe information is lost. The framework applies to sinusoidal phase-shifting patterns, and other structured-light configurations or underwater conditions may need fine-tuning with configuration-specific data.

item.title: Deep transformer-enhanced dynamic structured light for three-dimensional moving object imaging
item.description:
The problem

Phase-shifting profilometry (PSP) projects a sequence of sinusoidal fringe patterns, each shifted by a known amount, and recovers the 3D shape of a surface from the phase of the captured images. It is robust to ambient light and to changes in surface reflectivity, but it needs at least three images, and the object must stay still while they are taken. If the object moves, each surface point is lit by different projector pixels and seen by different camera pixels in each frame, so the phase steps between frames are no longer the intended ones. The result is ripples, phase-unwrapping errors or a failed reconstruction.

Faster projectors and cameras reduce the problem but raise hardware cost, and the effect of motion still remains. Most error-estimation methods handle motion only along the depth direction and do not address the pixel mismatch caused by motion in other directions. Tracking-based compensation models such as Lu’s work well within the X–Y plane but handle Z-direction motion poorly, and methods that estimate a single global translation miss local, pixel-level motion differences. When an object moves in an arbitrary direction, every surface point has its own displacement and therefore its own phase error.

How it works

The method keeps standard four-step phase shifting and adds two things: a learned tracker that finds where each pixel of one fringe image went in the next ones, and a pixel-wise model of the phase error that remains after that tracking. Both run inside a short sliding window of five frames.

  1. Model the motion-induced phase error. The projector cycles four-step fringes (π/2 apart) while the camera captures the moving object. The motion of each surface point is split into an in-plane displacement, which moves the point to another pixel (Δu, Δv), and a displacement along Z, which adds a phase error. The total phase error is the sum of the two.
  2. Track pixels with a transformer. The image sequence is split into windows of five frames, and the middle frame is the key frame. A COTR (COrrespondence TRansformer) network, initialised with its original pre-trained weights and fine-tuned on fringe images, matches query pixels in the key frame to the other four frames. A shared CNN backbone extracts features from both images, a transformer encoder–decoder relates them, and an MLP head predicts each match.
  3. Align the frames and solve for the Z error. The matches define a pixel-wise mapping that aligns all five frames so the same surface point is followed through the window. Within the short window, the Z-direction velocity is treated as constant, so each frame adds the same extra phase error ε, and frame n of the window (n = 1 to 5, key frame n = 3) carries a Z part of (n − 3)ε. Combining the intensities of the five frames gives three equations in the object phase Φ and ε. For small ε they reduce to a linear equation K1ε + K0 = 0, which is solved at every pixel, and the corrected phase Φ follows.
  4. Unwrap and reconstruct. The corrected wrapped phase is unwrapped with a three-frequency phase-shifting algorithm, using two sets of lower-frequency fringes projected alternately with the high-frequency ones, and converted into 3D shape with the calibrated camera–projector model.
  5. Slide the window. The window moves on by one frame, so each newly acquired image, together with the four before it, gives a new 3D shape of the object.

Results

RMSE 0.072 mm on a moving ceramic plate, against 1.401 mm for standard PSP and 1.352–2.028 mm for Guo’s, Lu’s and Wang’s methods (Section 3.2, Fig. 6).
RMSE 0.096 mm on a moving “Aphrodite” statue, against 1.129 mm for PSP (Section 3.3, Fig. 8).
Fringe-image matching error (AEPE) 0.47–0.83 px for the fine-tuned COTR, against 12.32–21.06 px for optical flow on five unseen objects (Table 1).
3D reconstruction RMSE 0.092 mm with COTR as the tracker, against 0.157, 0.181 and 0.490 mm with fine-tuned FlowFormer, GMFlow and RAFT in a combined-motion experiment (Table 2).

The system uses a high-speed camera at 512 × 512 pixels and 30 fps and a DLP projector. To fine-tune COTR, the authors captured 45 dynamic scenes of sculptures, toys and industrial parts on a shallow box of sand (about 5 cm deep), with 60 motions each, giving 2,700 pairs of pre- and post-motion fringe images (2,400 for training, 300 for validation). Ground-truth matches came from an extra blank image projected at each pose, on which a robust local optical flow method computed dense displacements. Training converged after about 1,400 epochs and took about 42 hours.

The ceramic plate was moved by a translation stage at 40° to the camera’s optical axis in 1 mm steps, with a 12-step phase-shifting measurement as ground truth. Standard PSP shows clear ripple distortion. Guo’s method smooths part of it, Lu’s method compensates only motion in the X–Y plane, and Wang’s method simplifies the phase-shift error, which leads to even larger errors. With steps of ±1, ±2 and ±3 mm, the RMS error of the proposed method stays below 0.1 mm (Fig. 6(f)). On the statue, PSP shows stripe artifacts and discontinuities along the edges, Guo’s method still has large errors at the edges, and Lu’s method leaves periodic ripples because Z-direction motion is not compensated; the proposed method recovers the contour more accurately.

The method was also tested on a static statue next to a rotating one, on a rotating fan model with a smooth, weakly textured surface, on a statue on a continuously rotating platform, and on objects that translate and rotate at the same time. Under combined translation and rotation, the rotation adds phase deviations of up to about 1 rad in the outer regions, and the method still keeps most surface areas accurate. The authors note its limits: when the translation along Z is too large, phase-error estimation can still fail (marked regions in Fig. 12); the authors suggest increasing the projection rate or combining the framework with geometry-constraint-based or Gray-code-based unwrapping. Because the estimate relies on a five-frame window, the method works reliably for small inter-frame motion; standard frame rates suffice for slow to moderate motion, while fast objects need high-frame-rate cameras and projectors.

item.title: A Reversible Grayscale Method Based on Bit-Field Multi-Channel Fusion Encoding
item.description:
The problem

Grayscale images are widely used because they cut computational complexity, storage and transmission cost. In many applications, though, the original colours are needed again later, so the conversion should be reversible: the grayscale image has to carry enough colour information to restore the RGB image.

Traditional reversible grayscale methods, such as histogram shifting and wavelet-packet data hiding, embed colour cues into the luminance channel. They usually impose extra transform-domain constraints or need several auxiliary channels, which adds computation and memory. Deep-learning methods reach high reconstruction fidelity but bring high inference latency, large models, limited interpretability and a strong dependence on training data.

How it works

The method needs no training. Each RGB pixel is converted to the HSV colour space, which separates the chromatic part (hue H, saturation S) from the luminance part (value V). The three components are quantized to a, b and c bits with a + b + c = 16 and written side by side into the bit fields (H in the high bits, V in the low bits) of one 16-bit grayscale pixel. Decoding reads the fields back with shifts and masks. The whole pipeline uses only quantization and bitwise operations, and it is exactly invertible except for the quantization error.

  1. Normalize. The three channels of an 8-bit RGB pixel are divided by 255, so they lie in [0, 1].
  2. RGB to HSV. The standard conversion gives hue H as an angle from 0° to 360°, saturation S and value V; H is then scaled to [0, 1).
  3. Allocate the 16 bits. The output pixel’s 16 bits are split into a bits for H, b for S and c for V. The split can follow the image statistics, with a and b proportional to the variances of H and S and c taking the rest. The paper also gives four example schemes; the balanced Scheme 1 uses (6, 4, 6).
  4. Quantize and pack. H, S and V pass through a non-linear (gamma) mapping that favours perceptually sensitive ranges, are quantized to 2a, 2b and 2c levels, and are packed as IG = (Hq ≪ (b + c)) | (Sq ≪ c) | Vq. The result is a single-channel 16-bit grayscale image.
  5. Decode. Bit masks and shifts recover Hq, Sq and Vq; inverse quantization and the standard HSV-to-RGB transform give the 8-bit RGB pixel back.

The choice of (a, b, c) trades accuracy between the channels. Because people are sensitive to hue changes, the authors recommend a ≥ 5 (32 hue levels) to avoid visible colour shifts, and c ≥ 6 (64 value levels) to prevent banding; b can be reduced for images with little colour. Hue is circular, so a non-linear quantization keeps errors small near 0°/360°, and Floyd–Steinberg error diffusion spreads the remaining quantization error spatially.

Results

Encoding 3.71 ms and decoding 7.01 ms per Kodak image with Scheme 1, against 175.30 / 125.24 ms for IDN and 2486.75 / 2453.82 ms for the CNN-based method (Table II).
PSNR 34.80 dB, SSIM 0.9726 on Kodak with Scheme 1; higher is better, and PSNR is below IDN (42.16 dB) and the CNN-based method (37.40 dB) (Table II).
PSNR 34.06 / 34.48 / 32.20 dB on Urban100 / BSD500 / McMaster with Scheme 1, with encoding and decoding times between 2.80 and 3.82 ms (Table III).

The method was evaluated on four datasets: Kodak PhotoCD (24 images), Urban100 (100 urban scenes), BSD500 (500 natural landscapes) and McMaster (18 images). It was compared with two learning-based invertible grayscale methods, IDN and a CNN-based method, using MAE, PSNR, SSIM, FSIM and LPIPS, and timed on an AMD Ryzen 9 7945HX with an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4060. Of the four bit-allocation schemes, Scheme 1 (6, 4, 6) gives the best balance; Scheme 2 (5, 5, 6) reaches the highest SSIM of the four on Kodak (0.9779), and Scheme 4 (6, 5, 5) is the fastest at 3.21 ms encoding and 4.49 ms decoding. The 16-bit files are also slightly smaller on Kodak: 633.20 KB for Scheme 1, against 721.47 KB for IDN and 660.87 KB for the CNN-based method (Table II).

The speed comes at a cost in fidelity. On Kodak, IDN reaches 42.16 dB PSNR and the CNN-based method 37.40 dB, against 34.80 dB here, and the authors note that a recent reversible data-hiding method reports 43.69 dB. They see the method as a lightweight, interpretable alternative for resource-constrained settings such as edge and embedded systems, and plan adaptive allocation algorithms and reversible compression to close the quality gap, and FPGA/ASIC implementations to further cut latency.

item.title: Calibration Method of Fringe Projection Based on High-Order Polynomial
item.description:
The problem

Phase-shifting profilometry (PSP) measures 3D shape by projecting sinusoidal fringes onto an object, recovering the phase of the deformed fringes in the camera image, and converting pixel coordinates and phase into 3D coordinates. That conversion is set by system calibration, and the traditional approaches are laborious. Phase-to-height mapping needs a large, precise calibration target and a precision translation stage, and its parameters depend on how accurately both are made and moved. Stereo-vision calibration takes the target coordinates and their image coordinates in the camera and the projector, and solves for the parameters by nonlinear optimisation. That is slow, and the accuracy depends on how well those image coordinates are measured.

A polynomial calibration model avoids the projector model and the translation stage: it directly fits the 3D world coordinates as a polynomial in the pixel coordinates (u, v) and the absolute phase ϕ. Higher orders describe this relationship more accurately, but the number of coefficients grows quickly, and fitting them by least squares becomes slow and unstable once the order exceeds 3. An earlier simplification removes redundant terms by principal component analysis, which speeds the fit up but lowers reconstruction accuracy.

How it works

The method keeps a high-order polynomial calibration model, which needs no projector model and no translation stage, and replaces least-squares fitting with a sparse greedy randomized Kaczmarz (SGRK) solver. SGRK combines the efficient iterations of the randomized sparse Kaczmarz method with the selection strategy of greedy algorithms: each step works on one well-chosen equation instead of the whole system.

  1. Collect calibration points. Fringes are projected onto a circle-grid board placed in several poses. The circle centres are the feature points: each gives its pixel coordinates (u, v), its absolute phase ϕ from three-frequency four-step phase shifting, and its world coordinates from Zhang’s calibration method.
  2. Set up the polynomial model. Each world coordinate X, Y and Z is written as an n-th order polynomial in u, v and ϕ, so calibration becomes a linear system W = Ax. The model has 60 coefficients at order 3, 105 at order 4 and 168 at order 5; the paper uses order 4 as its standard model, balancing accuracy and computing time.
  3. Choose an equation greedily. In each iteration SGRK computes the residual of every equation, keeps the rows whose residual exceeds a threshold, and draws one of them with probability proportional to its squared residual. Equations with large errors are therefore updated first, which speeds up convergence.
  4. Update and sparsify. The chosen row updates the coefficients by a weighted Kaczmarz projection, and a soft-threshold operation then sets small coefficients to zero, so the solution stays sparse.
  5. Iterate, then reconstruct. The loop runs until the relative standard error (RSE) of the coefficients falls below 10⁻⁶. To measure an object, the pixel coordinates and absolute phase of each point are put into the fitted polynomial to give its 3D coordinates.

Results

Standard ceramic sphere (25.0001 mm), 4th-order model: diameter deviation 0.0232 mm in 1.63 s with SGRK, against 0.0727 mm in 3.96 s with least squares (Table 2).
Standard step block, 4th-order model: average errors of 0.004 and −0.003 mm on the two step heights in 1.78 s, against 0.009 and 0.006 mm in 4.32 s with least squares (Table 1).
Ceramic doll: RMSE 0.0729 mm with SGRK versus 0.9250 mm with least squares, measured against a Mech-Eye Pro S Enhanced scan (Sec. 3, Fig. 9).

The system uses a DLP LightCrafter 4500 projector (912 × 1140 pixels), a CCD camera (1280 × 1024 pixels) and a 300 mm × 300 mm circle board with 30 mm between circle centres. Each method was compared on the full 4th-order model and on the PCA-simplified 4th-order model. SGRK was faster and more accurate in both cases: on the sphere the simplified model gave 0.0449 mm in 1.17 s with SGRK against 0.0932 mm in 3.17 s with least squares, and the simplified models were less accurate than the full one for both solvers (Table 2). The step block was measured three times after each calibration to check repeatability (Table 1).

The advantage holds at other orders too (Table 3). At order 3, SGRK gave a sphere diameter deviation of 0.0549 mm in 1.02 s against 0.1470 mm in 3.04 s for least squares; at order 5, 0.0177 mm in 2.31 s against 0.0400 mm in 6.15 s. The 5th-order model is more accurate than the 4th, but its 168 coefficients make the computation markedly longer, and both are more accurate than the 3rd-order model.

item.title: DeSC: Learning Deep Semantic Descriptor for NeRF Registration
item.description:
The problem

A Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) stores a scene inside a neural network. Large scenes are often split into several NeRFs, and images captured without reliable global camera poses produce NeRFs that each live in their own coordinate frame. To combine them, one has to estimate the rigid rotation and translation between two independently trained NeRFs: NeRF registration.

Existing methods rely on either geometry or rendered colour. DReg-NeRF samples a point cloud from each NeRF and regresses correspondences, but these point clouds are noisy and contain artifacts from inaccurate density estimates, especially when a NeRF is under-trained. VF-NeRF optimises with a photometric loss, which makes it vulnerable to textureless and highly symmetric cases. Both ignore the view-independent embedding that a NeRF computes internally for every 3D point, which carries both geometry and appearance. Using it directly is not straightforward either: the two NeRFs are trained separately, so their embedding spaces do not match.

How it works

DeSC treats each NeRF as a source of point features, not only of geometry. It samples a point cloud from each NeRF, extracts geometric features with a KPConv backbone, and adds a Deep Semantic Aggregation Module (DSAM) that turns the NeRF’s own embeddings into descriptors that agree across the two NeRFs. A Transformer and a coarse-to-fine matcher then find correspondences, and the pose is solved by SVD.

  1. Sample each NeRF. DeSC takes the centres of the non-empty voxels in each NeRF’s occupancy grid and keeps those whose density exceeds a threshold σt. KP-FCNN downsamples this point cloud hierarchically and extracts multi-level geometric features.
  2. Query embeddings around each sparse point. For every sparse point (a point of the coarsest downsampled level), a patch is formed from its k nearest dense points (from the next, denser level) within a radius τ. Each patch point queries the NeRF for its view-independent embedding, which is enriched with the point’s colour and density through a sinusoidal encoding, so that the features carry photometric information shared by both NeRFs.
  3. Aggregate with a texture-aware graph convolution. A graph convolution runs over each patch. Its edge weights emphasise points that are close to each other but have contrasting features, capturing local high-frequency texture. The output is fused with the geometric features to give the deep semantic descriptor.
  4. Add context and match. Geometric self-attention and cross-attention let each point cloud gather context from itself and from the other. Coarse correspondences are selected from the resulting features and refined on dense points with an optimal transport layer.
  5. Solve the pose. Outliers are removed, and SVD gives the rotation and translation that align the two NeRFs. During training, a density-aware photometric consistency loss also asks matched patches to have similar density-weighted colour.

Results

Registration recall (pairs with RMSE below 0.2 m) 97.7 % on Objaverse, against 92.1 % for the NeRF method VF-NeRF and 94.5 % for the point cloud registration method SIRA-PCR, with a rotation error of 2.57° (Table I).
90.6 %, 91.0 % and 88.1 % registration recall at 30 % overlap on DTU, LLFF and Mip-NeRF360, against 86.6 %, 88.5 % and 84.8 % for VF-NeRF (Tables III–V).
Removing all proposed modules lowers Objaverse recall to 93.2 % and raises the rotation error to 9.19° (Table VI).

The object-level benchmark is built from Objaverse: for each object, 120 rendered images are split into two blocks, each block is given a random transformation, and a separate NeRF is trained on each; 44 objects unseen during training are used for testing. Registration recall counts the pairs whose estimated transformation has an RMSE below 0.2 m. DeSC is compared with the NeRF registration methods DReg-NeRF and VF-NeRF, and with eight point cloud registration methods run on points sampled from the NeRFs. With uniform noise of 10 % of the scene size added, its recall is still 95.74 % (Table II).

On the real-scene datasets DTU, LLFF and Mip-NeRF360, each scene is split into image subsets with 30 %, 50 % and 80 % overlap. DeSC has the highest registration recall in all nine settings, and the margin is largest at 30 % overlap, although VF-NeRF reaches a slightly lower rotation error in some settings. In the ablation, adding the deep semantic aggregation, the photometric encoding, the texture-aware edge weights and the photometric consistency loss in turn raises Objaverse recall step by step, from 93.2 % with none of them to 93.9 %, 95.1 %, 96.9 % and 97.7 %.

The authors state two limitations. DeSC relies on NeRF’s implicit embeddings, so it does not apply directly to explicit representations such as 3D Gaussian Splatting, voxel grids or hash-based methods. Objects that are highly symmetric in both shape and texture, such as a traffic cone, yield symmetric features and can be matched wrongly, even when the rendered alignment looks plausible.

item.title: Fast Shape Retrieval Based on Differential Chain Code Descriptor and Fuzzy Contour Matching
item.description:
The problem

Matching a known shape in an image is a basic step in industrial inspection and measurement. Feature-based methods such as SIFT, SURF and ORB describe key points, but they perform poorly under heavy noise, blur or strong viewpoint change, and the many feature points make them computationally intensive. Template-based methods compare image patches directly, which is costly over large search spaces and sensitive to scale, rotation and illumination. This paper therefore matches contours, using the structural and topological information they carry.

A chain code turns a contour into a sequence of direction changes, so two similar shapes produce similar sequences and matching becomes sequence comparison. The catch is that the sequence is ordered: one noise point shifts the correspondence of the points after it, and the longer the code, the more points are misaligned and the larger the error.

How it works

The method first turns each contour into an ordered, evenly spaced point set and encodes it as differential chain codes. It then matches the local contour against the model in short segments, so that a noise point only disturbs the segment it falls in, and finally checks each candidate position geometrically.

  1. Extract, smooth and resample the contour. Run-length encoding of the binary image, a connectivity analysis and a depth-first search give the outer and inner contours, with points about 1 pixel apart. The points are smoothed with the mean of their neighbours and then sampled at a fixed distance, which reduces their number while keeping the shape.
  2. Encode the turning angles. Instead of computing an ordinary chain code first, each point and its two neighbours form two vectors, and the rotation angle between them is quantised into a differential code. The contour becomes a code sequence that does not change when the shape is translated.
  3. Match short segments. The code of the local contour is divided into short segments. Each segment slides along the longer model code, and at every position the cost is the sum of absolute code differences. Each segment produces one cost array as long as the model code.
  4. Combine the costs and pick candidates. A sliding window writes the minimum cost inside the window into its centre, which absorbs small shifts of the best position. The segment cost arrays are then combined into one total cost. The total forms valleys; positions with small cost are kept, and the centre of each valley becomes a candidate starting position.
  5. Verify with SVD. Fuzzy matching can also return look-alike or wrong positions. For each candidate, the local points are paired with the model points, a transformation is estimated by singular value decomposition (SVD), and the mean distance between the transformed pairs scores the match. The positions with the smallest mean distance are kept. An optional ICP step refines the final alignment.

Results

Lower mean distance than Halcon and Smart on all 8 test images: 0.376–0.601 for the proposed method, against 0.694–1.027 for Halcon and 0.642–0.958 for Smart (Table 1).
0.372–0.447 with ICP refinement, with standard deviations of 0.155–0.189, against standard deviations of 0.269–0.483 for Halcon (Table 1).

The test material is CAD drawings captured with the SmartFlash-2020 one-click measurement sensor, an instrument for large flat products with a measurement range of up to 300 × 200 mm. Each original image was rotated clockwise by 30°, 60°, 90°, 120° and 150° and matched against the original, and further experiments test matching under multi-target interference. For the quantitative comparison, Table 1 reports the mean distance and standard deviation between the matched contour and the ground truth on eight test images, for Halcon, a baseline referred to as Smart, the proposed method, and the proposed method followed by ICP.

The proposed method has the lowest mean distance of the three methods on every image; on test image 2, for example, it is 0.426, against 1.027 for Halcon and 0.715 for Smart. ICP refinement lowers the mean distance on seven images and leaves it unchanged on image 6 (0.376), with the largest reductions on images 8, 5 and 4 (0.601 → 0.372, 0.581 → 0.391 and 0.578 → 0.419). As future work, the authors plan more advanced smoothing, an improved fuzzy matching algorithm and the use of deep learning.

item.title: FPD: Fringe Photometric Deflectometry when Fringe Meets Photometric Stereo
item.description:
The problem

Many industrial parts are neither purely matte nor purely mirror-like. The back of a phone, for example, has a glossy logo on a surface whose specular reflection is weaker, and defects such as scratches and fingerprint smudges have to be found on both. Two established optical methods each cover only half of this. Photometric stereo (PS) recovers surface normals from images taken under several illumination directions; it works well on diffuse (Lambertian) regions but degrades where specular highlights appear. Phase Measuring Deflectometry (PMD) measures surface gradients from the reflection of sinusoidal fringes; it is accurate on specular surfaces but unreliable on matte areas, where fringe contrast is low.

As a result, existing inspection methods often fail to detect subtle defects when specular highlights or diffuse textures dominate. Few earlier works merge the two methods: one combined photogrammetry with PS, another fused line-structured light with PS but had difficulties in highly reflective areas.

How it works

FPD captures the data for both methods in one cycle, runs a PMD branch and a PS branch, and fuses their outputs pixel by pixel. The PMD branch also measures how specular each pixel is, and that measurement sets the fusion weights.

  1. One capture cycle. A projector displays three kinds of patterns: binary patterns that simulate four-quadrant illumination for PS, and horizontal (fringe-x) and vertical (fringe-y) sinusoidal fringes for PMD. The camera records 12 images per cycle.
  2. PMD branch. With four phase-shifted fringe images per pixel, the mean intensity is A, the specular component S is computed from the fringe modulation, and the diffuse component is D = A − S; glossiness is S / A. Multi-frequency unwrapping gives the absolute phase, whose x and y derivatives form the phase gradient magnitude P.
  3. PS branch. The four binary-pattern images, using the PMD specular and diffuse reflection maps as prior information, form an intensity matrix of images × pixels. Its singular value decomposition gives the surface normals, from which the surface gradients and the mean curvature H are computed, with CUDA acceleration.
  4. Weights from reflectance. Each pixel gets wPMD = S / (S + D) and wPS = D / (S + D). Glossy pixels lean on PMD, more diffuse pixels on PS, and the transition between them is smooth.
  5. Fusion. The result is R = wPMD·P + wPS·H. PMD dominates where fringes are reliable, PS where fine diffuse detail needs to be kept.

Results

Scratch on the glossy logo: missed by the PS mean curvature map, kept by PMD and by FPD (Fig. 4).
Fingerprint smudge outside the logo: missed by the PMD phase gradient map, kept by PS and by FPD (Fig. 4).
Defect detection in Smart3 (a commercial inspection software): PS-based detection fails on the strongly specular region, PMD-based detection fails where reflection is weaker, and the FPD result supports detecting both (Fig. 7).

The test object is the back of an iPhone, which shows both diffuse and specular reflection. It was imaged on a platform with a projector, a camera and mounting structures, with a 12-image cycle of binary, fringe-x and fringe-y patterns, and processed on a PC with an Intel Core i5-13500 CPU and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 GPU. The comparison is between the three reconstructed maps of the same capture: the PS mean curvature map, the PMD phase gradient map and the FPD fusion result, which the authors find more complete and consistent across both types of feature. Defect detection was then run on each of the three maps with Smart3, a commercial inspection software from OPT Machine Vision: scratch detection, and smudge detection by line extraction. FPD has also been integrated into commercial defect inspection software.

The authors name calibration of the integrated system and height measurement for complex surfaces as future work.

item.title: GCMA6D: Graph Convolution and Cross-Modality Attention Fusion for 6D Pose Estimation
item.description:
The problem

6D pose estimation recovers the 3D rotation and translation of an object relative to the camera, a step that robotic manipulation and augmented reality depend on. It remains hard for low-texture objects and under partial occlusion. Methods that use RGB images alone lack depth information, which limits their robustness in complex environments. RGB-D methods such as DenseFusion fuse colour and point-cloud features pixel by pixel, but they describe the geometry with PointNet, which may miss fine local detail. Methods that add local feature modelling, such as PVN3D, raise the computational cost, and the size and inference latency of large foundation models hinder real-time deployment.

GCMA6D builds on the pixel-wise fusion of DenseFusion, the baseline of its ablation study, and strengthens each part of it: graph convolution models local geometry, Large Kernel Attention sharpens the image features, and a cross-modality attention module lets colour and geometry inform each other before they are fused.

How it works

The network takes a single RGB-D image. It segments the object, extracts colour features from the image crop and geometric features from the object’s point cloud, fuses them with attention, and regresses the pose from every pixel of the object.

  1. Segment and crop. The semantic segmentation network from PoseCNN produces a mask for each object. The mask crops the colour image and cuts the object out of the depth map, which the camera intrinsics convert into a 3D point cloud. This suppresses background interference before any features are computed.
  2. Colour features with Large Kernel Attention. A ResNet18 backbone and a pyramid pooling module extract multi-scale features from the image crop. Large Kernel Attention, a depth-wise convolution, a depth-wise dilated convolution and a 1×1 convolution, builds an attention map that is multiplied with the features, so the network captures local texture and edges as well as longer-range context.
  3. Geometric features with 3DGCN and PointNet. A 3D graph convolutional network applies learnable 3D graph-convolution kernels to the neighbourhood of each point, followed by graph max pooling, to model local geometric structure. A PointNet branch processes the points with fully connected layers and obtains a global shape feature through max pooling.
  4. Cross-modality attention. The CMA-Net module takes the colour features (F1), the 3DGCN features (F2) and the PointNet features (F3). One dot-product attention uses F1, F2, F3 as query, key and value to enhance the colour features; a second uses F2, F1, F3 to enhance the point features. A Squeeze-and-Excitation module reweights the channels of both outputs and of F3, and the three are concatenated.
  5. Dense fusion and pose. The fused features of each pixel pass through shared MLPs and average pooling to form a global feature, which is appended to every pixel’s feature. Each pixel then predicts a rotation, a translation and a confidence; the most confident prediction is kept. Following DenseFusion, a small network then refines it iteratively by predicting residual poses.

Results

97.7 % mean accuracy on LineMOD (ADD(-S) within 10 % of the object diameter), against 94.3 % for DenseFusion (Table 2).
Each module alone improves on the 94.3 % baseline: graph convolution (3DGCN) 96.9 %, Large Kernel Attention (LKA) 96.2 %, cross-modality attention (CMA-Net) 95.4 % (Table 1).
92.9 % AUC (area under the ADD(-S) accuracy curve up to 10 cm) and 95.7 % of poses under 2 cm on YCB-Video, against 91.2 % and 95.3 % for DenseFusion (Section 4.4).

The evaluation uses two public datasets. LineMOD contains low-texture objects against complex backgrounds under varying illumination; 15 % of the images are used for training and 85 % for testing, and a pose counts as correct when its ADD distance (ADD-S for symmetric objects) is below 10 % of the object’s diameter. In Table 2, GCMA6D has the highest mean accuracy of the seven methods compared, ahead of TMFNet (96.8 %) and QaQ (95.3 %), and reaches 100 % on the symmetric eggbox and glue. The ablation study on LineMOD shows that the modules complement each other: any two together score 96.8–97.4 %, and all three give 97.7 %.

YCB-Video has 21 objects with varying levels of occlusion; testing uses 2,949 key frames from 12 videos. Accuracy is measured as the area under the ADD(-S) accuracy curve for thresholds up to 10 cm, and as the share of poses with an error below 2 cm. GCMA6D’s 92.9 % AUC is above SaMfNet (92.6 %), G2L-Net (92.4 %), MSCNet (91.5 %) and DenseFusion (91.2 %). The authors note lower accuracy on the large and extra-large clamps: the two look very similar, so PoseCNN’s segmentation struggles to produce precise masks for them. They also name highly symmetric or heavily occluded objects as a remaining limitation, and plan to improve the processing of background-masked regions.

item.title: Identifying frequency-domain operating deflection shapes and internal damage in structures using geometric vision method
item.description:
The problem

An operating deflection shape (ODS) describes how a structure deforms at each vibration frequency while it is in service. Because it does not require prior knowledge of the excitation, it offers an automatic way to assess dynamic behaviour and to detect damage. Measuring it is the hard part. Conventional contact sensors are bulky in operation and serve a single function, and non-contact laser vibrometers sample one point at a time and need complex calibration, which is impractical when many degrees of freedom are involved. Vision methods can measure dense surface motion, but stereo digital image correlation (stereo-DIC), which tracks speckle points across images and triangulates them, reconstructs displacement in the time domain first, where noise has to be filtered out and the filtering can remove high-frequency motion as well. Earlier frequency-domain triangulation methods use one camera that sees the object from several views through relative motion, so camera poses change between views, must be re-estimated at every step, and introduce phase delays.

Internal damage adds a second difficulty. Visual crack detection only sees surface defects, while vibration-based damage identification usually needs precise excitation information or contact sensors, and recent vision-based variants still rely on pseudo-excitation or heuristic steps such as denoising and clustering.

How it works

The method uses a stereo pair of still high-speed cameras with a fixed geometry. After calibration and rectification, every observed point is described by one parameter, its disparity, which makes the map from stereo image motion to the frequency-domain ODS linear. A wavelet transform of the resulting ODS fields then exposes internal damage.

  1. RANSAC calibration. Zhang’s planar-target method runs inside a RANSAC loop: random subsets of checkerboard corners are used for calibration until the averaged re-projection error meets a threshold. Corners that lose imaging precision in some poses therefore no longer bias the focal lengths, principal points and distortion factors.
  2. Stereo and temporal matching. Only the reference stereo pair is rectified. Each point of interest is matched along the epipolar line with spatial DIC, then tracked through the original left and right image sequences with temporal DIC. Rectification is applied to the tracked point coordinates rather than to whole images, which avoids interpolation errors.
  3. Depth parameterization. In the rectified geometry a point’s depth is d = Bf/δ, with baseline B, focal length f and disparity δ, so each point has one unknown instead of three. Its image motion is encoded in a state vector ξ(t) = x₁(t)/δ(t), where x₁(t) is the point’s image coordinate in the left camera.
  4. ODS in the frequency domain. The ODS is a linear function of the state-vector change, U(ω) = Bf · Δξ(ω), obtained with a discrete Fourier transform and no triangulation step. The ODS fields at all frequencies form the response spectrum, and each peak corresponds to a full-field ODS map.
  5. Wavelet damage identification. Each ODS field is treated as an image on the left reference grid. Damage due to stiffness loss shows up as a step in the ODS, and a Haar wavelet transform produces normalized coefficients that peak at the damage. The peak gives the location and the damage degree, a relative change in ODS amplitude that reflects the local stiffness loss.

Results

ODS amplitude at 17 Hz: 1.84 mm vs 1.86 mm from a displacement transducer, a 1.1% error, against 1.80 mm (3.2%) for stereo-DIC (Section 3.4, Fig. 7).
Mean 3D reconstruction error of the calibration target: 0.014 mm vs 0.085 mm with the standard Zhang’s method (Table 3).
Damage degree 20.8% vs a theoretical 18.9% (computed from the specimen’s stiffness parameters) on the plate specimen, located with a maximum error of 0.87 mm in the vertical direction (Section 3.4).

The test specimen is a 1.5 mm thick, 300 mm × 50 mm plate of 304 stainless steel with a blind hole, 8.0 mm in diameter and 1.0 mm deep, on the face the cameras do not see. An exciter drove it at 17 Hz, close to its first natural frequency, while the two cameras (2560 × 1920 pixels) recorded 5000 stereo pairs at 1000 fps. RANSAC calibration lowered the re-projection error from 0.088 to 0.039 (Table 2) and the mean 3D error of an 8 × 8 test target from 0.124 mm to 0.013 mm (Table 3). On the flat specimen, the depth error ranged from −0.06 to 0.09 mm (mean 0.02 mm), against −0.17 to 0.35 mm (mean 0.09 mm) with Zhang’s calibration (Fig. 6).

At the transducer location, the vision-based spectrum captured the complete set of peaks. Even at 34.4 Hz, the smallest amplitude of 0.14 mm was estimated within 0.01 mm, while stereo-DIC missed most of the components other than the resonance. The full-field ODS maps at 17.0, 51.2, 150.6 and 248.8 Hz show the amplitude falling and the shape growing more complex as frequency rises, and singular value decomposition of these fields gives the corresponding 3D mode shapes. The wavelet damage landscape peaked at 0.208; transformed to the specimen frame, the damage lies at (24.26, 195.13) mm against the actual (25.00, 196.00) mm.

The method was also applied to a 3D-printed resin blade with curved surfaces, a 340 mm chord and two internal defects (5 mm and 3 mm in diameter, 0.8 mm and 0.6 mm deep) under a 0–300 Hz sweep excitation. Spectra at three points along the chord gave six characteristic frequencies, and the corresponding ODS maps yielded the first six mode shapes without excitation information. Both defects were found, with damage degrees of 5.1% and 3.2% and maximum positioning errors of 1.08 mm and 1.11 mm.

The authors note two limits. The two separate cameras used here are not integrated enough for long-term monitoring, and they propose a compact biprism stereo optic as a path forward. The damage algorithm recovers the location and extent of internal damage but not its shape or orientation.

item.title: Parallel Grayscale Connected Component Analysis via Neighborhood Labeling and Global Region Mapping
item.description:
The problem

Connected component analysis (CCA) groups adjacent pixels with similar values into regions. It is a basic step in industrial defect detection, depth-map filtering and medical tissue identification. As sensors reach higher resolutions, industrial lines need it on megapixel images within milliseconds, without losing segmentation fidelity.

The existing options trade one for the other. Serial CPU algorithms such as region growing and flood fill work directly on grayscale intensity and keep fine structure and subtle gradients, but are too slow for high-throughput production lines. Fast GPU algorithms, such as OpenCV’s connectedComponents, are designed for binary images. They need a binarization step first, for example Otsu thresholding, which discards intensity information. Low-contrast defects, or adjacent depth planes with similar intensities, are then merged or lost.

Adapting the binary GPU algorithms to grayscale is not straightforward, according to the authors. Binary images mostly consist of sparse, distinct blobs, whereas grayscale images have dense, continuous gradients. Linking neighbours whose intensities differ by at most a threshold creates far more temporary equivalences between pixels. In label propagation and parallel union-find this leads to heavy atomic contention on global memory, which destroys the parallel speed-up.

How it works

The method runs entirely on the GPU and works on the raw grayscale or depth values. Two neighbouring pixels belong together if their intensities differ by at most a threshold τ. Instead of merging pixel by pixel, it first cuts the image into small local regions, finds where those regions touch, and then merges them in the much smaller space of region IDs.

  1. Local partitioning. Each pixel looks at four neighbours already passed in raster order: upper-left, up, upper-right and left. It attaches to the first one, in that fixed priority order, whose intensity differs by at most τ; if none qualifies, it becomes a root. All pixels decide in parallel. Pointer jumping (path compression) then gives every pixel the ID of its root. Because the mask only looks backwards, some shapes, such as U-shapes, are split into several preliminary regions.
  2. Boundary detection. To find where those regions should join, each pixel checks its three neighbours below: lower-left, down and lower-right. If a neighbour has a different label but an intensity within τ, the pair of region IDs is written to an edge list with one atomic index increment. The edges form a region adjacency graph, which is much smaller than the image.
  3. Global region mapping. A mapping table over region IDs starts as the identity. For each edge, the larger ID is mapped to the smaller one; chains are followed to their current roots, so a region connected to several others ends up in one component. A final flattening pass makes every entry point straight to its root, and one pass over the image replaces each pixel’s label by its root.
  4. Feature aggregation. Region statistics such as the area are counted in each GPU block’s shared memory, in a small hash table, and then added to global memory once per block. This cuts the number of global atomic operations from one per pixel to roughly one per region and block, and the integer sums are exact and deterministic. Components below a minimum area can be filtered out in the same pass.

Results

1.567 ms on a 1920 × 1080 depth image, against 155.79 ms for serial region growing and 156.60 ms for flood fill (Image 1 of Table 4), about 1.32 gigapixels per second.
Grayscale detail is kept: on the same image, the binarize-then-label OpenCV pipeline finds 27 components, region growing 2,543 and the proposed method 2,586 (Table 4). With region growing as the reference, the average IoU over 8 depth maps is 99.98%.
Runtime barely depends on scene complexity: across 8 images of the same size it stays between 1.567 and 1.704 ms, while region growing ranges from 152.55 to 284.79 ms (Table 4).

The algorithm is implemented in CUDA C++ and was tested on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 with an Intel Core i5-12500 CPU; times are averages of 100 runs and exclude data transfer. The test images are industrial depth maps and grayscale images from 400 × 300 to 4000 × 3000 pixels. The baselines are OpenCV connectedComponents on the GPU, which needs a binary image, and serial region growing and flood fill on the CPU, which work on grayscale like the proposed method.

According to the authors, the binary pipeline over-merges or misses subtle grayscale components after thresholding, while the proposed method gives finer region partitions. OpenCV is still much faster, since it labels a binary image: 0.194 ms against 0.865 ms at 1920 × 1080 (Table 2). Against the grayscale baselines the gap is large at every resolution: at 4000 × 3000 the proposed method needs 8.659 ms, region growing 763.75 ms. From 400 × 300 to 4000 × 3000 the pixel count grows 100 times and the runtime 24.4 times, from 0.355 ms to 8.659 ms.

As a correctness check, with binary input and threshold 1 the method finds exactly the same number of components as OpenCV and a classical two-pass algorithm on three test images, with 475, 12,484 and 91,737 components (Table 3). The authors attribute the small differences to region growing in the IoU comparison to floating-point differences between CPU and GPU.

A stage breakdown on a 1920 × 1080 image (Table 5) shows where the time goes: initial labeling 0.608 ms, boundary detection and mapping 0.693 ms, global region-ID merging only 0.028 ms, and final relabeling with statistics 0.165 ms. The threshold τ sets how fine the segmentation is; since the runtime hardly changes with the number of components, it can be tuned without a latency penalty. Because merging is transitive, a gradual intensity ramp stays one component as long as each step between neighbouring pixels is within τ. As future work, the authors name adaptive thresholding, topology-aware boundary rules and multi-GPU extensions.

item.title: Photometric stereo-based defect detection for lithium battery top covers
item.description:
The problem

Cylindrical lithium batteries pick up scratches and pits on their top covers during production, from collisions, friction and other external forces. Human visual inspection is still common, but it is inefficient, inaccurate and prone to human error. Ordinary 2D machine vision lacks depth information: on a reflective metal surface it struggles in bright and dark areas, and text or dirt is easily confused with real defects. 3D methods such as structured light and fringe projection detect defects more precisely, but they are costly and data-intensive.

Photometric stereo (PS) takes a middle path. It photographs the surface under several lighting directions and recovers surface normals and curvature from the brightness changes, which makes it effective at revealing subtle surface variations. Traditional PS, however, is limited to static objects, which does not suit a production line, and very subtle defects such as shallow scratches remain hard to detect.

How it works

The method changes both the hardware and the algorithm. A line-scan camera images the cover while it moves, and a four-partition spherical integrating light source is strobed so that consecutive scan lines are lit from different directions. The usual circular opening at the top of the dome is replaced by a narrow slit, which reduces shadow artefacts. The four images are then turned into albedo and curvature maps on the GPU with CUDA, the curvature map is enhanced, and defects are extracted with image processing.

  1. Time-division acquisition. The motion platform’s encoder emits a line signal. A frequency divider produces four signals that switch the four light partitions in turn while triggering the camera, so each scan line is lit by one partition.
  2. Four images in one pass. Sorting the interleaved lines by partition gives four images of the moving cover, each under a different lighting direction.
  3. Normals by least squares. Under the Lambertian model, a pixel’s brightness is I = ρ L · N, with surface reflectance (albedo) ρ, light direction L and surface normal N. Four lights give four equations per pixel, solved by least squares. The albedo image shows foreign objects and contaminants; the normals give the surface gradients and a mean curvature image, which shows scratches, wrinkles and other defects.
  4. Enhancement. Contrast stretching widens the grey-level differences in the curvature image. A weighted least-squares filter, an edge-preserving smoother, then suppresses the texture of the workpiece while keeping defects such as scratches.
  5. Defect extraction. A region of interest is selected and the image is filtered and resampled. A difference image is formed between the original and the preprocessed (filtered and resampled) image, then thresholded; morphological operations refine the regions, and defects are kept according to their shape and grey-level features.

Results

Detection rate 95.38% for scratches and 96.43% for pits, over 376 scratches and 336 pits in 100 images of aluminium alloy surfaces with known defects (Table 2).
Sharpness 77.06 vs 16.91 and variance 168.88 vs 41.03 for the enhanced image against the method of Ren et al. (ref. 12); entropy, peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and structural similarity (SSIM) are also higher (Table 1).

The system runs on an industrial computer with an Intel Core i5-12500 processor and an Nvidia GeForce RTX 3060 GPU. The light direction vectors are first calibrated with a ring light, and the four images captured along these directions are processed in parallel with CUDA to produce the albedo and mean curvature images. The enhanced curvature image was compared with the method of Ren et al. on five image-quality metrics: sharpness, information entropy, variance, PSNR and SSIM (the last two are peak signal-to-noise ratio and structural similarity). The proposed method scored higher on all five (entropy 4.70 vs 4.16, PSNR 12.37 vs 10.84, SSIM 0.527 vs 0.512), which the authors read as stronger defect contrast with the original image structure preserved. The authors also compared CPU parallel computation with Intel TBB against CUDA on the GPU over different image sizes, and found that GPU acceleration significantly improves computational efficiency.

Future work will extend the algorithm to non-Lambertian surfaces and further improve real-time processing efficiency.

item.title: Precision 3D volume measurement of transparent adhesives via spectrally optimized line laser scanning and enhanced centroid extraction
item.description:
The problem

Automated dispensing machines lay down adhesive by dots, lines and coatings in electronic packaging and precision manufacturing. Pneumatic dispensers meter the adhesive through air pressure and valve opening time, and pressure fluctuations make the discharge uneven: too much adhesive overflows, too little leaves weak bonding or poor airtightness. Measuring the volume that was actually dispensed gives the data needed to calibrate the discharge. Manual measurement with calipers is slow and inaccurate, ultrasonic methods are sensitive to material properties and the environment, and electrochemical methods struggle because most adhesives are dielectric. Optical non-contact 3D measurement works well, but mainly for opaque materials.

Transparent adhesive breaks the diffuse-reflection assumption behind structured light, photometric stereo and stereo vision. Light is reflected and refracted at more than one surface, the material has no surface texture, and the reconstruction becomes inaccurate or incomplete. Earlier laser-scanning work on transparent objects either relies on complex ray tracing, at a high computational cost, or uses a multi-stage stereo framework that remains sensitive to strong cross-reflections and needs more expensive hardware.

How it works

The system is a monocular line laser scanner: a violet laser projects a stripe onto the dispensed adhesive, a CMOS camera images it, and a mobile robotic platform moves the specimen under the sensor. Camera calibration is automatic. A calibration board on a precision lifting platform is stepped through known heights; at each height the system records a laser stripe image and, with the laser off and a fixed light on, an image of the board. Merging the two gives world coordinates for the stripe centre points, and all camera parameters are then estimated together and refined by maximum likelihood with Levenberg–Marquardt iterations. This replaces the conventional two-stage calibration (at least 15 board poses, then a separate camera-to-laser step), in which errors from the first stage propagate to the second. Each scan then passes through the following steps.

  1. Complementary spectral background optimization (CSBO). The adhesive is dispensed onto a green-yellow substrate. Green-yellow is the complementary colour of violet, so the substrate absorbs the violet laser light that passes through the adhesive and suppresses the scattering and reflections it would otherwise cause, without ray-tracing models or extra equipment.
  2. Candidate centre points. Each stripe image is mean-filtered. In every pixel row, a gradient test with direction-consistency checks finds candidate regions where the gray level rises and then falls by at least a threshold K. A gray-level centre of gravity, weighted by w(I) = I / (256 − I), gives one sub-pixel candidate centre per region.
  3. Dynamic weighted multi-factor scoring (DWMF-SS). Each candidate in a row is scored on continuity (how many neighbouring-row points lie within an offset threshold), gray-level intensity, and closeness to the point kept in the previous row, with weights 0.1, 0.8 and 0.1. Candidates darker than 10% of the brightest candidate in the row or wider than 20 pixels score zero, and the highest-scoring candidate is kept.
  4. Clean centre line and depth map. A second screening pass after scoring removes anomalous jump regions shorter than a minimum continuity length, and gaps shorter than an interpolation threshold are filled by linear interpolation. The calibration parameters turn each centre line into world coordinates, and all profiles are projected into a depth map of the adhesive surface.
  5. Volume. A datum plane is fitted by principal component analysis to platform regions of interest, and a rigid-body transformation rectifies the depth map to it. Connectivity-based segmentation (3D Otsu thresholding, run-length encoding, eight-neighbourhood connectivity) isolates the adhesive. Each pixel is treated as a prism of base Δx × Δy and height z, and the volume is V = Δx·Δy·Σz.

Results

Stripe centre RMSD (root-mean-square deviation from the true centre line) of 0.0682 pixels on a calibration board, against 0.2657 for Steger, 1.0253 for the gray-level centre of gravity and 0.1518 for thinning (Table 2).
1.62% mean relative volume error on the green-yellow substrate, against 4.41% on black and 8.29–8.76% on purple, pink and blue substrates (Table 4, Fig. 22).
0.0053 s per image for centre extraction, 4.66 times faster than Steger and 3.17 times faster than thinning (Table 3).

For centre extraction, the methods were first compared on a stripe image with strong edge-diffusion noise from a metallic surface. Steger’s method picked up noise points near the stripe edges, the gray-level centre of gravity failed under the noise, and thinning extracted a skeleton through noise points, while the proposed method gave a continuous, smooth centre line that follows the stripe. Against the true centre line on a calibration board, its RMSD is 74%, 93% and 55% lower than that of Steger, gray-level centre of gravity and thinning. The weights 0.1, 0.8 and 0.1 were chosen by comparing six weight sets on the noisy image. The method is 1.13 times slower than the plain gray-level centre of gravity because it processes extra candidate points, which the authors consider fast enough for industrial real-time use. In their system, an FPGA implementation reaches up to 18 kHz (about 55.6 µs per frame).

For volume, similar linear beads were dispensed onto green-yellow, blue, pink, purple and black substrates. Each specimen was weighed on a precision electronic balance as ground truth, and the measured volume was converted to weight with a density of 0.0011 g/mm³. Each substrate had five replicates, each measured 20 times and averaged. The green-yellow substrate gave the lowest error, with replicate errors between 1.11% and 2.25%. On the other substrates, the depth maps show varying degrees of surface distortion caused by internal optical interference. Six more complex beads on the green-yellow substrate gave errors of 2.38%, 5.57% and 8.59% for curvilinear patterns and 2.17%, 5.56% and 5.17% for annular ones (Table 5). The larger errors come from surface data missing in the depth maps: when the bead is thick or complex, it blocks the camera’s line of sight to the regions behind it, an inherent limitation of line laser triangulation. The authors point to two scans from different viewpoints as the usual remedy, and plan to extend the system to complex backgrounds and to supplement single-scan data.

item.title: SFRF6D: Selective Fewer-Reference Fusion for 6D Pose Estimation
item.description:
The problem

6D pose estimation recovers an object’s 3D rotation and 3D translation, the information a robot needs for precise grasping and assembly. Most existing methods depend on a CAD model of the object or on a large collection of reference images. Model-based methods match image features to the CAD model, which limits them in real settings where no model exists. Model-free methods such as Gen6D, OnePose and FoundationPose instead build a multi-view representation from many reference images or a video, and their cross-view alignment becomes hard to keep stable under severe occlusion or large viewpoint changes. Methods that need only a few references lose much of their matching ability when the reference views barely overlap.

SFRF6D sets out to estimate the pose with no CAD model and only a few RGB-D reference images whose poses are known, while staying robust when the object is heavily occluded.

How it works

SFRF6D first rebuilds a rough 3D shape of the object from the reference images and aligns it coarsely with the query. It then renders reference views from that coarse pose and matches them with the query through attention that is steered by 3D geometry, so that visible regions count and occluded ones do not. Finally it refines the pose and chooses among pose hypotheses by rendering and comparing.

  1. A few references, one query. The input is a small set of RGB-D reference images with ground-truth poses (four in the main experiments) and an RGB-D query image. A query mask segments the object.

  2. Coarse 3D shape. The reference view whose viewpoint is closest to the query becomes the anchor; a ResNet18 extracts its features and its depth map gives an initial object point cloud. The other references are transformed into the same world frame with their camera intrinsics and known poses, filling in the shape, which is then normalised to the range [−1, 1].

  3. Coarse alignment. An oriented bounding box gives the object’s centre (the mean of its points) and its rotation (the principal axes from PCA of the point covariance). Because this is still rough, rotation and scale are tuned by maximising the overlap (IoU), which gives the coarse alignment.

  4. Geometry-guided sparse attention. Reference point clouds are rendered from the query’s coarse pose. Normalised direction vectors between reference and query points build a top-K mask for cross-attention, with Gumbel-Softmax used for soft top-K sampling; pairs that fail to match are masked out, so attention concentrates on visible, relevant regions. A multi-scale fusion module weighs global against local features.

  5. Refine and select. Refine: the object scale and pose are optimised jointly: the pose by rendering the shape and minimising its projection error against the anchor image, and the scale by sampling scales within a range and choosing by IoU against the reconstructed shape. The relative pose to the query is then computed.

    Select: each pose hypothesis is rendered and compared with the query to give a feature vector; a self-attention module scores all hypotheses together, and top-K filtering selects the final pose.

Results
