Mean ADD(-S) accuracy 83.2 % on LM, LMO and YCB-Video with four reference images and 0.9 s per object, against 75.8 % for FS6D + ICP, 70.1 % for LatentFusion (both with 16 references) and 76.5 % for Any6D (Table 1).
67.3 % on the heavily occluded LMO, against 58.6 %, 53.5 % and 57.9 % for the same three methods (Table 1).
On LMO, replacing the geometry-guided sparse attention with plain fully connected attention lowers accuracy to 64.5 % (Table 2).

The comparison uses three BOP benchmarks: LINEMOD (LM), Occlusion LINEMOD (LMO), where object visibility can drop below 40 %, and YCB-Video (YCBV). Accuracy is the ADD(-S) score at a threshold of 0.1 times the object diameter. Among the methods that do not use a CAD model, SFRF6D is the most accurate on all three datasets (92.1 %, 67.3 % and 90.2 %) and the fastest. FoundationPose, which uses the CAD model, remains more accurate, with a mean of 89.7 % at 1.0 s; the authors describe SFRF6D’s precision as slightly lower, in exchange for needing no CAD model and less computation.

The ablation on LMO (Table 2) separates the parts. Removing the view selector, which chooses among the rendered views, and using all of them keeps accuracy close (66.2 %) but raises the time from 0.94 s to 1.32 s. The number of references matters most at the low end: one reference gives 57.3 %, two give 63.4 %, four give 67.3 % and eight give 68.1 % at 1.03 s, so the authors settle on four as the balance between accuracy and cost. With a single reference the reconstructed shape depends heavily on that one view, and features cannot be aligned robustly when occlusion or the viewpoint difference is large. The authors list pretrained foundation models, dynamic multi-object scenes and lighter models for mobile and edge platforms as future work.

item.title: Surface Smoothing based on Discrete Orthogonal Polynomial
item.description:
The problem

Triangle meshes are a versatile way to represent 3D objects in reverse design, rapid prototyping, 3D printing and virtual simulation. Meshes obtained by 3D measurement, however, carry noise introduced during scanning and digitisation, and it has to be removed in pre-processing. The difficulty is to remove the noise while preserving geometric features such as sharp edges as much as possible.

Early smoothing methods are isotropic and cannot preserve such features: a simple, fast Laplacian smoothing, for example, also contracts the surface. Anisotropic methods do better. Many of them smooth the face normals first and then update the vertices; methods that classify features during denoising often look only at local neighbourhoods and are susceptible to noise, and sparse formulations such as L0-minimisation preserve features but lead to a non-convex, slow minimisation.

How it works

The method also smooths normals first and then moves the vertices, with two changes. A face’s normal is estimated not from a single face or its immediate neighbours but from non-local similar structures: groups of faces in a wider neighbourhood that share its orientation. These normals are then filtered by fitting them with orthogonal polynomials, whose different orders do not interfere with one another.

  1. Normal tensor of a local structure. A single noisy face normal may not be accurate enough. For each face, the faces within r rings of neighbours around it (its r-ring) vote into a normal tensor, weighted by their distance and by the angle between the normals; the eigenvector of the largest eigenvalue is the representative direction of that local structure.
  2. Co-aligned local structure. Faces whose normal deviates from this direction by more than a threshold angle θth are removed, which eliminates faces with large errors from the structure. The threshold is set larger for noisier models.
  3. Non-local similar structures. The search is widened to an R-ring (R > r). Every co-aligned structure in it whose angle to the current one is within θth (40° for high noise, 20° for low noise) is added to the face’s set of non-local similar structures.
  4. Orthogonal polynomial filtering. The face normals of these structures are stacked as rows of a matrix, which is reshaped to be close to square (an n × 3 matrix has rank at most 3, so the reshape makes the low-rank fit meaningful). Discrete Legendre polynomial bases are built in the X and Y directions on [−1, 1], and the matrix is fitted with them. Where structures overlap, each face’s estimates are accumulated and divided by how often the face was used, giving its updated normal.
  5. Vertex update. Each vertex is moved according to the updated normals of the faces around it, and the mesh is updated over several iterations.

Results

Cube (noise 0.2 lₑ, lₑ being the mean edge length): MSAE 0.075 × 10⁻² (mean square angular error of face normals), against 0.135 × 10⁻² for the next-best method, UNF, together with the lowest vertex error, Ev 1.224 × 10⁻³ (Table 2).
Fandisk (noise 0.4 lₑ): lowest vertex error, Ev 5.983 × 10⁻³, against 6.976 × 10⁻³ for GNF (Table 2).
Cad (noise 0.3 lₑ): lowest normal error, MSAE 0.640 × 10⁻², against 2.529 × 10⁻² for SNF (Table 2).

The method is compared with seven others: L0-minimisation, the Bilateral, Unilateral and Guided Normal Filters (BNF, UNF, GNF), the L1-median filter, the Half-kernel Laplacian Operator (HLO) and Segmentation-Driven Feature-Preserving filtering (SNF). Synthetic test meshes are made by adding zero-mean Gaussian noise whose standard deviation σn is proportional to the mean edge length lₑ. Two errors are measured against the ground truth: Ev, a vertex-based positional error, and MSAE, the mean square angular error of the face normals. The new method has the lowest value on both measures for Cube and on one of the two for Fandisk and Cad; L0-minimisation has the lowest MSAE on Fandisk and SNF the lowest Ev on Cad. On Octaflower, SNF has the lowest Ev and MSAE (L1 ties it on Ev), and the paper’s close-up views show the method preserving local features.

On a raw scan of the Angel model, the method lags slightly behind SNF but denoises and preserves features better than the other methods. On the same scanned Bunny with noise at three levels, it performs well at 0.1 and 0.3 but has certain limitations at 0.5. The authors note that, like other methods, it has limited robustness against excessive noise and irregular triangulation; as future work they suggest partitioning the mesh and fitting the orthogonal polynomials separately on feature parts (corners and edges) and non-feature parts.

item.title: Volume Measurement Technology of Dispensing Transparent Adhesives Based on Line Laser Scanning
item.description:
The problem

Pneumatic dispensers meter adhesive through air pressure and valve opening time, and fluctuations in air pressure make the amount they deposit uneven. Too much adhesive overflows; too little gives weak bonding or poor airtightness. Measuring the volume of each dispensed bead provides the data needed to calibrate the discharge. For transparent adhesives, though, traditional optical 3D measurement methods show large errors or fail to reconstruct the bead completely.

A line-laser scanner works by locating a bright laser stripe in a camera image. On a transparent bead, part of the laser light travels into the adhesive and through it. That transmitted light causes internal scattering and reflection interference, which degrades the 3D reconstruction.

How it works

The method works on two levels. On the optical side, complementary spectral background optimization (CSBO) suppresses the transmitted light through the colour of the substrate alone. On the algorithmic side, an improved stripe-centre extractor collects several candidate points per image row and scores them, so that noise does not end up on the centre line. Geometry analysis then turns the reconstructed surface into a volume.

  1. Absorb the transmitted light (CSBO). A material absorbs light of one colour and shows the complementary colour, and green-yellow is the complementary colour of violet. The 3D sensor uses a violet laser, so the adhesive is dispensed onto a green-yellow substrate. The substrate absorbs the laser light that passes through the bead, which suppresses scattering and specular reflection without extra measurement tools or equipment.
  2. Find candidate regions in each row. After mean filtering, each pixel row of a stripe image is searched for candidate regions: a region starts where the grey level rises by at least a threshold K and ends where it falls by at least K. One row can contain several regions.
  3. One candidate centre per region. Within each region, a grey-scale centre of gravity with the weight w(I) = I / (256 − I) gives a candidate centre point; the weight emphasises the brightest pixels.
  4. Score and select (DWMF-SC). The dynamic weighted multi-factor scoring constraints method scores each candidate as 0.5 × continuity (how many points in the neighbouring rows lie within an offset threshold) + 0.1 × intensity + 0.4 × history (closeness to the point chosen in the previous row). Candidates darker than 10% of the row’s brightest candidate, or from regions wider than 20 pixels, score zero. The highest-scoring candidate is kept, one point per row.
  5. From centre lines to volume. All centre lines are projected into a depth map. A plane fitted by principal component analysis (PCA) to randomly sampled platform regions defines the datum, and a rigid-body transformation levels the depth map. 3D Otsu thresholding and eight-neighbourhood connectivity analysis segment the adhesive. Each pixel of the adhesive region then counts as a prism with base Δx × Δy and height z, so V = Δx·Δy·Σz.

Results

Average relative volume error 1.39% on the green-yellow substrate (maximum 1.55%), while the same method gives 9.05%, 8.03% and 8.63% on blue, pink and purple substrates (Table II, Fig. 13).
Continuous, smooth stripe centre lines on an image with strong surface roughness and edge diffusion noise, where the Steger and thinning methods pick up noise points and the gray-scale center of gravity method fails (Fig. 11).

For the volume experiment, a precision dispensing nozzle laid similar straight beads of transparent adhesive onto four substrates (green-yellow, blue, pink and purple), and each specimen was weighed on a precision electronic balance to obtain the reference value. Each specimen was scanned in a workshop environment and measured five times; the predicted weight is the measured volume times the adhesive density, 0.0011 g/mm³. On the green-yellow substrate the five relative errors range from 1.32% to 1.55%; on the other three substrates they range from 8.01% to 9.16%. The authors conclude that CSBO improves the 3D reconstruction accuracy of transparent adhesives.

The centre-line experiment uses a stripe image of a metallic part, where surface roughness makes the stripe profile uneven and the metallic lustre adds edge diffusion noise. The Steger method expects a Gaussian stripe profile and extracts multiple centre points near the noisy edges; the gray-scale center of gravity method, computed over the whole column, fails under the noise; and the thinning method extracts part of its skeleton from noise points. The proposed method follows the shape of the stripe with continuous, smooth centre points, which the authors attribute to the candidate points mechanism and the DWMF-SC selection.

item.title: VeinTr: Robust end-to-end full-hand vein identification with transformer
item.description:
The problem

Hand vein identification recognises a person from the vein pattern of the hand, imaged under near-infrared light. Typical systems follow four steps: locate the hand, extract a region of interest (ROI), extract features from it, and match the result against a database of enrolled hands. Earlier work built hand-crafted geometric or statistical descriptors, which suffer under perturbations such as illumination changes and noise; more recent methods learn the features with convolutional neural networks.

Even the learned methods still work on an ROI, usually cut from the palm. That brings two drawbacks. The preprocessing is complex, and accuracy depends on how robustly the ROI is extracted, which is hard in real applications. And the crop throws information away: the vein pattern across the whole hand is unique to each person, so a representation built from only part of it is potentially inferior to one that uses the full pattern.

How it works

VeinTr skips ROI extraction and takes the full-hand image directly as input. Its identification has only two steps, feature extraction and probe-to-database matching. The feature extractor combines a convolutional local feature encoder, a lightweight transformer and an MLP-based global feature decoder, and the whole network is trained end to end as a metric-learning task.

  1. No ROI crop. Conventional pipelines locate the hand and crop a palm ROI before extracting features, so veins outside the crop are lost. VeinTr feeds in the whole hand image instead.
  2. Local features. Convolution blocks (convolution, batch normalisation, PReLU) reduce the size of the 256×256 input while extracting local features, and three residual blocks refine them into a 64×64×64 local feature map.
  3. Global aggregation with attention. The feature map is cut into 16 patches of 16×16, which are flattened and projected to a lower dimension. Three multi-head attention layers with 8 heads relate every patch to every other one, enlarging the receptive field from local to the whole hand.
  4. One feature per hand. The global feature decoder flattens the attention output and applies a two-layer MLP with batch normalisation, giving a 512-dimensional hand vein feature. Training uses the ArcFace loss, which pulls features of the same hand together and pushes different hands apart.
  5. Probe-to-database matching. The normalised features of the enrolled hands form a database matrix D. A probe hand is assigned to the identity C with the highest similarity score, C = argmax(D · ‖VeinTr(p)‖), where ‖·‖ denotes normalisation.

Results

Correct recognition rate 99.85 % at 850 nm and 99.92 % at 940 nm on CASIA, the highest in the paper’s comparison with six hand-crafted and six deep-learning methods (Table 1).
Equal error rate 0.10 % and 0.09 % (the point where false accepts equal false rejects), against 0.51 % for the best hand-crafted method (NMRT) and 3.71 % for PVSNet (Table 1).
Trained on CASIA, 98.17 % on TPV and 97.62 % on PLUSVein without retraining (Table 2).

All methods in the comparison work on a palm or finger ROI; VeinTr is the only one that uses the full hand. On CASIA, all hand-crafted methods already exceed 90 % correct recognition and the earlier method NAF is close to saturation at 99.83 % and 99.50 %, so VeinTr’s lead in recognition rate is small (0.02 and 0.42 points); in equal error rate it is 0.41 points below NMRT and 3.61 below PVSNet (Table 1). For inter-dataset tests, VeinTr is trained on one dataset and tested on all three. Models trained on CASIA or TPV stay above 90 % correct recognition on every test set. PLUSVein is much smaller (420 images of 42 volunteers), and the model trained on it generalises less well, reaching 89.76 % on CASIA and 81.43 % on TPV.

The ablation study (all models trained on CASIA) shows that both parts of the network matter. Without the attention layers, the correct recognition rate drops to 83.43 % on CASIA, 65.14 % on TPV and 55.10 % on PLUSVein; without the residual blocks, it drops to 95.12 %, 75.07 % and 83.67 % (Table 3). With three attention layers the rate saturates on CASIA and peaks on TPV and PLUSVein; a fourth and fifth layer lower it, which the authors attribute to overfitting. Three residual blocks are chosen as a trade-off between recognition rate and computational cost. As future work, the authors plan to fuse full-hand vein information with full-hand print data.

item.title: Segmentation-Driven Feature-Preserving Mesh Denoising
item.description:
The problem

Mesh denoising recovers a clean triangle mesh from one contaminated by noise, for use in tasks such as 3D modelling, computer animation and industrial design. The difficulty is to remove the noise while keeping the features that define the shape: edges, boundaries and corners.

Many denoising methods based on face normals handle features by giving small weights to anisotropic surfaces, where neighbouring faces point in clearly different directions, and large weights to isotropic surfaces, where they point the same way. Even with small weights, though, the faces on anisotropic surfaces still affect the denoising outcome. Other anisotropic methods struggle when the features are buried in severe noise, and methods built on low-rank matrices are slow. Earlier attempts to guide denoising with a segmentation either hardly preserve sharp features between regions, need the number of clusters tuned by hand, cluster an already filtered mesh, or remain unsatisfactory at high noise levels.

How it works

The method partitions the noisy mesh into regions bounded by its features and then denoises each region separately, so that a face is never filtered together with faces from another region. For meshes with high noise (σn ≥ 0.3 le, in units of the mean edge length), face orientations are so distorted, or even flipped, that direct segmentation becomes unreliable; the mesh is then first pre-filtered by a convex optimisation, segmented, and the regions are mapped back onto the original noisy mesh.

  1. Why weights are not enough. In a normal-based filter, faces across a sharp edge get small weights but still take part in the update, and they still affect the denoised result near the edge.
  2. Test every edge. For each edge shared by two faces, the cosine between their normals is compared with a global threshold Nthr (the mean cosine over all edges of the mesh), and the L2-norm of an area-based edge operator D(e), built from the four vertices of the two triangles, is compared with a user-set threshold Dthr. ‖D(e)‖2 is 0 for a flat pair of triangles and grows as the dihedral angle sharpens.
  3. Grow regions from seeds. A seed face passes its label to an edge-connected face if the normal cosine exceeds Nthr or ‖D(e)‖2 is below Dthr; newly labelled faces become seeds in turn. When growth stops, a new seed is picked at random among the unlabelled faces, until every face belongs to a region.
  4. Refine small clusters. Noise can leave small clusters behind. Clusters with fewer than 50 faces are dissolved: each of their faces takes the neighbouring label with the largest sum of normal cosines over its 2-ring neighbourhood.
  5. Denoise region by region. An existing filter, here BNF, UNF, GNF or L1, updates normals and vertices using only faces of the same region, with its own parameters unchanged. The only extra parameter is Dthr.

Results

Lowest vertex error Ev on all six synthetic test models among the compared methods, tied with plain L1 on Casting (Table 2).
Dodecahedron, σn = 0.4 le: Ev falls from 13.808 to 3.878 (×10⁻³) when the segmentation backbone is added to the existing denoiser BNF, and from 6.832 to 2.695 with GNF (Table 2).
Icosahedron, σn = 0.4 le: with BNF, MAE drops by 62.4 % (9.859° → 3.712°) and Ev by 72.0 % (Fig. 15).

The quantitative tests add zero-mean Gaussian noise, scaled to the mean edge length, to six models with known ground truth (Cube, Casting, Double torus, Dodecahedron, Icosahedron and Cad). They measure the mean angular error of the face normals (MAE, in degrees) and the vertex-based mesh-to-mesh error Ev. The comparison covers seven existing denoising methods (L0, BNF, UNF, GNF, L1, HLO and TGV; BNF, UNF and GNF are the bilateral, unilateral and guided normal filters, and L1 is the L1-median filter), and the four open-source methods BNF, UNF, GNF and L1 are also run inside the segmentation backbone with the same parameters as their original versions. Embedding the backbone lowers MAE in 23 of these 24 model–filter pairs and Ev in 22 of them. For MAE the results are competitive rather than always best: TGV has the lowest MAE on Casting and L0 on Double torus. The gains in feature preservation show most clearly on the CAD-like Cube, Dodecahedron and Icosahedron, where L0, BNF and TGV leave larger errors along the edges.

Visually, the backbone preserves features on both synthetic and scanned meshes. On synthetic models it recovers the sharp tip of the Octaflower while keeping its curved regions, and the features of Fandisk under severe noise (σn = 0.4 le). On raw scans, whose noise is not Gaussian, it keeps the feathers of the Angel and the hair and lips of Wilhelm. Among segmentation methods used to guide the same denoiser (K-means, VSA, SDF and the proposed one), the proposed segmentation gives the lowest overall Ev (Fig. 8). The backbone also makes UNF and GNF less sensitive to their parameters (Figs. 25–28), and the refinement step reduces pits and rough edges (Fig. 29). The authors note one limitation: on a mesh with extremely sparse and irregular triangulation, such as a gear model, the segmentation is reasonable but the denoised shape does not fully recover the original shape, especially at the edges (Fig. 30).

item.title: SemReg: Semantics-Constrained Point Cloud Registration
item.description:
The problem

Point cloud registration finds the rotation and translation that line up two partially overlapping 3D scans of the same scene, so that they can be merged into one. Recent learned methods describe every point by the shape around it, let the two scans exchange information through cross-attention, and then match points. Shape alone is often ambiguous, though: partial scans of a bed and a table can look geometrically alike. Cross-attention also lets every region of one scan interact with every region of the other, including pairs that are unlikely to overlap, such as a chair in one scan and a table in the other. These superfluous interactions lead to wrong matches.

Indoor scans captured with RGB-D cameras come with colour images, and semantic understanding is far more mature for 2D images than for 3D geometry. An earlier cross-modal method, PCR-CG, added image colour to the 3D features, but it uses only colour, not the semantic content of the images, and its features remain inconsistent.

How it works

SemReg is a 2D–3D cross-modal network. It keeps a standard 3D backbone for shape features and adds a semantic signal taken from the RGB frames, which it uses in three places: inside attention, at matching time, and in the training loss.

  1. Two scans with their colour frames. The input is a pair of partially overlapping point clouds, each with its RGB images. A KPConv backbone downsamples each cloud and extracts local shape features.
  2. Semantic features from the images. A pretrained DINOv2 network, kept frozen, extracts features from the RGB images. Using depth and the camera parameters, these are projected onto the 3D points and added to the shape features in self-attention.
  3. A semantic prior guides cross-attention. For each source point, SemReg finds the target points whose semantic features closely resemble its own and places a Gaussian over 3D distance around each one. The mixture of these Gaussians, the Gaussian Mixture Semantic Prior (GMSP), weights cross-attention so that features interact mainly between semantically similar regions.
  4. Matching within similar semantics. The Semantics Constrained Matching module sets the score of a candidate pair to zero when the semantic prior says the two points belong to unrelated regions. During training, a Semantics Aware Focal Loss supervises only pairs that are semantically related.
  5. Pose from the surviving matches. The final rotation and translation are estimated from the correspondences with RANSAC, and can be refined further with ICP.

Results

Registration recall 94.7 % on 3DMatch and 75.9 % on 3DLoMatch, the highest of all methods compared on both (Table 1).
95.4 % and 77.4 % after ICP refinement (Table 2).
Replacing all four semantic components (semantics constrained matching, semantics aware focal loss, semantic self-attention and GMSP-guided cross-attention) with standard counterparts drops recall to 92.1 % and 66.5 % (Table 3).

The evaluation uses 3DMatch, an indoor RGB-D benchmark, and its low-overlap split 3DLoMatch (scan pairs with 10–30 % overlap). Registration recall is the share of scan pairs whose estimated transformation is accurate to within 0.2 m (RMSE). SemReg leads on both splits, ahead of SIRA-PCR on 3DMatch and GeoTransformer on 3DLoMatch, and in the paper’s ICP-refinement comparison its margin over the next-best method grows to 1.5 and 2.9 points. The semantic components matter most when overlap is small: they account for 9.4 points of recall on 3DLoMatch, against 2.6 points on 3DMatch. In one extreme case with 12.53 % overlap, where the only shared object is a chair, the semantic prior still locates the chair in the target scan and the registration succeeds, while GeoTransformer fails.

SemReg matches at a coarse level, with 0.1K–1K correspondences per pair against 6K–7K for dense methods such as GeoTransformer. Its inlier ratio (the share of correspondences within 0.1 m under the ground-truth transformation) is therefore lower than that of some competitors, although its registration recall is higher. Results on the outdoor KITTI dataset are reported in the supplementary material. The method needs RGB images aligned with the scan, so it does not apply directly to standalone point clouds; the authors suggest rendering images from the point cloud as a future workaround.

item.title: Reconstruction of transparent objects using phase shifting profilometry based on diffusion models
item.description:
The problem

Phase shifting profilometry (PSP) projects a set of sinusoidal fringe patterns onto an object, recovers the phase from the captured intensities and turns it into 3D shape using the system calibration. Because it relies on the correct intensity of the captured fringes, it works well for objects with diffusely reflecting surfaces. On a transparent object such as glass, the projected fringes are reflected by the front and the back surface at the same time, and some light bounces several times between the two surfaces before reaching the camera. The captured pattern is then an aliased mixture of several fringe patterns, and the phase computed from it does not describe the surface being measured.

Earlier work on transparent objects falls into reflection-based methods (for example heating the surface with a laser and imaging it with an infrared camera, which is time-consuming), refraction-based methods that trace light through the object, and deep learning methods. This paper keeps a standard PSP set-up and instead removes the unwanted light from the fringe images themselves.

How it works

The authors model each captured fringe image as a sum of the front-surface pattern, the back-surface pattern, the multiple-reflection pattern and background light. They then train a conditional diffusion model to generate only the front-surface pattern from the aliased one, and pass the generated patterns to ordinary PSP.

  1. Three light paths. Fringes reach the camera after reflection from the front surface (F), a single reflection from the back surface (B), and multiple reflections between the two surfaces (M). F and B are normally the strongest components and M the weakest.
  2. A sum to undo. Each captured fringe image is S = F + B + M + A, where A is the background light. Only F, together with the background light, can be used to reconstruct the front surface, so a network p is trained to sample an estimate F* ∼ p(S; θ).
  3. Training. The front-surface pattern x0 is captured after spraying a developer onto the object, which gives clean front-surface fringes, together with the aliased pattern y of the same scene. Gaussian noise e is added to x0 in a forward diffusion process (T = 2600 steps, β rising linearly from 0.0001 to 0.002), and a U-Net with residual blocks, given the noisy pattern xt, the step t and the condition y, learns to predict the noise.
  4. Sampling. Starting from pure Gaussian noise, the trained network, conditioned on the captured aliased pattern y, estimates and removes noise one step at a time until t = 0, giving the front-surface pattern F*.
  5. Conventional PSP. The estimated patterns are processed with the 4-step PSP algorithm to obtain the wrapped phase and the 3D shape of the front surface.

Results

RMS reconstruction error 0.0420 mm for a transparent cube and 0.0423 mm for a transparent hemisphere (Table 1).
0.0437 mm for a translucent object and 0.0388 mm for a partially-transparent object (Table 1).

The set-up uses a 2048 × 1536 camera, a 1280 × 1024 DLP projector and 4-step PSP. The authors tried simulation and pasting cardboard stickers onto the surface to obtain clean front-surface fringes, but simulated images differed too much from real ones and stickers are hard to apply to non-planar objects, so the dataset was built by spraying a developer. For each object, 15,000 image pairs were used for training and 1500 for testing, with the objects placed at random positions and poses. The test objects are an acrylic transparent cube (25 mm side), a glass transparent hemisphere (20 mm radius), an acrylic translucent object and a glass partially-transparent object.

For each object, the estimated front-surface pattern is compared with the pattern captured after spraying the developer, in intensity, in wrapped phase and in the reconstructed shape. The intensities are not strictly identical, but the estimated patterns have the same characteristics, and the phase values in the object regions closely agree. The translucent object is a case where refraction-based methods do not work, because light cannot pass through the object to be refracted. Partially-transparent objects are hard for most existing methods because the transparent and the solid parts need different reconstruction algorithms; here, light that does not come from the front surface is simply treated as noise and removed by the diffusion model.

The authors note one limitation: because the generated patterns start from Gaussian noise, some residual noise, invisible in the images, remains and can reduce the accuracy of the phase and of the 3D reconstruction. Using more diffusion steps reduces it, but they found that this increases the computational cost of both training and sampling.

item.title: TopFormer: Topology-Aware Transformer for Point Cloud Registration
item.description:
The problem

Point cloud registration estimates the rotation and translation that align two partially overlapping scans. Most learned methods describe each point by its local geometry, match the descriptors, reject outliers with RANSAC and solve for the transformation. Recent Transformer-based methods work on a sparse, sub-sampled set of points and let every sparse point attend to all the others, and some add the points’ relative positions so that attention knows where each point sits.

Sub-sampling throws away fine-grained structure, though, and relative position does not help when two sparse points are close to each other in space but far apart along the surface. The paper’s example is the top of a chair next to the corner of a desk: the two points have similar local geometry because they lie in the same neighbourhood, and their relative position barely separates them because they are close in Cartesian space. Their features become ambiguous and lead to wrong matches. In the dense point cloud the difference is easy to see, since the route from one to the other along the surface is long; in the sparse points it is hard to observe.

How it works

TopFormer follows a coarse-to-fine registration pipeline and adds one ingredient: a topological structure encoding that tells the Transformer how each pair of sparse points is connected along the surface. Because the sparse points are a subset of the dense points, this surface information can be measured on the dense cloud and handed to the sparse points, which the authors call a sparse-through-dense strategy.

  1. Close in space, far along the surface. A KPConv encoder extracts local features at a sparse and a dense level. Two sparse points such as a chair top and a desk corner can look alike to it, and their relative position does little to separate them.
  2. Sparse points inside the dense graph. Down-sampling uses furthest point sampling, so every sparse point is also a dense point. On the dense points, TopFormer builds a K-nearest-neighbour graph, keeping only edges shorter than a radius τ.
  3. Geodesic distance by shortest path. For two sparse points p and q, Dijkstra’s algorithm on the dense graph gives the geodesic distance from p to q, the length of the shortest route along the surface.
  4. Direction from normals, independent of their sign. Normals estimated by PCA are unoriented, and scans can be in arbitrary poses, so the normals are hard to re-orient consistently. TopFormer therefore uses the sines of the angle between the normal at p and the vector from p to q, and of the angle between the two normals; flipping a normal turns an angle α into π − α and leaves the sine unchanged.
  5. Encoding inside attention, then matching. The geodesic distance, the Euclidean distance and the two sines are mapped by a sinusoidal function into the topological structure encoding, which is added to the keys of self-attention. Cross-attention then lets the two clouds exchange information; sparse points are matched from a confidence matrix, the matches are refined at the dense level with an optimal transport layer, and RANSAC estimates the final rotation and translation.

Results

Registration recall (share of scan pairs aligned to an RMSE below 0.2 m) of 92.4 % on 3DMatch and 75.1 % on 3DLoMatch with 5,000 correspondences, against 92.0 % and 75.0 % for GeoTransformer (Table 1).
On KITTI, 99.8 % registration recall with a relative translation error of 6.7 cm, the lowest in the comparison (Table 2).
Removing the topological structure encoding lowers recall to 89.7 % and 67.4 % on 3DMatch and 3DLoMatch (Table 3).

The indoor experiments use 3DMatch and its low-overlap split 3DLoMatch, which holds the scan pairs with 10–30 % overlap. Registration recall is the share of pairs whose estimated transformation has an RMSE below 0.2 m, computed with 50K RANSAC iterations. TopFormer’s registration recall is the highest, or tied for highest, at every correspondence number tested (5,000 down to 250) on both splits, and its feature matching recall on 3DMatch stays between 98.4 % and 98.7 %.

Its inlier ratio is below GeoTransformer’s at 5,000 correspondences (71.7 % against 71.9 % on 3DMatch, 37.2 % against 43.5 % on 3DLoMatch), but higher at smaller numbers, for example 82.8 % against 76.0 % on 3DMatch and 53.1 % against 46.2 % on 3DLoMatch at 1,000. On the outdoor KITTI odometry data, most of the compared methods already reach 99.8 % recall; TopFormer matches that, with a rotation error of 0.27°.

The ablation study shows that both parts of the encoding contribute. Without the geodesic distance, registration recall falls from 92.4 % to 90.3 % on 3DMatch and from 75.1 % to 72.3 % on 3DLoMatch; without the normal-based directional terms it falls to 91.9 % and 73.9 %. Dropping the encoding entirely, which leaves a vanilla Transformer, costs 2.7 and 7.7 points of recall, and the inlier ratio falls by 8.6 and 5.6 points.

item.title: A Point Cloud Contour Extraction Method based on Plane Segmentation
item.description:
The problem

Extracting contour features from point clouds is used in industrial inspection, robot operation and related fields. Point clouds from real devices contain noise and carry no topological relationships between points, which makes contours hard to detect. Plane detection has been approached with Hough transforms, region growing and iterative RANSAC; boundary extraction with triangular meshes, breakline sorting with B-spline fitting, and the alpha shape algorithm. Alpha shapes can extract the inner and outer contour points of polygons, but for point clouds with a large data volume its time complexity is high.

Plain RANSAC has a weak spot of its own: it tolerates obvious noise, but points just off the plane, such as those of an adjacent plane, fall within the distance threshold and introduce errors. The paper targets the contours of the surfaces of an object, here the contours of the chips on a circuit board.

How it works

The method has two stages. Plane segmentation fuses RANSAC with PCA to split the cloud into planar point sets. Contour extraction then turns each plane into a 2D image, finds its boundary from the image gradient, and maps the boundary points back into 3D space.

  1. RANSAC proposes planes. Three far-apart points are drawn at random and a plane is fitted through them; points within a distance threshold dth of the plane join its set. After Niterate iterations the largest set is kept as the current plane and removed from the cloud, and the search repeats until fewer than Nminnum points remain.
  2. PCA refines and cleans the planes. Each set is refitted by PCA: the plane passes through the centroid, and its normal is the eigenvector of the covariance matrix with the smallest eigenvalue. Two planes whose normals differ by less than 15° are merged if more than 90% of their points lie within dth of the other plane; plane pairs with too few points are removed. This repeats until no plane can be merged or removed.
  3. Flatten each plane into an image. A rotation matrix turns the planar point cloud parallel to the XOY plane, and a projection with focal lengths and offsets maps it into a 2D image. Pixels holding object points are set to 0, all others to 1.
  4. Find the boundary from gradients. The image is smoothed with a Gaussian filter, and the gradient magnitude and direction are computed. A preliminary edge pixel is kept as a boundary point only if its value is the largest among its neighbours along the gradient direction.
  5. Map back to 3D. The boundary pixels are transformed back through the projection and the inverse rotation, giving the contour points in 3D space.

Results

Contour of one chip in 64.614 ms, against 745.253 ms for alpha shapes, on the same 62,668-point cloud (Table 1).
919 boundary points (a denser, continuous outline) found by the proposed method, against 514 for alpha shapes (a sparse, broken outline) (Table 1).

The experiments extract the contours of the chips on a circuit board, running on an Intel i7-12700 CPU with 16 GB of memory. For plane segmentation, the method is compared with region growing and conventional RANSAC on the same data. On the chip shown below, region growing also takes in a neighbouring region and RANSAC a strip attached below the chip, whereas PCA-RANSAC returns the chip surface alone; the paper describes its result as the one least affected by noise.

For boundary extraction the method is compared with the alpha shape algorithm. On a single chip, alpha shapes returns a sparse, broken outline, while the proposed method returns a denser, continuous one in less time.

item.title: Gap measurement method based on projection lines and convex analysis of 3D point clouds
item.description:
The problem

The gap between the lower surface of a relay and the ground (the base the relay stands on) is a critical factor in relay quality: it affects the relay’s conductivity and reliability, and for a qualified relay it must be less than 0.07 mm in the working state. Common displacement sensors each have drawbacks: eddy-current sensors must be customised to the measured part and are relatively costly, inductive sensors are disturbed by temperature, humidity and electromagnetic interference, capacitive sensors need a high-voltage supply and have large nonlinear error, and photoelectric sensors cope poorly with ambient light.

Optical measurement avoids contact, but each kind has a limit. Two earlier vision methods for measuring levitation gaps, Pixel Area and SelfConvNet, trade speed against accuracy: Pixel Area is fast but less accurate, SelfConvNet more accurate but slow. 2D methods also lose depth, including in occluded areas, which limits their accuracy. 3D point clouds keep that information, but their disorder and sparsity make the measurement time-consuming. On top of this, metal surfaces are prone to defects such as pits and burrs because of the limits of machining.

How it works

The method combines two measurement models. A 2D projection-line model measures the gap from a backlit image of it; a 3D surface point-cloud model locates the support surface between the relay and the ground and measures the gap against it. In inspection, the fast 2D model runs first and the 3D model checks the relays that pass.

  1. Backlit projection image. A highly directional backlight shines through the gap; it suppresses the diffraction of the illuminating light so that the edges image clearly. The camera sees the relay’s lower edge l0 and the base edge l1 as two clear straight lines with a bright gap between them.
  2. Projection lines. After guided filtering, which smooths noise while preserving edges, vertical search lines cross the region of interest, and on each line the two points with the largest Sobel gradient mark the edges. A line-deviation index discards points that differ from both neighbours by more than a threshold, which removes the noise points caused by burrs. Least-squares lines are fitted to the remaining points, and the pixel distance d between them is converted to millimetres with D = k·d, where the coefficient k is averaged over measurements of known gaps.
  3. Point-cloud clean-up. A line-laser profiler captures the relay’s lower surface as a 3D point cloud. A point is treated as an outlier when too many of its neighbours lie farther than a distance threshold. Connected-component segmentation then splits the surface into separate regions.
  4. Convex hull and centroid. Fitting a surface to the point cloud is complex, and its efficiency and accuracy are hard to guarantee together. Instead, the method builds the convex hull of the surface points with a fast convex-hull algorithm and computes the relay’s centroid, weighting each material part by its density. An object comes to rest when the resultant force and moment on it are zero, so the hull face that the centroid, projected along gravity, falls on is the support surface. The gap is the vertical distance from the points of the lower surface to this plane.
  5. Two-stage inspection. The projection-line model is the coarse stage and screens every relay. Relays that pass go to the point-cloud model, the fine stage, for a second measurement.

Results

Combined 2D + 3D model: average error 0.0054 mm, maximum error 0.009 mm on gaps of 0–0.1 mm, the lowest of the five models compared (Pixel Area, SelfConvNet, projection-line, point-cloud and combined; Fig. 17).
Misjudgement (false-drop) rate 0.05% at 182.4 ms per relay for the combined model on 11,931 relays, against 2% at 236.8 ms for the point-cloud model alone and 5% at 19.8 ms for the projection-line model alone (Table 2).
Average error 0.0087 mm for the point-cloud model and 0.016 mm for the projection-line model (Fig. 17).

The experiments use a 4000 × 3000 camera with a highly directional backlight for the 2D images and an OPT-LPE50 3D laser profiler for the point clouds. The models are compared with Pixel Area and SelfConvNet. For accuracy, gaps from 0 to 0.1 mm at equal steps were set on a single relay. Pixel Area had the largest errors (maximum 0.047 mm, average 0.038 mm), followed by the projection-line model (0.021 and 0.016 mm), SelfConvNet (0.02 and 0.0095 mm) and the point-cloud model (0.015 and 0.0087 mm). In the linearity test, the point-cloud model followed the true gap more closely than Pixel Area and SelfConvNet, and the combined model was the most linear.

In the factory inspection test, 11,931 relays were measured, 9,247 good and 2,684 defective. The projection-line model was both more accurate and faster than Pixel Area (6.6%, 48.5 ms), and the point-cloud model beat SelfConvNet (2.6%, 510 ms) on both counts. The combined model had the lowest false-drop rate (the share of relays misjudged) and was faster than both the point-cloud model and SelfConvNet, meeting the requirements of real-time on-site inspection. Manual inspection of mis-detected relays showed surface defects of varying degree, particularly pits and burrs. At a pit, edge occlusion makes the projection image show the lower surface at line b rather than at the pit bottom, line a, so Pixel Area, SelfConvNet and the projection-line model, which all work from projection images, lose accuracy there. The point-cloud model measures the distance between the entire surface and the support surface, which makes it less susceptible to pits. The authors sum up the trade-off: 2D methods are simple and fast but limited by the missing dimension and more prone to errors from surface defects, while 3D methods are more accurate and reliable at the cost of longer processing time.

item.title: Generative deep-learning-embedded asynchronous structured light for three-dimensional imaging
item.description:
The problem

Structured light measures 3D shape by projecting a sequence of stripe images, called fringe patterns, onto an object and photographing them from a second viewpoint. The surface bends the stripes, and the stripe phase at each pixel encodes depth. In fringe projection profilometry (FPP), one of the most popular forms of the technique, the camera must capture each pattern while it alone is on screen. That requires synchronisation between projector and camera, usually a hardware trigger signal.

Synchronisation is a practical burden. Hardware trigger circuits are found in expensive industrial equipment, while affordable consumer devices often have no interface for them, even though the cameras in smartphones, tablets and laptops now offer high resolution and frame rates. Software synchronisation waits longer than the exposure time between patterns, which lowers the frame rate and does not always work stably. Signal wires also limit how far apart camera and projector can be and are susceptible to electromagnetic interference. If projector and camera simply run independently, though, the projector can switch patterns in the middle of an exposure, and the photo records a blend of two neighbouring patterns: an aliased fringe pattern (AFP). Computing phase directly from such images leads to reconstruction errors. Earlier work on unsynchronised structured light used simple binary (black-and-white) patterns or addressed other aspects of asynchrony; to the authors’ knowledge, asynchronous capture with the widely used sinusoidal fringes had not been studied.

How it works

The mixing itself has a simple form. Each pixel of an AFP adds up what the two patterns contributed during the exposure, and the split depends on the moment the projector switched (Eq. 5 of the paper). The mixing does not move pixels; it is the same at every location, a property that suits a convolutional network. The switching moment, however, is unknown and very difficult to measure, so recovering two images from one is an ill-posed, one-to-many problem. The paper treats it as image generation: a generative network learns to produce the two clean patterns, and standard phase-shifting reconstruction then applies unchanged.

  1. Synchronised capture (the reference). Each exposure sees exactly one projected pattern, so each photo holds one clean pattern.
  2. Asynchronous capture. Projector and camera each run at their own constant speed, with the camera faster so that every pattern is captured. A pattern switch inside an exposure produces an AFP that integrates the two neighbouring patterns. The paper addresses mixes of two patterns.
  3. Separation with APSNet. APSNet (aliased fringe pattern separation network) is an encoder–decoder based on U-Net: four encoding blocks with max pooling, then a decoder that upsamples with skip connections back to full resolution. It maps one AFP to the two patterns it was mixed from. It is trained as the generator of a conditional generative adversarial network (GAN): a discriminator judges generated pattern pairs against real ones, and two further loss terms, mean-squared error and structural similarity, keep the generated patterns statistically close to the projected ones. Equal weights for the adversarial, mean-squared-error and structural-similarity terms gave the smoothest training (Fig. 8).
  4. Phase. Each AFP mixes two neighbouring patterns, so three consecutive AFPs, which share a pattern with their neighbours, give four successive patterns, each shifted by a quarter period. The well-established four-step phase-shifting algorithm computes the wrapped phase, and adding the fringe order (multiples of 2π) unwraps it into a continuous phase map.
  5. 3D shape. The continuous phase is converted into the object’s 3D shape with an established FPP reconstruction model.

The training data come from a real system: an industrial camera (2048 × 1536 pixels), a DLP projector (1280 × 1024) and a self-developed microcontroller that delays the camera by a set time Δt after the projector. With Δt = 0 the system captures ordinary, non-aliased fringes. The source patterns were five sets of 256 × 256 sinusoidal fringes with 50 to 90 periods, each in four phase shifts (0, 0.5π, π, 1.5π), captured with delays from 1 to 10 ms in 1 ms steps. This gave 1500 AFPs, each paired with its two source patterns: 1125 for training and 375 for testing.

Results

Within 0.008 mm of the synchronised reconstruction along a depth profile of a statue, with a standard deviation of 0.003 mm. Depth computed directly from the AFPs is off by −5.000 to 3.600 mm, with a standard deviation of 1.713 mm (Fig. 13).
Wrapped phase within 0.035 rad of the synchronised phase along a sampled line (Fig. 11).
Absolute error below 0.006 mm on a propeller and a 3D-printed bolt, objects with large-curvature surfaces absent from the earlier tests (standard deviations 0.002 and 0.001 mm; Fig. 16).

The test objects, including statues, a car model and a sphere, were not seen by the network during training or validation. Every comparison treats the reconstruction from synchronised patterns as the benchmark. Reconstructing directly from the AFPs loses much of the shape, while the shape from APSNet’s patterns is remarkably close to the benchmark (Fig. 12). In the paper’s summary, this improves reconstruction accuracy by three orders of magnitude over using the aliased fringes directly.

The network was trained only on sinusoidal patterns, yet it also separated aliased binary patterns projected onto a sphere, a car model and a statue, without further tuning (Fig. 14). It also handled a multi-object scene of a propeller prototype, a 3D-printed bolt and a statue, with different colours and reflective materials (Fig. 15). The method assumes that each photo mixes two patterns. If the projector runs much faster than the camera, more than two patterns fall within one exposure; the authors name this more complex aliasing as a limitation and a direction for further work.

item.title: WTAYOLO: A Detection Model for Weak Scratches on Metal Surfaces
item.description:
The problem

Scratches on lithium-battery surfaces affect the batteries’ electrochemical performance and safety in operation, so they must be found during quality control. On highly reflective metal this is hard. The aluminium alloy reflects light strongly and is very sensitive to lighting, while shallow scratches have little depth, blurred contours and minimal contrast with the surrounding surface. Scratches are also randomly placed and irregularly shaped, and many look much like the surface itself.

Photometric stereo, which images the surface under light from several directions, gives detailed surface topography without complex laser equipment, so it suits fine scratches on reflective metal. On the algorithm side, U-Net-style networks are widely used for defect segmentation, and YOLO networks are fast and accurate. According to the authors, few studies have applied YOLO segmentation to metal scratches, and balancing accuracy, model size and real-time performance remains difficult. This paper builds a scratch segmentation model, WTAYOLO, on the YOLOv11n baseline and feeds it photometric stereo images.

How it works

WTAYOLO keeps the structure of YOLOv11n and replaces its C3K2 modules with C3K2-WTAConv. Inside each bottleneck, a new convolution, WTAConv, combines wavelet-transform convolution (WTConv) with the CBAM attention module.

  1. Photometric stereo images. The metal surface is imaged by a photometric stereo system, which reduces interference from surface reflections and brings out the scratches.
  2. Wavelet convolution for a large receptive field. WTConv splits its input with a 2D Haar wavelet transform into a low-frequency and three high-frequency components, applies small convolution kernels to each, and reconstructs the output with the inverse transform. Repeated over two levels, this gives a large receptive field while the parameters grow only logarithmically, avoiding the cost of large kernels.
  3. Channel and spatial attention (CBAM). The output of the wavelet convolution passes through CBAM. Channel attention pools the feature map globally (average and max), passes both descriptors through a shared MLP and weights each channel; spatial attention pools along the channel axis, applies a 7×7 convolution and weights each location. This strengthens important features and suppresses background.
  4. Segmentation. The modified backbone and neck feed YOLOv11’s segmentation head, which outputs scratch masks.

Results

mAP50 of 0.868, the highest of the compared methods: 5.1 points above the YOLOv11n baseline (0.817), and above YOLOv8n (0.799), YOLOv5n (0.74), U-Net (0.582) and Otsu thresholding (0.289) (Table 2).
Parameters do not grow: 2.727 M against 2.834 M for YOLOv11n, at 10.1 GFLOPs against 10.2 (Table 3).
Both parts help: wavelet convolution alone raises mAP50 to 0.854; adding the attention raises it to 0.868 (Table 2).

The test rig is a photometric stereo system built from an OPT camera (IMX183 sensor, 5472×3648), a 35 mm OPT lens and an OPT ring light (Table 1). With it the authors captured 566 images of scratched metal sheets at 1200×1200 pixels, annotated at pixel level by experts, and split them into 510 training and 56 validation images. All models were trained with the same parameters.

The comparison covers Otsu thresholding, U-Net, YOLOv5n, YOLOv8n and YOLOv11n. In the authors’ examples, Otsu fails to suppress background noise, so the scratches are obscured; U-Net partly overcomes the background but misses low-contrast scratches, leaving incomplete results; the YOLO networks suppress the background and use multi-scale information, and WTAYOLO segments the weak scratches best. WTAYOLO also has the highest precision (0.942) and recall (0.736).

On size, WTAYOLO has 16.3% fewer parameters than YOLOv8n (3.258 M) and 3.8% fewer than YOLOv11n. Adding the attention costs only 0.003 M parameters. By comparison, the larger YOLOv11s reaches 0.841 mAP50 with 10.067 M parameters and 35.3 GFLOPs. The extra modules do cost time: WTAYOLO needs 20.9 ms per image against 14.5 ms for YOLOv11n (Table 3). The authors judge that this still meets the time constraints of industrial inspection, and name optimising the algorithm for real-time detection as future work.

item.title: Kinematic target surface sensing based on improved deep optical flow tracking
item.description:
The problem

Phase-shifting profilometry (PSP) measures 3D shape with one projector and one camera. The projector casts at least three phase-shifted sinusoidal fringe patterns onto the object, the camera records how the object’s height distorts them, and the phase recovered from the set of images gives the surface. Because several images are combined, the influence of ambient light and surface reflectivity is removed, which gives PSP high accuracy and robustness. However, PSP requires the object to stay still while the fringe images are captured: if it moves between captures, the images no longer line up and the phase calculation picks up errors.

If the object’s movement is known, as a rotation matrix and translation vector, the motion can be built into the phase calculation and the error removed. The difficulty is measuring that movement from images covered in fringes. Earlier work tracked markers placed on the object, and later work used SIFT features. The periodic fringes are “noise” to SIFT and cause mismatches, so the SIFT-based methods project the fringes in one colour channel of a colour camera and filter that channel out first, which needs colour equipment with a higher cost and lower frame rate than monochrome cameras. Another method tracks the object in the fringe images directly, but it is limited to 2D translation and cannot follow a rotating object.

How it works

The method tracks the object in the fringe images themselves, with an affordable monochrome camera, and handles any 2D movement, rotation included. A modified RAFT optical-flow network estimates where every object pixel has moved, a selection step keeps only the accurate estimates, and the resulting motion is fed into the phase calculation.

  1. Motion breaks PSP. The fringes stay fixed while the object rotates and translates between captures, so each pixel sees a different part of the surface in each image. The paper models this by evaluating the reference phase at the moved coordinates in every fringe image.
  2. Correlation by NCC instead of dot product. A feature encoder maps two consecutive fringe images to feature maps at 1/8 resolution, and a context encoder processes the first image. The original RAFT compares all pairs of features by a dot product; under fringe illumination the light intensity around a feature point changes as it moves through the fringes. The improved network uses normalised cross-correlation (NCC), which normalises local lighting variations, to build the 4D correlation volume and a four-level correlation pyramid.
  3. Iterative flow updates. Starting from zero flow, a GRU-based update operator looks up the correlation pyramid and refines the flow over several iterations. The 1/8-resolution result is upsampled to full resolution, giving a displacement for every pixel.
  4. Keep only accurate points. RANSAC first removes obvious outliers. Then a rotation matrix and translation vector are fitted, each point is moved by them, and points that land more than a threshold (such as 0.5 pixel) from their tracked position are discarded. The fit and the check are repeated until every remaining point meets the threshold.
  5. Reconstruct with the motion. The final rotation matrix and translation vector describe the object motion, and the correct phase of the moving object is computed from them, giving its surface.

Results

RMS error 0.082–0.098 mm across five moving objects, against the reconstruction of each object when static (Table 1).
Comparable to the SIFT-based method (0.078–0.089 mm), which relies on a colour camera to separate the fringes (Table 1).
Only the points with accurate optical flow (about 12 thousand) are used to fit the motion (Section 3).

The system uses a 1280 × 720 projector and a camera of the same resolution, with 4-step PSP. For training, 2000 pairs of fringe images before and after movement were captured and split 8:1:1 into training, validation and test sets. Labels came from images without fringes taken at the same positions, where SIFT gives the rotation and translation, from which each pixel’s motion is derived. The training loss converged to 0.25 pixels after 900 epochs. Counting a point as correct when its estimated displacement is within half a pixel of the SIFT-based ground truth, the NCC-enhanced network yields more correct points on the fringe images than the original RAFT (Fig. 10).

The same trained network was applied to four further objects (Fig. 13), and each was reconstructed while moving. The RMS errors of the proposed method are slightly above those of the SIFT-based method for every object, which the authors describe as comparable, while removing the need for colour equipment. The method covers movement in a 2D plane; reconstructing objects with complex 3D movement is left to future work.

item.title: Deep learning-enabled 3D multimodal fusion of cone-beam CT and intraoral mesh scans for clinically applicable tooth-bone reconstruction
item.description:
The problem

Orthodontic treatment and implant surgery are planned on 3D models of the teeth and the bone that holds them. Two kinds of scan feed these models, and each sees only part of the picture. Cone-beam CT (CBCT) is an X-ray scan that shows whole teeth, crowns and roots, inside the jaw bone. But CBCT measurements can be up to 6.9% smaller than the real objects, depending on resolution, and CBCT often fails to capture the biting surfaces accurately because of dense enamel, dental restorations, implants and orthodontic appliances. An intraoral scanner (IOS) projects light onto the teeth and records a digital impression as a surface mesh. Its measurements shrink by as little as 0.9%, making it the most accurate of the 3D digital modalities, and it captures the bite and tooth positions well, but it shows only the crowns and gums, nothing below the gum line.

Combining the two gives what clinicians need: precise crowns on the correct roots, inside the surrounding bone. Doing this by hand is slow. Both scans must first be segmented, which is hard because anatomy varies from patient to patient. The CBCT usually shows the upper and lower jaws together, often in a bite where teeth touch, while the IOS records each jaw separately. Experienced experts need at least five hours per patient, even with interactive software and semi-automatic tools, and a fully automatic, clinically applicable solution had yet to be developed.

How it works

Deep Dental Multimodal Fusion (DDMF) is an automatic pipeline with three modules: segment the CBCT, segment the intraoral scan, then fuse the two. The fused model takes the crowns from the IOS and the roots and bone from the CBCT.

  1. Segment the CBCT. TSTNet, a network built on the Swin Transformer, labels every pixel of each 2D CBCT slice as tooth, alveolar bone or background, and 3D meshes of the teeth and bone are reconstructed from the result. Training needs labels on only about 20 of the 300–600 slices in a scan. An extra training head, tooth error calibration (TEC), corrects error-prone pixels at the tooth–bone boundary; it is removed at inference, so it adds no inference time.
  2. Segment the intraoral scan. IOSNet labels each face of the IOS mesh as gum or as one of 32 teeth, numbered in the FDI system. Two new training losses help: a centroid loss keeps the predicted centre of each tooth in place, so that two teeth are not recognised as one (or one as two), and a boundary loss sharpens tooth–tooth and tooth–gum borders. The gum is then separated, leaving numbered crowns.
  3. Split the jaws in the CBCT. A point-curvature feature, the average angle between a vertex’s surface normal and those of its neighbours, marks the boundaries where teeth meet. Removing the highest-curvature vertices separates the individual teeth; the removed vertices are merged back, and the teeth are grouped into upper and lower jaws.
  4. Register. The IOS crowns of each jaw are aligned with the matching CBCT jaw in two stages: a global registration (RANSAC on FPFH features) gives a rough initial alignment, and point-to-plane ICP at three scales refines it.
  5. Replace the crowns and fuse. CBCT crown points that lie close to the IOS crown are removed and replaced with the IOS points, and Poisson reconstruction turns the merged points into one mesh. The FDI tooth numbers come from the IOS, so the fused teeth are identified individually without instance-level annotation of the CBCT slices.

Results

Average surface distance of 0.17 mm between the fused models and expert-made ground truth, over 1,003 teeth in 50 cases (Chamfer distance 0.20 mm, Hausdorff distance 0.37 mm; Table 3).
20–25 minutes per patient, against 300–400 minutes for human experts (Table 6).
94% of CBCT meshes split correctly into upper and lower jaws, against 42% for a Gaussian-curvature method and 24% for DBSCAN, on 50 patients, 31 of them in a closed bite with tight contacts (Table 5).

The study used a large real-world dataset: 503 patients with both CBCT and intraoral scans, plus 28,559 further intraoral scans, collected from hospitals and clinics in 25 provinces of China from 2018 to 2021. The ground-truth fused models were made by a committee of human experts and had been used successfully in clinical practice. The errors were small and consistent across tooth types; the first and second molars showed slightly larger errors, mainly because they are larger. Since CBCT resolution ranged from 0.125 to 0.5 mm, an error of one to two pixels is acceptable for many clinical applications, as validated by human experts and a clinical applicability test. On 20 cases, DDMF also had lower errors than reconstruction from CBCT alone (Fig. 4C–E). The paper reports no other fusion baseline, as no systematic solution existed for this task.

Each segmentation module outperformed the compared networks. TSTNet reached a Dice coefficient of 93.99% in 5-fold cross-validation, with 50 test patients per fold, ahead of UNet, UNet++, the standard Swin Transformer and the other baselines (Table 1). IOSNet (trained on 28,000 scans) reached a mean intersection over union (mIoU) of 93.70% on lower-jaw scans and 95.70% on upper-jaw scans, 1.77 and 3.52 points above DCNet, the strongest baseline (Table 2).

The framework has been integrated into clinical software that assists orthodontic treatment planning. The authors also name its limits. The jaw splitting and registration steps may fail in 6–10% of cases, which then need manual correction, and segmentation may still be error-prone in extremely complicated cases, such as patients with metal artefacts or root canal therapy. The method has been evaluated mainly from an algorithmic perspective, and the authors call for rigorous multicentre clinical trials.

item.title: Weighted Point Cloud Normal Estimation
item.description:
The problem

Raw point clouds from scanners carry no normals and are often corrupted by noise, yet accurate normals help downstream tasks such as noise filtering and surface reconstruction. The classic approach, PCA, computes each point’s normal from the covariance of its neighbours; it is simple but tends to blur details and is fragile on noisy data. Learning-based regressors such as PCPNet and Nesti-Net are more robust to noise, but they ignore that neighbouring points contribute differently to the central point’s normal, which can make them inaccurate on complex surfaces. Surface-fitting methods such as DeepFit and AdaFit adapt well to complicated geometry but become less robust under severe noise.

How it works

The method regresses the normal of each point from a local patch around it, and it learns to weight the points of that patch by how relevant they are to the central point. Training has two stages: a contrastive pre-training stage that teaches the point encoder and weight regressor to relate patches to normals, and a normal estimation stage that fine-tunes them together with a normal regressor.

  1. A local patch. For each point, the patch contains its N nearest neighbours (N = 700 in the experiments). The patch is normalised to a unit sphere and aligned with a rotation R computed by PCA on the patch.
  2. Uniform weights fall short. Regressing the normal with every point weighted equally lets less relevant neighbours pull the estimate away from the true normal.
  3. Learned point weights. A point encoder built from DGCNN’s EdgeConv layers produces per-point features, and an MLP weight regressor predicts a weight for each point. The training target is the squared cosine between the central point’s ground-truth normal and each neighbour’s ground-truth normal, so points with similar normals count as more relevant. The weights multiply the features element-wise, F′ = W ⊙ F.
  4. Contrastive pre-training. A second branch encodes the central point’s ground-truth normal with MLPs. Both features pass through projection heads, and a temperature-scaled cross-entropy loss pulls each patch–normal pair together while pushing apart the other pairs in the batch. The weight loss is added to this loss.
  5. Weighted normal regression. The pre-trained encoder and weight regressor are fine-tuned with a normal regressor of fully connected layers, trained with a cosine loss plus the weight loss. The predicted normal is normalised and rotated back with R⁻¹.

Results

Average normal-angle RMSE 17.42° over the four noise levels of the PCPNet shapes with Gaussian noise, the lowest of all compared methods (AdaFit 17.66°, DeepFit 18.14°, best PCA setting 20.23°) (Table I).
Lowest error at the 0.60 %, 0.84 % and 1.20 % noise levels (noise as a share of the bounding-box diagonal), e.g. 21.48° vs 21.94° for AdaFit at 1.20 % (Table I).
On the PCPNet validation set, the full pipeline reaches 14.46°, against 21.15° for the baseline trained with the cosine loss alone (Table II).

The synthetic test set contains 19 PCPNet shapes, each with four Gaussian noise levels (0.36 %, 0.6 %, 0.84 % and 1.2 % of the bounding-box diagonal); the method is compared with PCA, the surface-fitting methods DI (Deep Iterative), DeepFit and AdaFit, and the regression methods PCPNet and Nesti-Net. At the lowest noise level DeepFit is slightly ahead (13.18° vs 13.25°); the method’s advantage appears as the noise grows. The ablation shows that both ideas matter: without the weight regression the error is 14.70°, and without the contrastive pre-training it is 18.21°.

On raw scans from the Kinect Fusion dataset, compared against the clean normals the dataset provides, the method has lower error than AdaFit and Nesti-Net on the three shapes shown. On the Paris-rue-Madame street scans, where no ground truth exists, its normals are tidier on complex areas such as a window lattice while keeping features such as a building eave and a car light. Used as input to point cloud filtering, its normals give the best filtering result by Chamfer distance, and in Poisson reconstruction of a sharp Star shape they give a more accurate tip.

item.title: 3D reconstruction of moving object by double sampling based on phase shifting profilometry
item.description:
The problem

Phase-shifting profilometry (PSP) is one of the most commonly used 3D measurement techniques, valued for its high precision, robustness and full-field measurement. A projector casts at least three phase-shifted sinusoidal fringe patterns onto the object, and a camera views them from another angle. The object’s height distorts the fringes, and the 3D shape is computed from the phase of the deformed fringes and the system parameters. Because several images are needed, traditional PSP requires the object to stay static during reconstruction. Once it moves during fringe projection and capture, errors are introduced.

Earlier work tracks the object’s motion and compensates the resulting error, estimates the motion between the 3D data of adjacent frames, or uses a high-speed imaging system with shifted Gray code. One approach that estimates motion from the object’s start and end states is limited to uniform motion, and deep-learning methods that recover phase from a single fringe pattern need time-consuming network training and are hard to run in real time. The authors therefore look for a motion-error compensation method suited to real-time phase-shift measurement.

How it works

The method changes how the images are captured and how the phase is computed. The camera is triggered twice during every projected fringe pattern, so two images taken under the same fringe differ only by the object’s motion. With the motion known from tracking, a least-squares model recovers the object’s phase from three consecutive images, and overlapping groups of three images give one phase map each.

  1. Two shots per fringe. A trigger control device is added to the camera and projector. The projector projects N fringe images at a set rate and triggers the camera twice in each projection cycle: I11 and I12 are captured while fringe I1 is projected, I21 and I22 while I2 is projected, and so on.
  2. Separate motion from phase shift. Two images taken under the same projected fringe, such as I11 and I12, have no PSP phase shift between them (δ1 = 0), so they differ only by the object’s motion. Images taken under different fringes also carry the PSP phase shift δ2 = 2π/N. The three images I11, I12 and I21 are therefore analysed together.
  3. Track the motion. The rotation matrix and translation vector describing the object’s motion are obtained by tracking the object. From them follows the coordinate transformation (fn, gn) that relates each point’s position before and after the motion.
  4. Solve for the phase by least squares. Each of the three images is written as A + B cos(ϕ + δk) + C sin(ϕ + δk), where A, B and C are unknowns and ϕ is the reference-plane phase at the transformed coordinates. Minimising the squared error over the three images (N = 3) leads to a linear system D X = E for X = [A B C]T, and the phase change caused by the object is φ = tan−1(−C/B). The object is then reconstructed from the phase and the system parameters.
  5. Multiplex the images. Every three consecutive images give one object phase map, so the groups overlap and a new frame starts with each new image. Traditional PSP needs three projected patterns for each frame.

Results

Simulated object moving 10 pixels between fringe patterns: the proposed method reconstructs the block, while traditional PSP on the same images gives large errors (Figs. 5 and 6).
Two images per projected fringe, captured through a trigger control device on the camera and projector (Fig. 1).
One object phase map from every three consecutive images, by multiplexing the fringe images (Fig. 2).
Shooting frame rate twice the projector’s highest frame rate, because the camera shoots twice per fringe.

The method is verified by simulation. Fringe patterns are simulated for a static object and for an object that moves from left to right by 10 pixels between each two fringe patterns. For comparison, the static patterns are reconstructed with traditional PSP. In the moving case, images taken under the same projected fringe contain only the object’s motion, while images under different fringes contain both the fringe phase shift and the motion. The rotation matrix and translation vector of the motion are computed by tracking the object, the phase is computed with the proposed model, and with multiplexing every three images give an object phase map. These phase maps at different frames give a high-frame-rate 3D reconstruction of the moving block (Fig. 5). Traditional PSP applied to the same images shows large errors (Fig. 6).

In their conclusion, the authors note that the method only needs a newly derived formula and the projection of the first two fringe patterns of a three-step phase shift to reconstruct the moving object, and that it doubles the shooting frame rate at low cost without losing the advantages of PSP. The comparison with traditional PSP is shown visually in Figs. 5 and 6.

item.title: 3D reconstruction of the moving object with double-shooting based on phase shifting profilometry
item.description:
The problem

Phase-shifting profilometry (PSP) is one of the most commonly used 3D measurement techniques, valued for its high accuracy, robustness and full-field measurement. A projector casts at least three phase-shifted sinusoidal fringe patterns onto the object, and a camera views them from another angle. The object’s height distorts the fringes, the phase of the fringes describes that distortion, and the phase plus the system parameters give the 3D shape. Because several patterns are used, traditional PSP requires the object to stay still: if it moves while the patterns are projected and captured, measurement errors appear.

Frame rate is a second limit. A projector typically shows 8-bit fringe patterns at up to 120 Hz, while a camera easily exceeds 1000 Hz, so the frame rate of the reconstructed point clouds is limited by the projector. Defocusing a projector that shows binary patterns can exceed 1000 Hz, but the amount of defocus is hard to control and quantify, and high-speed cameras and projectors raise the cost considerably. The paper asks how to reconstruct moving objects at a high frame rate with low-cost equipment.

How it works

A trigger controller is added between the camera and the projector, so the camera captures each projected fringe pattern twice and collects more fringe information about the moving object. The paper then analyses how the object’s motion changes the phase across three consecutive images, builds a fringe model that includes the motion, extracts the phase under this mixed phase shift, and reuses the captured images to obtain more reconstructed frames.

  1. Double shooting. The projector shows its N phase-shifted patterns at its normal rate, and the camera is triggered twice within each projection period. Every projected pattern therefore yields two camera images of the moving object.
  2. Mixed phase shift. Two images taken under the same pattern differ only by the phase shift caused by the object’s motion. Images taken under different patterns contain this motion-induced shift as well as the ordinary PSP phase shift. For three images I1, I2, I3, the shifts are δ1 = δ2 = 0 and δ3 = 2π/N.
  3. Fringe model with motion. An object motion tracking algorithm computes the rotation–translation matrix that describes the object’s motion. It gives the coordinate transform (fn, gn) between images, and each image is written as In = a + B cos hn + C sin hn, with hn = ϕ(fn, gn) + δn, where ϕ is the phase of the reference plane and a is the ambient light intensity.
  4. Least-squares phase. For each pixel, a, B and C are found by minimising the squared difference between the model and the captured images. B and C carry the phase change φ caused by the object’s shape (B = cos φ and C = −sin φ), so it is read as φ = arctan(−C / B).
  5. Image reuse. The captured images are reused: every three adjacent images give one frame of object phase, whereas traditional PSP builds each frame from its own group of images. A new phase frame therefore appears with each new image, rather than after a full set of patterns. This raises the reconstruction frame rate of the moving object while the projector speed stays limited.

Results

Mean error on the moving object against the static reconstruction: 0.1575 mm with traditional PSP, 0.0344 mm with the proposed method (Table 1).

The experimental system consists of an industrial camera (OPT-CC1-048A-RM-G, 1800 × 1600 pixels), a projector (TJ-S50, 1280 × 720 pixels) and a motorised translation stage. The measured object is a mask. The camera runs at 20 frames/s, the stage moves at 20 mm/s, and the field of view is 70 mm × 80 mm. The mask is first reconstructed at rest with traditional PSP, and this result serves as ground truth for the error evaluation.
