On the moving stage, the two images taken under one projected pattern contain only the object’s motion, while images under different patterns contain both motion and fringe phase shift. The rotation–translation matrix comes from an object motion tracking algorithm, and every three adjacent images give one phase map. The proposed method reconstructs the moving mask, whereas traditional PSP applied to the moving object shows large errors.

The authors name the accuracy of the object tracking algorithm as the most important limitation: it directly sets the reconstruction accuracy, and existing tracking algorithms have difficulty describing large motions. The method can only reconstruct objects undergoing 2D translation; because of the limits of motion tracking, it cannot handle 2D rotation or 3D motion. It does not require the object to move at constant speed, but the camera must capture clear fringe images of the moving object.

item.title: Random screening-based feature aggregation for point cloud denoising
item.description:
The problem

Point clouds captured by sensing devices are contaminated by noise from the environment and the limited precision of the devices, which corrupts the geometry they describe. Traditional optimisation-based denoising needs careful parameter tuning and can struggle to remove noise and preserve features at the same time. Learning-based methods ease the tuning, but they are usually trained on data with uniform point distributions and densities, and they become less robust when the noise is severe or the point density varies.

A common way to fully exploit point position information is to fuse the features of larger patches into smaller sub-patches. That technique is typically used when the training data has a uniform point resolution, which can make the network less robust on points with varying sampling density. This paper instead screens points at random and fuses the denser patch’s global feature into the remaining points.

How it works

The network denoises each point from its local patch. An encoder extracts point features; two random screening-based feature aggregation modules then each drop half of the points at random and fuse the global feature of the denser patch (the patch before screening) into the half of the points that remain. Finally, point-wise weights decide how much each remaining point contributes to the displacement that moves the noisy point towards the clean surface.

  1. Build a local patch. For each noisy point, the neighbours within a ball of radius r (5 % of the bounding-box diagonal) form a patch. The patch is translated to the origin, scaled to a unit sphere, rotated into a canonical pose by PCA, and padded or downsampled to N = 500 points.
  2. Encode and screen. A graph-based encoder with Dense Blocks produces an N × C feature matrix. The network extracts a global feature from it and randomly keeps half of the point features.
  3. Fuse dense into sparse. The global feature is copied N/2 times and concatenated with the features of the screened sub-patch; an MLP turns them into an N/2 × 2C matrix. The sparser sub-patch now carries richer geometric information from the denser patch.
  4. Repeat once more. The same screening and fusion run again, leaving N/4 points with 4C channels each. In the paper’s ablation, this two-stage cascade is more effective than a single aggregation layer.
  5. Weight and move. The network regresses a weight for each of the N/4 points; a weighting loss trains points closer to the tangent plane of the patch centre to receive higher weights. The weighted features are max-pooled and decoded into a displacement vector, which is added to the noisy point. Training combines this weighting loss with a surface proximity loss.

Results

Lowest average errors on the PUNet test set: Chamfer distance (CD) 2.25 and point-to-mesh distance (P2M) 0.65 (×10⁴), against 2.40 and 0.75 for MoDNet, the next best (Table 1).
CD 2.299 and P2M 0.920 on 1,792 CAD shapes from the ABC dataset, against 2.511 and 1.104 for MoDNet and 2.719 and 1.302 for Score (Table 2).
In the ablation, the full pipeline reaches P2M 0.961, against 1.149 without feature aggregation and 1.407 without the weighting loss (Table 3).

The network is trained on PUNet’s 40 training shapes, with Gaussian noise of 0.5 % to 2 % of the bounding-sphere radius added on the fly. The PUNet test set has 20 shapes at 10,000 and 50,000 points, each with 1 %, 2 % and 3 % noise; the method has the lowest Chamfer distance (CD) and point-to-mesh distance (P2M) in most of these settings and on average. On real depth-camera scans from the Kinect Fusion dataset, whose noise differs from Gaussian noise, it has the lowest P2M on all three scans shown (Fig. 4), and it also leads on the irregularly sampled icosahedron above. The Paris-rue-Madame street scans, captured by a mobile laser scanner, have no ground truth, so that comparison is visual only (Fig. 6).

Two further checks support the design. Keeping half of the features at each screening step gives the lowest P2M, 0.961, against 1.270, 1.254 and 1.251 for ratios of 1/3, 2/3 and 3/4 (Table 4). Compared with the cascaded scale feature aggregation used in earlier work, the method performs similarly at lower noise levels but preserves geometry better under severe noise (Fig. 7). The denoised point clouds can also be turned into meshes with Poisson reconstruction, where the paper shows more accurate results on edges and complicated regions (Fig. 8).

item.title: Towards uniform point distribution in feature-preserving point cloud filtering
item.description:
The problem

Raw point clouds from scanners contain noise, so they are usually filtered before upsampling, surface reconstruction or other downstream use. A good filter should move the noisy points back onto the underlying surface, keep sharp edges and corners, and leave the points evenly spread. Existing methods tend to manage only part of this. Position-based methods such as CLOP smooth well but, since they ignore normals, tend to smear sharp features. Normal-based methods keep sharp edges better, but their filtered points are often unevenly distributed, and some that include a repulsion term still leave gaps near the edges. Deep learning methods need noisy training data with ground truth and work on local patches; they too give uneven distributions, even with a repulsion loss, and sparse or unevenly sampled inputs are hard for them.

The paper builds on the edge-aware point update of an earlier low-rank filtering method. On its own, that update moves points towards sharp edges, where they concentrate and leave gaps beside the edge. These gaps hurt downstream steps such as upsampling and surface reconstruction.

How it works

The method has two phases. It first smooths the point normals, then updates the point positions using those normals. The position update minimises the sum of two terms: an edge-aware data term that approximates the noisy surface while preserving geometric features, and a repulsion term that controls the point distribution.

  1. Noisy input. The input is a noisy point cloud with normals. If it has only positions, initial normals are estimated with principal component analysis (PCA).
  2. Normal filtering. The normals are smoothed with bilateral filtering. The quality of the filtered points depends heavily on the quality of these normals.
  3. Data term. For each point and each neighbour in its local patch, the update adjusts the angles between the vector joining the two points and their normals so that the vector becomes perpendicular to both normals. This brings points onto the underlying surface and preserves sharp features, but used alone it moves points towards the edges and leaves gaps.
  4. Repulsion term. A repulsion term based on point coordinates and normals pushes neighbouring points apart perpendicular to the neighbour’s normal, with a weight that decays smoothly with distance. A parameter µ sets its strength.
  5. Iterate. Both terms are combined in one gradient-descent update per point (Eq. 6 of the paper), computed on a patch of the k nearest neighbours and repeated for t iterations. Most experiments use k = 30, µ = 0.3 and t = 5 (Table 1).

Results

Average Chamfer distance 5.80 × 10−5 on five models with synthetic noise, the lowest (lower is better) of the seven methods compared; the next best, RIMLS, averages 7.12 × 10−5 (Table 2).
Average mean square error 15.69 × 10−3, again the lowest average (Table 3).
0.91–28.16 s per model, faster than CLOP, TotalDenoising, PointCleanNet and Pointfilter on all nine models timed (Table 5).

The method is compared with a position-based method (CLOP), two normal-based methods (GPF and RIMLS) and three deep learning methods (TotalDenoising, PointCleanNet and Pointfilter, abbreviated TD, PCN and PF). The quantitative tests use five models with synthetic Gaussian noise of 0.5 % or 1.0 % (Bunnyhi, Rockerarm, Icosahedron, Dodecahedron and Kitten). The method has the lowest Chamfer distance on four of the five models and the lowest mean square error on three. On raw scans (Nefertiti, BuddhaStele, Realscan and David) there is no ground truth, so these are compared visually; the paper reports that its method keeps details such as sharp edges, the steps of BuddhaStele and facial features better than the others. The authors attribute the low errors to the more uniform point distribution: RIMLS, for example, gives comparable visual results in some cases but larger errors in most, owing to its uneven distribution. Without the repulsion term, some points concentrate at the edges.

Further tests cover point density, noise levels from 0.5 % to 3.0 %, irregular sampling, holes and an indoor scene. The authors state two limitations: as a normal-based method it depends on the quality of the input normals, and it may give less desirable results at very high noise (1.5 % is already more challenging than 0.5 % and 1.0 %). Big holes that severely disrupt the surface are also hard to fill, and the best neighbourhood size k depends strongly on point density.

item.title: Automated reconstruction of multiple objects with individual movement based on PSP
item.description:
The problem

Phase shifting profilometry (PSP) projects several phase-shifted sinusoidal fringe patterns, normally at least three, onto an object and recovers its shape from the phase seen by a camera. Because it needs several images, the object has to stay still while they are captured. If it moves, the captured patterns no longer line up with each other and the designed phase shift between them is violated, so errors appear in the result.

The authors’ earlier work handled movement by describing it with a rotation matrix and a translation vector and building this information into the reconstruction model. It could also reconstruct several isolated objects, but only when they all had the same movement. In practice it is more common for objects to move differently, and existing methods introduce errors when multiple objects with individual movements are reconstructed.

How it works

The method gives every object its own movement description. It first finds the objects, then follows each one through the fringe sequence, computes its rotation and translation separately, and finally retrieves the phase of each object with that object’s movement.

  1. Separate fringes from the object image. The fringe patterns are projected in red and captured by a colour camera. The red component carries the fringes for phase retrieval; in the blue component the fringes are filtered out, leaving a pure object image for tracking and feature extraction.
  2. Identify the objects. In the blue image, OTSU automatic thresholding separates the objects from the background. Thresholding can split an object into several parts, so a dilation step merges them again, and the contour of each object gives its bounding box.
  3. Track each object with KCF. The object inside each bounding box is used as a template, and the Kernelized Correlation Filters (KCF) tracker finds its new bounding box in the next fringe image. The new box then serves as the template for the images that follow.
  4. Estimate each object’s movement. SIFT finds feature points and their correspondences between the object before and after movement. From these points, singular value decomposition (SVD) gives a rotation matrix and translation vector for each object.
  5. Reconstruct object by object. With its own movement information, the phase of each object is retrieved from the red component by a least-squares solution of the reconstruction model that includes the movement, and the object is reconstructed. This repeats until the last object is done.

Results

RMS error 0.0773 mm with the proposed method, against 8.981 mm with traditional PSP, for two car models moving individually, measured against the static-object 6-step PSP reference (Section 4, Fig. 10).

The experiment uses a colour camera (Allied Vision Manta 504C, 2452 × 2056) and a projector (Wintech DLP PRO 4500, 912 × 1140). Two car models are measured with 3-step PSP using red fringes while each one rotates and translates on the reference plane in its own way. The reference is a 6-step PSP reconstruction of the static objects. Traditional PSP shows clear movement-induced errors, which are most serious where the height changes sharply, such as at the edges of the objects; with the proposed method these errors are removed. The method can also reconstruct only selected objects and ignore the others, by choosing the objects of interest after identification.

The authors state the conditions of the method. It considers only rigid objects with two-dimensional movement. Object identification works best with a large enough intensity difference between objects and background, and because dilation enlarges the objects, they must keep some distance from each other. The fringe colour should differ strongly from the object colour, and when ambient light is weak, blue background light should be added to the projected pattern. There is no limit on movement speed, but the capture must be fast enough to give clear images.

item.title: Gaussian Curvature Filter on 3D Meshes
item.description:
The problem

Triangle meshes from 3D scanners and other acquisition pipelines are often noisy, and a noisy mesh has higher Gaussian curvature than its noise-free counterpart. Reducing Gaussian curvature therefore smooths and denoises a mesh, and driving it to zero everywhere gives a developable surface, one that can be flattened onto a plane without distortion and is easy to manufacture.

The classical way to minimize Gaussian curvature is Gaussian curvature flow, and it has two problems. It computes Gaussian curvature explicitly, which implicitly assumes the surface is second-order differentiable, a condition real meshes rarely satisfy. It also needs a small time step to stay numerically stable, so it is slow, and in the paper’s tests the step size had to be tuned per mesh. Dedicated denoising methods, mostly built on vertex or face normals, bring their own difficulty: many manually set parameters and strong prior assumptions, and on models rich in texture they can damage the original features while removing noise.

How it works

The filter rests on one observation. On a developable surface, every point has another point arbitrarily close to it that lies on its tangent plane (Theorem 1 of the paper). So the Gaussian curvature at a vertex can be reduced by moving the vertex until one of its neighbours falls on its tangent plane. If a neighbour already lies there, the vertex does not move. The filter never computes Gaussian curvature itself and needs no second derivatives.

  1. A neighbour on the tangent plane. On a developable surface such as a cylinder, a cone or a tangent surface, a point x always has a nearby point x0 on its tangent plane. On a discrete mesh that point need not be a vertex, so the filter takes the 1-ring neighbours (the vertices directly connected to it) as candidates and uses one of them as an approximation.
  2. Domain decomposition. A colouring step (Algorithm 1) gives every vertex a label that none of its neighbours has. Each colour set is updated in turn, so a vertex moves while its 1-ring neighbours stay fixed. This is what keeps the iteration convergent, and the independent sets also make the algorithm easy to parallelise.
  3. Moving distance without constraint. For vertex vi, compute the distance from each 1-ring neighbour to the tangent plane of vi and take the smallest absolute value as the moving distance |d|.
  4. Moving distance with constraint. For feature preservation, the normal of each neighbour is also used (the unit cross product of its two adjacent edges). Every edge from vi to a neighbour is projected onto the normal of vi and onto every neighbour normal, 5 edges × 6 normals (the normal of vi and the five neighbour normals) = 30 distances for a five-neighbour ring, and the smallest absolute value is taken. At a vertex on a plane, an edge or a corner, some normal is perpendicular to an edge, so |d| = 0 and the vertex keeps its position.
  5. Vertex update. The vertex moves to v′ = v + |d|·δ, where δ is the unit vector opposite to the differential coordinate (the vertex minus the centroid of its neighbours), which approximates the reverse normal direction. Boundary vertices are not moved. Repeating this over all colour sets for a set number of iterations, the filter’s only parameter, lowers the Gaussian curvature of the whole mesh.

Results

Lowest mean square angular error (MSAE) on all four test meshes in the denoising comparison with seven methods, e.g. 9.72 on Armadillo (noise σn = 0.3 times the average edge length le) against 12.15 for the best compared method (Table 3).
Gaussian curvature distribution closest to the ground truth: KL divergence from the ground-truth distribution (lower is better) 0.08, 0.05 and 0.02 on Armadillo, Bunny and Vaselion, the lowest of all methods, and 0.07 on Max Planck, tied with one other method (Table 3).
56.39 s against 1016.41 s for standard Gaussian curvature flow on Max Planck, 100 iterations each, about 18 times faster (Table 1).

The paper tests two properties. For Gaussian curvature minimization, it compares the filter with Gaussian curvature flow on the Max Planck head and the Vase, without noise and with noise of 0.3 times the average edge length le. Both projection strategies lower the Gaussian curvature energy faster than the flow. Without the constraint the filter converges after about 10 iterations, but details are lost and the angular error rises again after its first rapid drop; with the constraint it converges after about 40 iterations and keeps details while removing noise. Against the developability method of Stein et al. (SIGGRAPH 2018), both reach similar results on noise-free meshes, with lower energy for the filter. On the noisy bunny the filter reaches a Gaussian curvature energy of 83.48 against 323.21 and an MSAE of 11.86 against 12.59, in 37.90 s against 1571.10 s (Table 2). On the noisy mask, the method of Stein et al. produces a singularity, while the filter does not (Fig. 7).

For denoising, the filter runs 40 iterations and the seven compared optimization- and filter-based methods use their default parameters. Besides the lowest MSAE, it reaches the lowest Gaussian curvature energy of all methods on each of the four meshes; the paper reads the low MSAE as the best preservation of geometric features. On two real scans with unknown noise, an angel and a rabbit, it removes noise while keeping geometric features (Figs. 13 and 14). Without the geometric constraint, the filter can denoise but cannot preserve features. As future work, the authors plan a parallel version of the filter for very large meshes on the GPU.

item.title: HLO: Half-kernel Laplacian Operator for surface smoothing
item.description:
The problem

Meshes captured by scanners or other sensors always carry noise, and they have to be smoothed before shape analysis, animation or rendering. The challenge is to remove the noise while preserving features and resisting shrinkage. The uniform Laplacian, which compares each vertex with the centroid of its neighbours, smooths effectively, but being isotropic it wipes out features and shrinks the surface. The paper also analyses feature points: on a sharp edge the surface is not differentiable, so the second-order derivative that the Laplacian approximates does not exist, and applying the uniform Laplacian to such a vertex with all its neighbours does not make sense. Most feature-preserving methods instead rely on face or vertex normals, and many of them consist of multiple steps and numerous parameters that are difficult to tune, especially on complex models.

How it works

HLO keeps the simplicity of the uniform Laplacian but applies it to half windows, subsets of a vertex’s neighbours, instead of the whole neighbourhood. For every vertex it generates all of these half windows, computes a Laplacian on each, and keeps the one with the least energy. The surface is then updated iteratively with these half-kernel Laplacians.

  1. The full window fails at features. The uniform Laplacian compares a vertex v₀ with the centroid v′₀ of all its neighbours. At a vertex on a sharp edge the surface is not differentiable, so this operator is not applicable there; in practice, smoothing with it wipes out features and shrinks the mesh (Fig. 2).
  2. Split the neighbourhood into half windows. Each neighbour in turn, say A, is paired with the neighbour D that is closest to the plane through v₀, A and v′₀. The line A–D divides the neighbours into a left and a right half window.
  3. Half-window Laplacians. The uniform Laplacian is computed on each half window separately, giving vectors such as d₁ and d₂.
  4. Project onto the full-window direction. A half-window Laplacian also shifts the vertex sideways, which can flip or degenerate triangles. It is therefore projected onto the direction n of the full-window Laplacian, δ = (d·n)n. According to the paper, this ensures small Laplacian magnitudes at feature vertices and large ones elsewhere, so non-features are smoothed and features preserved.
  5. Pick the least energy and iterate. A vertex with |NV| neighbours has 2|NV| candidate half windows. HLO keeps the one with the smallest energy, the length of its Laplacian plus the vertex’s distance from its original position, and uses it to update the vertex. The only parameter is the number of iterations.

Results

One parameter, the number of iterations, against three to six for the compared normal-filtering and L0 methods (Table 1).
Fastest in every runtime test, for example 1.81 s on Armadillo (43,243 vertices) against 5.68 s for the next-fastest method, UNF, with 10 vertex iterations each (Table 3).
Lowest normal error (MSAE, lower is better) in 4 of the 9 test cases, for example 9.33 × 10⁻² on Armadillo with noise σn = 0.5 lₑ against 9.59 × 10⁻² for L0 minimisation (Table 2).

HLO is compared with the uniform and cotangent Laplacians and with seven denoising methods: the bilateral mesh filter, the unilateral, bilateral and guided normal filters (UNF, BNF, GNF), L0 minimisation, cascaded normal regression (CNR) and non-local low-rank normal filtering (NLLR). Synthetic tests add zero-mean Gaussian noise whose standard deviation σn is proportional to the mean edge length lₑ; real tests use models scanned with Microsoft Kinect and the scanned Angel and Rabbit. Against the uniform Laplacian, HLO significantly alleviates shrinkage and gives much lower average vertex errors on the Julius model; the cotangent Laplacian is more geometry-aware but tends to create sharp “thorns”. Because HLO builds on the uniform Laplacian, which unfolds flipped triangles (shown in red in the figure below) during smoothing, HLO is less sensitive to high noise than most of the compared methods. For the normal error MSAE, L0 minimisation and HLO are usually the best two. The vertex error Ev (a positional error against the ground-truth mesh) does not always agree with the visual comparison, because unfolding flipped triangles can move vertices far from their ground-truth positions. HLO was the fastest method in the runtime comparison, although its code had not been optimised or parallelised.

The authors note limitations. HLO has difficulty recovering smooth sharp edges on CAD-like models with few vertices, because it is not an edge-based operator; on real scanned CAD-like models with many vertices its results are comparable to the other methods. Like previous works it keeps the open boundaries of the input fixed, which can sometimes give undesired results.

item.title: Iteratively weighted principal component analysis and orientation consistency for normal estimation in point cloud
item.description:
The problem

A point cloud is only a set of 3D coordinates. Many later steps, such as denoising, segmentation, surface reconstruction and visualisation, also need a surface normal at every point, so normal estimation is a basic operation in point cloud processing. The classical method, by Hoppe et al., fits a plane to each point’s nearest neighbours with principal component analysis (PCA) and takes the plane’s normal. It assumes the neighbourhood is close to a plane, and it does not perform well where points are sparse or where the surface has sharp edges: for example, normals can turn gradually around a right angle instead of following the true edge (Fig. 2).

Where point density varies and sharp features occur, the normal directions of adjacent points can also be inconsistent, some pointing inside and some outside. Reconstruction methods such as ball-pivoting and Poisson need consistently oriented normals. Wrong normals at sharp features blur those features after reconstruction, and inconsistent orientations can break the reconstructed surface.

How it works

The method keeps PCA plane fitting as its core and adds two things around it. To make the normals more robust and reliable, it weights every neighbour by distance and by normal similarity and repeats the weighted fit a few times; the authors call this Iteratively Weighted PCA (IWPCA). To make the orientation consistent, it first flips normals using the centre of the cloud and then propagates orientation along a minimal spanning tree (MST).

  1. Local plane fit. A Kd-tree finds the k nearest neighbours of each point, and a least-squares plane is fitted to them. The normal is the eigenvector belonging to the smallest eigenvalue of the neighbourhood covariance matrix.
  2. Bilateral weights. IWPCA centres the covariance matrix on the point itself and weights each neighbour twice. The spatial weight decreases with the neighbour’s distance from the point, controlled by σd, usually half the kNN search radius. The normal weight decreases as the neighbour’s normal departs from the point’s normal, controlled by σn, usually 15° to 30°. In the first pass every point’s normal is set to (1, 0, 0), so the normal weight starts out uniform.
  3. Iterate. Each new pass uses the normals of the previous pass in the normal weight. More iterations give a better estimate but cost more time; the authors recommend 2 or 3, and the last pass is the result.
  4. Pre-flip towards the outside. The centre of the whole cloud is computed, and every normal that points towards it is flipped.
  5. Propagate along a minimal spanning tree. Prim’s algorithm builds an MST over neighbouring points, with edge weight 1 − |ni · nj|. Starting from the root, each child’s normal is flipped when its dot product with its parent’s normal is negative.

For sharp parts, the normals can additionally be smoothed with the same spatial and normal weights (bilateral weighted smoothing). In the authors’ tests this made the normals on sharp parts more robust but lowered their reliability, so they recommend it only when needed, since IWPCA already improves robustness at edges by itself.

Results

Four test models from the Stanford Computer Graphics Lab: Stanford bunny (34,835 points), cube (39,846), sharp cone (50,000) and a scanned surface (30,443), all with σn = 30° and σd = 0.5 (Table 1).
Stanford bunny runtime: 564 ms for PCA, 697 ms for one IWPCA iteration, 896 ms for three (Table 1).
2 or 3 iterations recommended (Section 4.1).
Sharper cube edges and corners in Poisson reconstruction from IWPCA normals than from classical PCA normals (Fig. 8).

The comparisons in the paper are visual. On the cube, IWPCA improves the robustness of the normals at the sharp edges, and after the MST re-orientation the reliability, robustness and orientation consistency of all normals improve and the shape of the cube is clearer (Fig. 7). When the cube is reconstructed with the Poisson method, the edges and corners obtained from IWPCA normals are sharper and clearer than those from classical PCA normals (Fig. 8). On the sharp cone, classical PCA gives unsatisfactory normals at the tip, leaves some normals uncomputed and points many bottom normals inward; IWPCA improves robustness at both the top and the bottom (Fig. 9). On the scanned surface, the pre-flip and MST propagation (steps 4–5) turn inconsistent normals so that the vast majority point to the raised side (Fig. 11).

IWPCA costs more computation than classical PCA, and its runtimes include the normal re-orientation. With one iteration it is slower than PCA; with three iterations it is somewhat faster than running classical PCA three times. The experiments ran on Windows 7 (64-bit) with an Intel Core i7-5650U CPU at 2.20 GHz and 8 GB RAM. The neighbourhood size k and the weight parameters σd and σn are hard to determine and were chosen from experience; the authors suggest deriving them from local curvature, noise distribution and point density in future work.

item.title: Parallel Curvature Filter for High Performance Image Processing
item.description:
The problem

The curvature filter smooths and denoises an image by implicitly reducing a curvature energy, such as Gaussian curvature, mean curvature or total variation. It treats the image as a surface and repeatedly applies a cheap local operator to every pixel, each pass lowering the regularisation energy. The filter is fast, but many images that need enhancing are high-resolution or must be processed in real or near-real time, and on a CPU a large image such as 2048 × 2048 still takes minutes.

The most expensive part of the filter is a set of eight convolutions over the image. Inspired by the way GPUs run the convolutions of convolutional neural networks, the authors parallelise these convolutions on the GPU.

How it works

Each iteration of the curvature filter enumerates eight candidate moves for every pixel, picks the smallest one and applies it. PCF computes the eight candidates for all pixels at once with convolution kernels on the GPU.

  1. The image as a surface. The image intensity U is interpreted as a surface over the pixel grid. The curvature regularisers all work on the local 3 × 3 neighbourhood around each pixel.
  2. Eight tangent-plane projections. A surface can be locally approximated by its tangent plane. In the 3 × 3 neighbourhood, eight tangent planes through neighbouring pixels are enumerated, giving eight projection distances d1 … d8 for the centre pixel.
  3. Eight convolutions on the GPU. Each distance is computed for every pixel at once as a convolution of the image. These eight convolutions are the most computationally expensive part of the algorithm; PCF runs them in CUDA and uses the GPU’s shared memory to accelerate them.
  4. Pick the smallest distance and update. For every pixel, the distance dm with the smallest magnitude is selected (ABSMIN) and added to the pixel: Ut+1 = Ut + dm. The smallest distance indicates the closest fit to the desired geometry and to the original image.
  5. Iterate. Repeating the update regularises the image surface step by step, which the paper shows by plotting the intensity along one line of the image after 10 and 30 iterations.

Results

33.2 gigapixels per second on a single GPU.
About 87 s on the CPU versus about 6 s on the GPU for 3,000 iterations on the same image (Fig. 3).

The CUDA implementation was run with GPU block sizes from 16 to 32 on an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1080 Ti (3,584 CUDA cores, 11,264 MB of global memory, 49,152 bytes of shared memory per block) and compared with the original curvature filter on an Intel Xeon E5-1620 v4 CPU at 3.50 GHz. In Fig. 3 the computation time grows with the number of iterations on both, but far more slowly on the GPU. The authors conclude that this speed makes the filter suitable for real-time applications such as video processing and biomedical image processing.

The paper also applies Gaussian-curvature and mean-curvature versions of PCF to a photograph and plots the intensity along one line after 10 and 30 iterations. In both, the profile becomes smoother as iterations accumulate; judging from these profiles, the authors find the mean-curvature PCF more efficient at smoothing than the Gaussian-curvature PCF (a comparison of smoothing, not of running time).

item.title: Sequencing in Transformation of Rasterized 3D Models
item.description:
The problem

A rasterized 3D structure is built from discrete, equal-sized parts, the way a picture is built from pixels: voxels in a computer, and cubes, bricks or food cans in the physical world. Such parts are easy to process as data, easy to reuse and suited to mass production. The thesis asks how to change one such structure into another. It frames this as a transformation from a source structure to a destination structure, and looks for an efficient sequence of operations that a machine can follow, with efficiency measured by an application-dependent cost function. Building a structure from a material palette is a special case, in which the source is the palette.

The difficulty is that the problem is discrete. Even deciding which part goes where is a combinatorial problem: for n parts there are n! possible assignments. The lowest-cost assignment is not necessarily executable either. A suction gripper can only pick parts on the top surface, a LEGO brick cannot be picked while other bricks cover or surround it, and a brick cannot be placed where it would hang in the air. Sequencing therefore has to trade the total amount of work against physical feasibility, and for bricks also against how many of the source parts are reused.

How it works

The thesis studies three cases that, in its words, represent the majority of sequencing problems for transforming and shaping rasterized structures: pick-and-place of homogeneous voxels (Chapter 3), pick-and-place of heterogeneous LEGO bricks (Chapter 4), and folding of voxel chains (Chapter 5). The explainer follows the thesis’s worked voxel example step by step, then places the other two cases alongside it.

  1. Align and classify. Both mesh models are rasterized into voxels. Assuming they are already aligned vertically and only translation is allowed, an exhaustive search in the horizontal plane finds the alignment with the largest overlap. Voxels present only in the source are movers (M), voxels present only in the destination are voids (V), and overlapped voxels stay where they are. If the numbers of M and V differ, the extra voxels go to, or come from, a linear stack.

  2. Price every move. The cost function models a three-axis Cartesian machine that moves sideways only at a clearance plane zmax: the cost cij of moving mover i into void j is cij = |xj − xi| + |yj − yi| + 2zmax − zi − zj. Pairing every M with a V at minimum total cost is an assignment problem, which the Hungarian method solves in O(n3) time instead of comparing n! options.

  3. Respect top access. With a vacuum suction gripper, only voxels on the top surface can be picked or placed. Pairing all M and V at once (the global optimisation strategy, GOS) gives a lower bound on the cost, but the pairs may deadlock. The local optimisation strategy (LOS) builds the cost matrix only from the M and V that are currently accessible, applies the Hungarian method, and moves those pairs.

  4. Update and repeat. After each round the top surfaces change, a new cost matrix is built, and the process repeats until every M has been placed. In the worked example LOS reaches a total cost of 27, the same as the GOS lower bound. Two simpler baselines are also compared: a greedy strategy (GSS) that moves only the single cheapest accessible pair at each step, and a random one (RSS).

  5. Extend to bricks and chains. Bricks (LEGO). Voxels are merged into bricks layer by layer. The rigid approach (RT) generates both brick layouts before transformation, and the flexible approach (FT) generates the target layout on the fly, preferring brick types that are movable on the source. Each approach is combined with three strategies for routing bricks through a buffer and a stock (see the figure below), giving six algorithms, RT1–RT3 and FT1–FT3, named after the approach and the strategy number.

    The algorithms are scored by cost (the number of pick-and-place actions), reuse rate (the share of source bricks that end up in the target) and an overall performance that grows with reuse and falls with cost.

    Chains. A shape is turned into a 1D string by finding a Hamiltonian path through its voxels. The path is made possible either by pruning and appending voxels or by dividing each voxel into 4 (2D) or 8 (3D) sub-voxels. The fold is then planned from the difference between the start and target joint angles.

Results

LOS near the GOS lower bound, in seconds instead of over an hour: for wall → pyramid (1,643 M-V pairs), LOS costs 60,199 against the GOS lower bound of 60,021, and computes in 9.5 s against 4,440 s (Table 3.1).
LEGO reuse against cost: in the Growlithe → Charmander transformation with colour information, FT3 reuses 56.1% of the source bricks with 3,203 pick-and-place actions, while FT1 reuses 69.3% with 6,015 (Test 3, Fig. 4.13).
FT3 has the best overall performance averaged over 56 transformations at each of seven model sizes; RT2 is the best of the rigid algorithms (Fig. 4.9).

The voxel strategies were tested on eight models (wall, pyramid, starfish, cube, igloo, castle, stairs and the Eiger mountain), each rasterized to between 2,250 and 2,550 voxels and transformed into every other. GOS always gives the lowest cost but does not by itself define a feasible sequence, and it is the slowest, because it runs the Hungarian method once on a very large cost matrix. LOS is second in cost, GSS slightly worse, and RSS clearly worse but fastest. The work is set by the number of M-V pairs, not by model size: wall → pyramid needs 1,643 pairs, while the more similar pyramid → igloo needs only 325. Across rasterization resolutions, the total cost grows about linearly with the number of pairs, and so does the time of LOS, even though the Hungarian method itself is O(n3). LOS stands out for the balance it strikes between cost and computation time. Its stated limitation is the top-access constraint, which rules out overhanging structures. Bricks that lock together, like LEGO, can form overhangs, which motivates the LEGO chapter.

For LEGO, eight triangle-mesh models were converted to brick models. In the average over all pairwise transformations, cost rises linearly with model size, and Strategies 1, 2 and 3 cost successively less. Strategies 1 and 2 reach very similar reuse rates, so the thesis concludes that disassembling the whole source up front is not worthwhile. FT reuses more bricks than RT, but its bricks tend to be smaller than the best fit, which gives weaker structures with internal sliding planes and more bricks in the target. FT3 reaches a reuse rate comparable to the best RT algorithms, and in the transformations from one model to the other seven it matches the reuse of FT1 and FT2 at a much lower cost. With colour information (114 colours, and exterior bricks must match in colour as well as shape), reuse falls but does not drop to zero, because interior bricks may take any colour. The thesis notes that the overall-performance metric is empirical, and that the relative ranking may change in scenarios that define cost differently.

Two directions are left as future work: adding force analysis such as finite element analysis, so that intermediate structures as well as the final one are stable, and transforming at the level of modules (groups of parts moved as a whole) rather than single parts, which the thesis expects to improve both reuse rate and cost.

item.title: Transformation of LEGO Models
item.description:
The problem

Container stacking raises a practical question: how can containers be moved efficiently from one stack to another? This paper studies a remotely related question with LEGO: build a new LEGO model using bricks taken from an existing one. Many algorithms turn a 3D shape into a LEGO model, but constructing a LEGO model from the bricks of another model had not been explored in open literature. The task has two goals that pull against each other. Every pick-and-place (PnP) of a brick costs one move, and as many bricks of the source model as possible should end up in the target.

Physical constraints make the order of moves matter. A brick fully or partly under other bricks cannot be picked, and a brick cannot be placed where it would hang in the air. The authors also treat a top-surface brick that is completely surrounded by other bricks as not movable, because freeing it would take extra moves.

How it works

The source model is taken apart from the top down and the target is built from the bottom up, layer by layer. Two basic approaches, rigid transformation (RT) and flexible transformation (FT), decide how the target’s bricks are chosen, and three strategies decide where each brick comes from: straight from the source, from a buffer of bricks already removed, or from a stock with an unlimited supply. Combining them gives six algorithms, RT1–RT3 and FT1–FT3, which use seven brick shapes.

  1. Moves and constraints. Each PnP of one brick (source to buffer, source to target, buffer to target or stock to target) counts as a cost of 1. Only movable bricks, those with nothing on top and not fully surrounded, can be picked.
  2. Rigid or flexible target. In rigid transformation (RT), the target LEGO model is generated before the transformation, with large bricks used first on each layer. In flexible transformation (FT), the target is built from an interim voxelized model on the fly: a scoring rule weights each brick type by how many movable bricks of that type the source currently offers, so source bricks are used first.
  3. Strategy 1. The source is disassembled completely into the buffer, and the target is built from the buffer, with the stock filling in bricks the buffer lacks.
  4. Strategy 2. Movable source bricks go straight to the target. If none matches, the buffer is searched; if it has none either, one more layer of the source is disassembled into the buffer to uncover new bricks. The stock is used only when the source is gone.
  5. Strategy 3. No buffer. A matching movable source brick goes straight to the target; otherwise the stock supplies one.

The algorithms are compared with three metrics: the cost C, the number of PnP needed to build the target; the reuse rate R = Nr/Ns, the share of the source’s Ns bricks that end up in the target; and an overall performance P = V·R/C, where V is the number of voxels in the target model.

Results

FT3 gives the best overall performance of the six algorithms, averaged over all 56 ordered pairs of the eight models, at each of seven model sizes; among the RT algorithms, RT2 is best (Fig. 7c).
Strategies 1 and 2 reach very similar reuse rates, so disassembling the whole source upfront is not worthwhile (Fig. 7b).
Ball to house with colour matching: FT3 reuses 73.0 % of the bricks at 2673 PnP, against 74.8 % at 4502 PnP for FT1 (Fig. 8).

The algorithms were tested on eight triangle mesh models converted to LEGO. In the first test, model A was transformed into each of the other seven models at about 2500 voxels per model. In the second, all eight models were transformed into each other at seven model sizes. Cost grows linearly with model size, and cost drops from Strategy 1 to 2 to 3 at every model size. An FT algorithm costs more than its RT counterpart because FT builds a target with more bricks. FT3 reaches a reuse rate comparable to the best RT algorithms. RT3’s reuse rate is much lower than RT1’s and RT2’s: when the target bricks are fixed in advance and there is no buffer, matching source bricks are hard to find, and on average more than half of the target bricks come from the stock. Reuse rate is not very sensitive to model size above 1700 voxels per model; smaller models reduce it.

The third test added colour: exterior bricks must match the surface colour, while interior bricks may take any colour. For the ball-to-house transformation, RT1 and RT2 reuse 61.9 % and 59.9 % of the bricks, and RT3 only 9.2 % (Fig. 9). The authors note the trade-offs: FT’s higher reuse comes with more and smaller bricks, giving weaker structures with internal sliding planes; the overall performance metric is empirical, and other scenarios may weigh cost differently. The study moves one brick at a time; reusing groups of bricks as modules is left to future work, and the results may not be directly applicable to a specific industrial application such as cargo container stacking.

item.title: Pick-and-place process sequencing for transformation of rasterized 3D structures
item.description:
The problem

Buildings can be put together from bricks or prefabricated components; in the same way, a structure can be assembled from equal-sized parts, or voxels, by pick-and-place (PnP): a machine picks up one part and places it somewhere else. The paper frames the task as transforming one rasterized structure (the source) into another (the destination). Building from a material palette is the special case in which the source is the palette. The question is which sequence of moves the machine should follow so that the total work is as small as possible.

Two things make this hard. Deciding which part goes where is an assignment problem: a brute-force search compares n! sequences, and the structures in the experiments have about 2,250 to 2,550 voxels each. The cheapest mapping is also not necessarily executable. The machine studied here is a Cartesian robot with at least three axes and a vacuum suction gripper that holds parts by their top surface, so it can only pick or place a voxel on the top surface of a structure.

How it works

The input is a closed triangle mesh for each shape. Each mesh is rasterized into voxels, with a flood fill to mark the interior. The two voxel models are then aligned, and the remaining work is motion sequencing: deciding which voxel moves where, and in which order.

  1. Align and classify. The structures are assumed to be aligned vertically already, and only horizontal translation is searched, exhaustively, to maximise their overlap. Voxels present only in the source are Movers (M), voxels present only in the destination are Voids (V), and overlapped voxels stay in place. If there are more M than V or the other way round, the extra voxels go to or come from a palette, a linear stack.
  2. Cost of one move. Moving Mi to Vj costs cij = |xj − xi| + |yj − yi| + 2zmax − zi − zj, measured in voxel sizes (Eq. 1). The part is lifted to the clearance plane zmax, moved in x and y only at that height to avoid collisions, and lowered onto Vj.
  3. Hungarian method on the full cost matrix. The costs of every M–V pair form an n × n matrix. The Hungarian method, with time complexity O(n³), returns the n pairs with the minimum total cost. This Global Optimization Strategy (GOS) gives a lower bound on the total cost, not a valid motion sequence.
  4. Top-access constraint. Lowest-cost pairs do not necessarily lead to a feasible sequence. In the paper’s eight-voxel example, one minimum-cost pairing (total cost 27) can be executed in a suitable order, but an equally cheap alternative deadlocks after two moves.
  5. Local Optimization Strategy (LOS). LOS builds the cost matrix only from the M and V on the top surfaces and applies the Hungarian method to it; when there are more M than V, it leaves some M out of that stage. The M left out are those that make the total cost of the chosen pairs minimum. The resulting pairs can be moved in any order. The top surfaces are then updated and the process repeats until all M have been moved. In the example, LOS needs two stages and its total cost, 27, happens to equal the lower bound.

The paper compares LOS with two further strategies that also produce valid sequences. The Greedy Selection Strategy (GSS) uses the same top-surface cost matrix but, without the Hungarian method, moves only the single lowest-cost pair at each step. The Random Selection Strategy (RSS) moves a random top-surface pair at each step.

Results

Wall → castle, 2,153 M–V pairs: LOS reaches the GOS lower bound of 91,192 in 14.9 s, while GOS itself takes 10,718 s (Table 1).
Starfish → castle, 2,016 pairs: total cost 75,891 for GOS (lower bound), 76,065 for LOS, 77,929 for GSS and 88,209 for RSS (Table 1).
LOS takes 1.8–30.4 s for every transformation in Table 1; GOS takes 6.1–10,718 s (Table 1).

The strategies were tested on eight models (wall, pyramid, starfish, cube, igloo, castle, stairs and the Eiger mountain), rasterized to similar sizes of 2,250 to 2,550 voxels, by transforming every model into every other. Times are for a C++ program on an Intel Core i3-2310M 2.10 GHz PC with 8 GB of RAM. The amount of work depends on the number of M–V pairs, not on the number of voxels: pyramid → wall needs 1,643 pairs, but pyramid → igloo only 325, because the two shapes are more similar and align better. In cost, GOS is best because it gives the lower bound, but its pairs do not define a motion sequence and are sometimes not feasible at all. LOS is second, and its stages define the sequence directly; GSS is slightly worse than LOS but clearly better than RSS. In time, RSS is fastest, GSS and LOS are similar, and GOS, which runs the Hungarian method once on one huge matrix, is the slowest. The authors conclude that LOS gives an appealing balance between cost and processing time, and that it outperforms the other strategies that generate feasible sequences.

Repeating starfish → castle at six resolutions, from 139 to 2,016 M–V pairs, the total cost grows about linearly with the number of pairs, and so does the time of every strategy except GOS. Although LOS uses the O(n³) Hungarian method, its time does not grow cubically with resolution. All results come from computer simulation. The top-surface constraint also rules out overhanging structures, such as a room with a ceiling or a wall with windows; the authors suggest that the LOS approach, which first selects the voxels that satisfy the constraints and then optimizes the M–V pairs, can carry over to other parts and constraints.

item.title: Plasmon-induced transparency in coupled triangle-rod arrays
item.description:
The problem

Electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) is a quantum interference effect that removes light absorption in an atomic medium. It opens a spectrally narrow transmission window with extreme dispersion, which is attractive for sensing and slow light. Plasmonic nanostructures can mimic it with classical field interference, an effect called plasmon-induced transparency (PIT). PIT involves strong coupling between two distinct plasmon modes in one unit cell: a highly radiative “bright” mode with a broad resonance, and a subradiant “dark” mode with a narrow one. Their destructive interference gives a narrow transparency window.

The unit cell is the building block of plasmonic molecules and metamaterials, and small structural variations from fabrication errors can significantly degrade its optical function. This paper studies a coupled triangle-rod unit cell: it identifies the bright and dark resonators, and measures how the PIT window changes when the geometry is varied in small, controlled steps.

How it works

Each unit cell is a gold nanotriangle whose apex points at a gold nanorod. Light arrives at normal incidence, polarized either along the rod (H) or across it (V). Finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulations of the field and charge distributions identify which part of the cell is the bright resonator and which is the dark one, and fabricated arrays are measured with a microspectrophotometer.

  1. The unit cell. An equilateral nanotriangle (side 400 nm) sits below a nanorod (550 nm long, 80 nm wide). Both are 50 nm of gold on quartz, arranged with a 2 µm period. The gap g between the apex and the rod and the sideways offset Δd are the parameters that are varied.
  2. The bright mode. Under V polarization the nanotriangle resonates as a dipole. Light polarized across the rod cannot directly excite the rod’s longitudinal plasmons.
  3. The dark mode. The localized surface plasmon at the triangle tip excites the rod through its near field. The rod responds with a multipolar mode (labelled j = 2) with three charge parts, and serves as the dark resonator.
  4. The transparency window. Destructive interference between the bright and dark modes raises a transmission peak (III) out of the broad valley. On either side, dip I is the in-phase (bonding) and dip II the out-of-phase (antibonding) coupling of the triangle’s dipole with the rod’s multipole. Under H polarization there is only one broad dipolar dip.
  5. Tuning by geometry. The gap g and the offset Δd set how strongly the two modes couple, so changing them reshapes or removes the window.

Results

A polarization-dependent PIT window: under V polarization a transmission peak rises from the broad valley, while H polarization shows only one broad dipolar dip, in both FDTD simulation and measurement (g = 20 nm, Δd = 0 nm; Fig. 2).
25 fabricated geometries: gap g from 20 to 60 nm in 10 nm steps, offset Δd from 0 to 120 nm in 30 nm steps (Fig. 4).
At Δd = 120 nm the window disappears for every gap tested; the offset has a much stronger effect on the PIT window than the gap (Fig. 5).

The simulated and measured spectra of a sample with g = 20 nm and Δd = 0 nm agree well overall. The measured PIT peak is slightly red-shifted, which the authors attribute mainly to shape tolerance and to refractive-index differences between simulation and experiment.

All arrays were measured under V polarization. Individual spectra vary slightly from array to array, possibly because of defects or inconsistency in the characterization system, but a general trend holds. At a fixed gap of 20 nm, the window gradually disappears as the offset grows. At a fixed offset, the transmission of the window gradually increases as the gap grows. Overall, at large gap or large offset the PIT effect becomes very weak, and at the largest offset of 120 nm it disappears whatever the gap: the coupling between triangle and rod is then too weak to excite the rod’s dark mode. Because small, controlled changes of g and Δd can mimic fabrication errors, the authors note that such variations should be considered when designing and evaluating PIT-based devices.
